The tale ends with Thaurbad's death and a debate among listeners over whether the entity acted as an agent of mischief in service to Clavicus Vile or of insanity under Sheogorath, an uncertainty the Sage deliberately leaves unresolved. The narrative serves as a cautionary legend about the perils of daedric bargains and enchanted tools.
topic_desc_basic: The third volume of Waughin Jarth's series, recounting the Great Sage's tale of the scribe Thaurbad Hulzik. After Thaurbad tries to discard his enchanted quill, the bound daedra Feyfolken reasserts control, warping his writing and perceptions until his demise. The narrative deliberately leaves ambiguous whether the entity serves Clavicus Vile or Sheogorath, offering a cautionary legend about daedric bargains.

title: How Orsinium Passed to the Orcs
topic_desc: Menyna Gsost's narrative recounts the 3E 399 legal duel between the Breton Lord Bowyn and the Orc Gortwog gro-Nagorm over a tract between Menevia and Wayrest. When both presented equal claims, Imperial law mandated armed combat. Gortwog chose Orcish armor and steel longswords; Bowyn chose the arena. An elderly Orc servant named Tunner, formerly of the Cursed Legion, trained Bowyn in heavy armor technique but secretly colluded with Gortwog, arranging the duel's rescheduling to a post-feast evening. Saturated and sluggish, Bowyn paradoxically learned to let the armor's joints guide movement rather than fighting against them. Gortwog won after three hours and named the land Orsinium. The account blends legal procedure with a practical treatise on Orcish armor, suggesting the mail rewards composure over force. Tunner's loyalty to his people frames the narrative with quiet Orcish solidarity.
topic_desc_basic: A historical account by Menyna Gsost describing how Gortwog gro-Nagorm won the land called Orsinium through a legal duel against the Breton Lord Bowyn in 3E 399. The duel was fought in Orcish armor with steel longswords. Gortwog prevailed and named the territory after the ancient Orcish homeland. The work also serves as instruction on fighting in heavy Orcish mail.

record_links.display_name: How Orsinium Passed to the Orcs

title: Ice and Chiton
topic_desc: Pletius Spatec's historical narrative recounts an episode from 2E 855, during Tiber Septim's conquest of Tamriel. Imperial commander Beatia of Ylliolos and her guard, ambushed and separated from their forces in northern Skyrim, take refuge in a ruined Reman-era keep. Finding only two dilapidated suits of chitin armor, Beatia devises a desperate diversion: she and Lieutenant Ascutus don the brittle shells and sprint across a frozen bay, drawing enemy cavalry onto treacherous ice. The aged chitin deflects arrow fire yet stiffens at the joints, slowing their flight. Their weight and impact fracture the ice behind them, causing the pursuing cavalry to plunge into the frigid water while the armored pair barely scrambles to safety. The account serves as a practical illustration of chitin armor's distinct properties—its resilience against projectiles and its susceptibility to rigidity and environmental degradation.
topic_desc_basic: A historical account by Pletius Spatec set in 2E 855, during Tiber Septim's conquests. Imperial commander Beatia of Ylliolos and Lieutenant Ascutus use degraded chitin armor to survive a desperate flight across a frozen bay in Skyrim, drawing enemy cavalry onto thin ice. The tale illustrates chitin armor's ability to deflect arrows despite becoming stiff and brittle with age.

title: Incident in Necrom
topic_desc: Jonquilla Bothe's tale recounts a Temple-commissioned expedition to clear a vampire-infested cemetery near Necrom. A hired party of four—including the underestimated illusionist Massitha—battles the savage Quarra bloodline within a Second Era Cyrodilic mausoleum. While the warriors dismiss Illusion as merely casting light or silence, Massitha's paralysis spells prove critical in combat. The mission succeeds but costs the warrior Phlaxith his life, and Massitha suffers a vampire's wound. When her surviving companions plot to steal her reward share, assuming her School useless for pursuit, Massitha uses invisibility to reclaim her gold, demonstrating Illusion's practical and deceptive power. The narrative serves as an instructive anecdote on the School's versatility.
topic_desc_basic: A story by Jonquilla Bothe about a Temple-hired group clearing vampires from a cemetery near Necrom. The party's illusionist, Massitha, proves her School's worth by using paralysis to survive combat and invisibility to reclaim her reward after her companions attempt to steal her share.

title: Last Scabbard of Akrash
topic_desc: A dramatic tale by Tabar Vunqidh set in 3E 407 Tear, following Peliah, daughter of the Dres slaver Minegaur. She secretly learns sword repair from a master armorer to maintain her father's prized blade, Akrash, which she provides to her Khajiit lover and family slave, Kazagh. Kazagh uses Akrash to murder local slave-traders, earning the sobriquet The Lopper. The slavers erroneously suspect an Outlander. After a poisoned needle fells Kazagh, Minegaur kills him with Akrash, only to be fatally stabbed by Peliah. The narrative intertwines armorer techniques with a tragic critique of Morrowind's slave trade, though its precise historical veracity remains uncertain.
topic_desc_basic: A tragic tale by Tabar Vunqidh set in 3E 407 Tear. It follows Peliah, daughter of a Dres slaver, who secretly repairs her father's sword Akrash for her Khajiit lover to use in murdering slave-traders. The story details armorer techniques alongside its dramatic plot, culminating in the deaths of the lover, the father, and the blade finding its final scabbard.

title: Lord Jornibret's Last Dance
topic_desc: A traditional poetic ballad alternating between women's and men's choruses, recounting the exploits of Lord Ogin Jornibret of Gaer at the winter ball hosted by the Queen of Rimmen. Jornibret, notorious for leaving maidens in tears, selects a fair partner and demonstrates surprising grace while dancing in ornate hide armor. As the dance concludes, the maiden reveals herself to be a man in a ursine-hide helm—the same figure who had spoken with Jornibret earlier—having disguised himself to teach the lord a humiliating lesson. The tale serves as a popular illustration of light armor's agility in social and martial contexts alike.
topic_desc_basic: A traditional song telling of Lord Ogin Jornibret of Gaer, a notorious charmer at the Rimmen court's winter balls. After he selects a maiden for a dance, his partner reveals a deep voice and a bear-helm disguise, turning Jornibret's expected conquest into public humiliation. The verse highlights the surprising grace achievable in hide armor.

title: Night Falls On Sentinel
topic_desc: Boali's tale unfolds in a Sentinel tavern, where a young woman named Haballa hires the retired kidnapper Jomic. Jomic recounts how he and his collaborators abducted the frail Crown Prince Arthago decades earlier on the royal family's behalf, leaving the Underking as a scapegoat. He then expounds on the seventy-one prime pain centers across the body and how a club can incapacitate or kill without bruising. Satisfied by his confession, Haballa reveals King Lhotun's crest and her mission to avenge her abducted brother, beating Jomic with a cudgel while counting his pain centers. The narrative blends a revenge drama with an unreliable narrator's instructional discourse on blunt weaponry.
topic_desc_basic: Boali's tale follows Haballa, who hires the retired kidnapper Jomic in a Sentinel tavern. Jomic confesses to abducting the frail Crown Prince Arthago decades earlier on the royal family's orders, framing the Underking, and explains how a club exploits bodily pain centers. Revealing King Lhotun's crest, Haballa avenges her brother by beating Jomic with a cudgel.

title: Palla, Book I
topic_desc: Vojne Mierstyyd's first-person narrative recounts a young Illusion initiate's obsessive infatuation with a dead woman. Stationed at the Mir Corrup Mages Guild, the narrator discovers a mysterious black disc among a deceased magister's effects, which an Enchantment instructor urgently orders destroyed, recognizing it as a necromantic artifact intended for resurrection. Later, while attending a Tales and Tallows ball at the estate of a young Redguard woman named Betaniqi, the narrator encounters a statue depicting her mother, Palla, locked in mortal combat with a monstrous figure. The narrator falls instantly and fatally in love with the sculpted image of this deceased warrior. The account, told from the infatuated narrator's subjective perspective, establishes a tragic conjurer's obsession that presumably drives the necromantic ambitions explored in the subsequent volume.
topic_desc_basic: A first-person account by Vojne Mierstyyd, an Illusion initiate at the Mir Corrup Mages Guild. After discovering a forbidden necromantic disc meant for resurrection, the narrator attends a ball and becomes fatally infatuated with a statue of the deceased Redguard warrior Palla, setting the stage for a tragic conjuration.

title: Palla, Book II
topic_desc: Vojne Mierstyyd's account concludes a Mages Guild initiate's tragic infatuation in Mir Corrup. Obsessed with a statue depicting a fierce Redguard warrior slaying a beast, the narrator steals a necromantic disc to resurrect the woman he loves, named Palla. Abandoning Illusion for Enchantment, he channels the artifact for months, only for it to shatter during a storm. When he confesses his failure to the warrior's daughter Betaniqi, she reveals that Palla was the monster; her mother was Xarlys. The narrator then encounters the resurrected creature awaiting him in the dark. The tale serves as a cautionary legend about obsession and the perils of misidentified desire, while embedding Magister Ilther's discourse on enchantment as a catalyst for deepening latent magicka.
topic_desc_basic: Vojne Mierstyyd's tale concludes a Mages Guild initiate's tragic obsession with a statue of a Redguard warrior. He steals a necromantic disc to resurrect his beloved, Palla, but the artifact shatters. The warrior's daughter then reveals Palla was the monster, not her mother. The narrator meets the resurrected beast in the dark.

title: Realizations of Acrobacy
topic_desc: A narrative account by Master Rhunen Zebavi detailing his traveling acrobatic troupe's encounter with House Telvanni Councilors Gothren and Neloth. After Neloth's guards tortured the performers—killing their Khajiit member S'Rabba—the troupe retaliated by infiltrating Tel Naga and stealing Mehrunes' Razor. Rhunen then presented the artifact to Gothren, leveraging acrobatic prowess to shift the Telvanni power balance. The work serves as both an adventure tale and a practical demonstration of acrobatic disciplines, emphasizing genuine physical mastery over illusion.
topic_desc_basic: Master Rhunen Zebavi recounts his troupe's theft of Mehrunes' Razor from Tel Naga after being tortured by Master Neloth's guards, later presenting the artifact to rival Councilor Gothren.

title: Response to Bero's Speech
topic_desc: A polemical treatise by the Battlemage Malviser, written in rebuttal to the privately printed lecture of the illusionist Berevar Bero. Bero argued that the School of Destruction is a shallow discipline and that Battlemages rely on other magical schools, even proposing that Destruction be merged into Alteration. Malviser counters by challenging Bero's historical examples—disputing claims regarding Zurin Arctus, Hethoth, and Welloc—and by asserting that Destruction requires mastery over complex factors such as delivery methods, elemental forces, target responses, defenses, and subtle generational curses. He rejects the proposed merger with Alteration and concludes that an illusionist's attack on Destruction is fitting, as Illusion concerns masking the truth.
topic_desc_basic: A polemical rebuttal by the Battlemage Malviser against the illusionist Berevar Bero. Bero argued that the School of Destruction is shallow and should be merged into Alteration, citing historical Battlemages who relied on other schools. Malviser disputes these historical claims and defends Destruction as a complex, subtle discipline requiring mastery of elemental forces, delivery methods, and curses.

title: Silence
topic_desc: A fictional tale by Ganpheril Kimeth, framed as an adventurer's memoir, that serves as a practical treatise on the Illusion spell Silence. The narrative follows the warrior Oristian Silverthorn, who seeks to slay the rogue battlemage Egroamaro at Indoranyon. A retired University of Gwylim instructor teaches Silverthorn the spell, explaining that it bends sound like glass bends light, extinguishing it as a physical entity. Silverthorn later uses the spell to prevent the battlemage from casting, slaying him effortlessly. The story concludes with a comedic inversion: Silverthorn returns home to his anxious wife Liah and uses the same spell to silence her relentless worrying, wryly reflecting that while he could have killed the mage without it, surviving his wife required Silence. The work propagates the doctrine that Illusion manipulates physical phenomena.
topic_desc_basic: A fictional tale by Ganpheril Kimeth illustrating the practical use of the Silence spell. The warrior Oristian Silverthorn learns the spell from a retired University of Gwylim instructor to defeat the battlemage Egroamaro, preventing him from casting. Silverthorn later uses the same spell to silence his relentlessly worrying wife, humorously demonstrating the spell's everyday utility.

title: Smuggler's Island
topic_desc: Quarde Anarion's tale follows two moon sugar smugglers, Harithoel and the Khajiit S'Riizh, shipwrecked on a barren island after a storm drowns their twelve-person crew. With no fresh water, Harithoel learns to spear golden fish, gradually mastering the weapon's technique of anticipating a target's movement. S'Riizh, feigning crippled helplessness, secretly observes and applies this same principle. When their contact vessel finally arrives after two months, S'Riizh reveals he can walk, tricks Harithoel into removing a crate concealing a rigged spear, and kills him—having learned that a fortune divided by one exceeds a fortune divided by two. The narrative functions as a dark instructional treatise on spear technique, using its brutal twist to illustrate the core lesson.
topic_desc_basic: Quarde Anarion's tale recounts two shipwrecked moon sugar smugglers stranded on a barren island. Harithoel learns to spear fish to keep them alive, mastering the technique of anticipating where a target will move. His Khajiit companion S'Riizh, secretly feigning injury, observes and applies this same principle to murder Harithoel upon rescue, claiming the entire cargo.

title: Surfeit of Thieves
topic_desc: A cautionary tale by Aniis Noru recounting the doomed robbery of two thieves, Heriah and Indyk, at Ald Olyra castle. Lured by the wealth of a hermetic Order of St. Eadnua, Heriah infiltrates the armory while Indyk provides a distraction. Mistaken for an expected guest called Lady Tressed, Heriah is ushered into a bizarre feast where robed figures introduce themselves with reversed names. The gathering's true nature is revealed when an hourglass empties: the celebrants are monstrous creatures, Indyk lies dead and drained, and Heriah realizes too late that her assumed identity, spelled backwards, marks her as their dessert. The narrative serves as a grim warning about overconfidence in security and infiltration.
topic_desc_basic: A cautionary tale by Aniis Noru about two thieves, Heriah and Indyk, who target a wealthy hermetic order at Ald Olyra castle. Mistaken for an expected guest, Heriah joins a strange feast of robed figures using reversed names. When an hourglass empties, the celebrants reveal themselves as monsters, and Heriah realizes too late that her assumed identity, spelled backwards, marks her as their next meal.

title: The Armorer's Challenge
topic_desc: Mymophonus's historical account chronicles the armoring contest commissioned during Empress Katariah's reign to equip Imperial forces campaigning in Black Marsh. When the Imperial Council objected to Katariah's preferred armorer, the Argonian freedman Hazadir, favoring the renowned Imperial artisan Sirollus Saccus instead, a champion's trial was decreed. Saccus crafted exquisite ebony armor and an enchanted dai-katana, while Hazadir supplied simple, swamp-adapted gear. In the flooded arena, Hazadir's lightweight scaled armor and spear bested Saccus's heavy, mobility-restricting equipment. Hazadir's victory earned him the commission, and his regional expertise quelled the Armanias insurrection. The narrative, which concludes with Saccus departing for Morrowind to study Argonian methods, serves as a lesson on practical adaptation over sheer craftsmanship, though the author's perspective may favor Katariah's ultimately vindicated judgment.
topic_desc_basic: Mymophonus recounts a famous armoring contest from Empress Katariah's reign. The Imperial artisan Sirollus Saccus crafted heavy ebony armor and an enchanted dai-katana, while the Argonian freedman Hazadir supplied simple, swamp-adapted gear. In a flooded arena simulating Black Marsh, Hazadir's lightweight equipment triumphed over Saccus's cumbersome finery, demonstrating the value of environmental adaptation in warfare.

title: The Axe Man
topic_desc: An anonymous account of the Morag Tong assassin Minas Torik, whose exclusive preference for axes puzzled the author. Torik recounted his youth as an abused servant at his uncle's failing saltrice plantation in Sheogorad. His duties—scouring floors, hauling a heavy bell-chain, and sweeping with a long duster—conditioned the exact motions of his later killing technique. When his uncle announced his departure for Skyrim without him, Torik seized an allegedly Dwemer axe and killed the man using those ingrained movements, then effortlessly cleaned the scene. The narrative, presented as Torik's own testimony, offers a chilling perspective on how brutal servitude forged his proficiency.
topic_desc_basic: An account of the Morag Tong assassin Minas Torik, who preferred axes above all weapons. The book recounts how Torik's abusive servitude at his uncle's Sheogorad saltrice plantation conditioned the sweeping and striking motions he later used to murder his uncle with an axe, a crime that went undetected.

title: The Black Arrow, Volume 1
topic_desc: Gorgic Guine's memoir recounts his youth as a footman serving the reclusive, Imperial Duchess of Woda in her fortified Valenwood palace. The Duchess despises the nearby village of Moliva and its archery academy, founded by the retired master Hiomaste. Guine befriends several students, including the Dunmer Missun Akin and the Breton Prolyssa, who dreams of joining the Quill Circus. Prolyssa demonstrates remarkable acrobatic skill by leaping through the jungle canopy, explaining her technique of anticipating landings. The narrative provides an outsider's perspective on cultural tensions between the aristocratic Imperial presence and Bosmer traditions, while offering practical insight into acrobatic movement. The account is framed as personal recollection, its reliability shaped by the narrator's admitted youth and limited social experience at the time.
topic_desc_basic: Gorgic Guine's memoir describes his service as a footman to the reclusive Duchess of Woda in Valenwood and his friendship with students at Master Hiomaste's nearby archery academy. The work offers personal observations on cultural tensions and acrobatic technique through his encounters with the Breton student Prolyssa.

title: The Black Arrow, Volume II
topic_desc: The second volume of Gorgic Guine's memoir recounts events at the palace of the Duchess of Woda in Valenwood. The Duchess schemes to relocate the village of Moliva and Master Hiomaste's archery school to make way for her sister Lady Villea's new palace. When the school burns under suspicious circumstances, killing Hiomaste and a student named Prolyssa, a Dunmer archer named Missun Akin exacts retribution. Over successive mornings, black ebony arrows forged at Dagoth-Ur pierce the Duchess's portrait despite exhaustive security, culminating in an impossible shot through the keyhole of the palace door that strikes the Duchess herself. Guine, formerly a palace servant and later a bard, recounts the tale with evident awe at Akin's marksmanship, though he admits he never confirmed the archer's method directly. The narrative blends admiration for extraordinary skill with an unmistakable tale of noble cruelty punished.
topic_desc_basic: A memoir by Gorgic Guine describing the downfall of the Duchess of Woda in Valenwood. After her palace burns Master Hiomaste's archery school, the Dunmer archer Missun Akin fires ebony arrows through the palace keyhole into her portrait nightly until one strikes the Duchess herself. The tale celebrates extraordinary marksmanship and is studied by those honing the bow.

title: The Buying Game
topic_desc: A treatise on mercantile strategy by the Khajiiti trader Ababael Timsar-Dadisun. The author frames bargaining as a polite, universal game requiring social awareness rather than aggression. He advises offering roughly sixty percent of the asking price, feigning budgetary constraints rather than criticizing wares, and resisting merchant flattery. Timsar-Dadisun stresses regional literacy, noting that rural merchants are not easily fooled and that provincial prejudices—such as suspicion toward Argonians in Morrowind or wariness of Khajiit and Bosmer everywhere—shape transactions. He also recounts personal regret over delaying purchases, arguing that occasional impulsiveness secures rare opportunities. The work blends practical advice with anecdotal observation from a seasoned Dunmer-based trader.
topic_desc_basic: A mercantile guide by the trader Ababael Timsar-Dadisun. It presents bargaining as a polite, strategic game across Tamriel, advising buyers to offer fair reductions, feign poverty rather than insult wares, and understand regional merchant types and prejudices. The author also warns against passing up rare goods, arguing that timely purchase often outweighs waiting for a better price.

title: The Cake and the Diamond
topic_desc: A cautionary narrative by Athyn Muendil detailing an encounter in an Ald'ruhn cornerclub with the renowned Breton alchemist Abelle Chriditte. When a thief presents a stolen diamond, Chriditte offers to trade invisibility potions for the gem's remnants. Exploiting the patrons' suspicion, she proposes they share a demonstration cake to prove it is unpoisoned. Having drugged Muendil to act as her unwitting mouthpiece, she applies diamond dust to only one side of the cutting blade, consumes the dosed half, and vanishes invisibly into the night with the gem. The account illustrates practical alchemical principles, contrasting野外 self-taught techniques with Mages Guild conventions, while warning of the craft's potential for cunning deception.
topic_desc_basic: A tale by Athyn Muendil recounting the renowned alchemist Abelle Chriditte's cunning deception in an Ald'ruhn cornerclub. Chriditte tricks a thief out of a stolen diamond by promising invisibility potions, then uses a drugged accomplice and a cleverly dusted cutting blade to consume the only functional dose and vanish with the gem.

title: The Dowry
topic_desc: A wealthy landowner tests suitors for his dour daughter by demanding wealth, intellect, and the ability to make her smile. A mysterious suitor passes the first two trials using stolen dowry gold, then reveals he burgled the vault beforehand. The daughter laughs at the audacity, and they marry. The publisher's note explicitly identifies this as a common folktale motif, noting the characters behave unlike the Dwemer, whose marriage customs remain unknown. A fringe theory citing this and other Marobar Sul tales proposes the Dwemer never disappeared but disguised themselves among Chimer and Altmer to evade Azura's gaze.
topic_desc_basic: Part ten of Marobar Sul's fictional Ancient Tales of the Dwemer. A suitor wins a dour maiden by burgling her dowry to fund his courtship. The publisher notes the tale reflects common folklore rather than genuine Dwemer culture, and mentions a fringe theory that the Dwemer disguised themselves to hide from Azura.
aliases: Ancient Tales of the Dwemer Part X

title: The Dragon Break Re-Examined
topic_desc: Fal Droon's treatise argues that the Dragon Break—a supposed metaphysical rupture in linear time—is a late Third Era fabrication rooted in a prosaic scholarly error. He contends that the Encyclopedia Tamrielica, published in 3E 12, misread the Alessian priesthood's visionary year as a standard calendar year, inflating the Order's lifespan from roughly 150 years to the legendary 1,008. Droon attributes the Dragon Break doctrine to eschatological cults obsessed with Tiber Septim's rise and Numidiumism, later perpetuated by uncritical scholarly inertia. The text references the fall of the Septim Dynasty as an established event, an anachronism suggesting either temporal displacement or deliberate unreliability. The author's name, Fal Droon, is itself an anagram of 'Darn Fool,' further marking the work as potentially satirical or self-undermining rather than straightforward scholarship.
topic_desc_basic: This revisionist treatise by Fal Droon disputes the reality of the Dragon Break, attributing the concept to a dating error in the Encyclopedia Tamrielica that misread Alessian visionary trances as calendar years. Droon calls the doctrine a late Third Era invention fueled by eschatological cults. Anachronistic references and the author's anagrammatic name cast doubt on the work's reliability.

title: The Firsthold Revolt
topic_desc: Maveus Cie's account recounts a conspiracy against Queen Morgiah of Firsthold, the Dunmer wife of King Reman on Summerset Isle. Lady Gialene, the king's Altmer concubine, secretly arms the xenophobic Trebbite Monks and mercenaries with her father's gold, timing the uprising for Reman's absence on a pirate campaign. The narrative centers on Morgiah's cunning defense: she feints a battlemage ambush while deploying archers, exploiting the rebels' own reflection spells to render their healers useless. The revolt collapses, Gialene is exiled, and her advisor Kael is executed. The work reads as dramatic historical fiction rather than sober chronicle, and its reliability regarding private conversations and motives is uncertain. Widely circulated as a Mysticism primer, it illustrates spell reflection as an unconventional battlefield tactic.
topic_desc_basic: A popular historical account by Maveus Cie describing a failed revolt in the Summerset Isle city of Firsthold. Altmer conspirators and Trebbite Monks rose against Queen Morgiah, a Dunmer, but were defeated through her cunning use of magic and deception. The work is valued as a Mysticism instructional text.

title: The Four Suitors of Benitah
topic_desc: A fable by Jole Yolivess recounting the tale of Oin Parnafacasis, a impoverished gardener who yearns for his childhood friend Benitah Gorgoth, now a wealthy widow. When Benitah declares she will only marry the strongest, most intelligent, most enduring, and most agile man in Morrowind, Oin enlists the healer Yakin Bael to teach him Fortify Attribute spells for each trait. Under assumed names, Oin bests renowned champions in each discipline. Upon overhearing that Benitah invented these tests to ward off fortune-hunters while awaiting her childhood protector, Oin reveals himself. The narrative serves as an instructional allegory for Restoration magic, detailing the visualization and magicka manipulation required to fortify strength, intelligence, endurance, and agility.
topic_desc_basic: A fable by Jole Yolivess about the gardener Oin Parnafacasis, who uses Fortify Attribute spells learned from the healer Yakin Bael to best a series of renowned champions. Oin undertakes this to win his childhood friend Benitah, a wealthy widow who set these impossible tests to deter fortune-hunters. The tale serves as an instructional allegory for Restoration magic.

title: The Gold Ribbon of Merit
topic_desc: A short fictional work by Ampyrian Brum set in High Rock, framing a practical discourse on marksmanship within a tale of class resentment. Stryngpool, an academy-trained aristocrat, condescendingly tutors Templer, a battle-scarred soldier whose family lost its land to Stryngpool's. Stryngpool demonstrates proper stringing, draws, and release techniques—including methods he attributes to Bosmer and Khajiit archers—while Templer seemingly struggles. The story reveals its ironic twist when Templer's allegedly wild shot actually arcs into the valley mansion, piercing Stryngpool's prized gold ribbon of merit through a shattered window. The narrative thus contrasts academic theory against raw, purposeful skill while embedding genuine archery instruction.
topic_desc_basic: A fictional tale by Ampyrian Brum about two old friends in High Rock who meet for archery practice. The privileged Stryngpool instructs the veteran soldier Templer in proper bow technique, but Templer seemingly errant shot deliberately arcs into the valley, striking Stryngpool's prized award through his mansion window.

title: The Hope of the Redoran
topic_desc: Turiul Nirith's treatise on the treacherous nature of omens, framed around a House Redoran legend. A dying mother prophesied her newborn son Andas would bring hope to House Redoran, be mighty in mind and arm, and suffer no harm from spell, blade, illness, poison, or spilled blood. Dubbed the Hope of the Redoran, Andas grew up invulnerable and arrogant, eventually claiming his cousin Athyn's councilor seat. Athyn challenged him to single combat. Guided by his Hammerfell teacher Shardie, Athyn recognized the omen's literal loophole and armed himself with a club, battering Andas to death without shedding blood. Nirith suggests the omen's promised hope may have referred to Athyn all along, illustrating how prophecies can function as deceptive traps, perhaps crafted by Boethiah.
topic_desc_basic: A cautionary tale by Turiul Nirith about the deceptive nature of prophecy. It recounts the legend of Andas, a Dunmer noble prophesied to be invulnerable to blades, poison, and spilled blood. His cousin Athyn exploited the omen's literal wording by killing him with a club, proving that prophecies can be misleading traps.

title: The Horror of Castle Xyr
topic_desc: Baloth-Kul's one-act play depicts Imperial Guard Captain Clavides investigating Castle Xyr in Scath Anud after an Ashlander dies of unnatural frostbite. The maid Anara appears ignorant of her master Hordalf Xyr's secret cellar, filled with corpses of diverse races subjected to systematic magical experimentation. A delivered ledger reveals not necromancy but prolonged Destruction spell torture, annotated in red ink by a correspondent. The final revelation implicates the maid herself as Iachilla Xyr, her identity eroded by slow poisoning. The play functions as both thriller and commentary on Telvanni impunity, Imperial jurisdictional limits, and the capacity for magical atrocity. Its unreliable narration, dramatic irony, and staged format invite skepticism about how comfortably Imperial authority confronts wizard-lord predation in Morrowind's remote reaches.
topic_desc_basic: A one-act play by Baloth-Kul dramatizing an Imperial Guard investigation at Castle Xyr in Scath Anud. The captain discovers a hidden cellar of corpses subjected to systematic Destruction magic torture by the Telvanni lord Hordalf Xyr and a correspondent. The play ends with the revelation that the maid Anara is herself the disguised noble Iachilla Xyr, her memory eroded by slow poisoning.

title: The Importance of Where
topic_desc: Part III of Marobar Sul's Ancient Tales of the Dwemer, this fable recounts the warrior Fangbith slaying monsters that plague Othrobar's flocks. His mentor Joltereg teaches that 'where' matters more than 'when': Fangbith must strike the five vital points and, crucially, slay the second beast at the stronghold so the chieftain witnesses the kill. A publisher's note reveals the tale is an old Ashlander story repackaged with Dwemer-sounding names. The Great Mountain is Red Mountain, and the referenced strongholds suggest Ashlanders once inhabited fortress ruins found across Vvardenfell, though scholars debate their builders. The double meaning of 'where'—striking location and battlefield location—reflects Ashlander riddle traditions.
topic_desc_basic: Part III of Marobar Sul's Ancient Tales of the Dwemer, this fable teaches that 'where' one strikes matters more than 'when.' A publisher's note reveals it is actually an old Ashlander tale repackaged with Dwemer names, offering evidence that ancient Ashlanders lived in strongholds rather than wickwheat camps.

title: The Locked Room
topic_desc: A cautionary tale by Porbert Lyttumly recounting the downfall of the cruel locksmith Arthcamu. His methodical Redguard pupil Yana, whom he tormented for her slow, exploratory approach to lockpicking, ultimately traps him inside a room with a ravenous vampire ancient. Yana's supposedly pick-proof lock forces Arthcamu to rely on her despised careful methods, but his panicked failure leaves him at the creature's mercy. The key hangs around the vampire's neck—a final, fatal irony mocking his earlier boast that she would never open a lock even with the key before her.
topic_desc_basic: A cautionary tale by Porbert Lyttumly about the Redguard pupil Yana who traps her cruel locksmith mentor inside a locked room with a hungry vampire. Her supposedly pick-proof lock and the key dangling from the vampire's neck deliver a fatal irony.

title: The Mirror
topic_desc: A tragic Bjoulsae tale by Berdier Wreans recounting the Battle of Ain-Kolur. The warrior Mindothrax, an undefeated defensive fighter who advocates prioritizing shield over blade, meets his death in single combat with a mercenary who mirrors his exact technique. As he dies, Mindothrax realizes the mercenary is his twin brother, Jurrifax, sold by their mother in infancy. A Reachmen witch perceives the truth but remains silent. The narrative serves as a vehicle for defensive combat philosophy, citing blademaster Gaiden Shinji, while exploring fate and the literal and figurative mirrors that destroy those who face themselves.
topic_desc_basic: A Bjoulsae tale by Berdier Wreans following Mindothrax, an undefeated defensive fighter who preaches prioritizing the shield over the blade. At the Battle of Ain-Kolur, he duels a mercenary who perfectly mirrors his technique. As he dies, Mindothrax recognizes his killer as his twin brother, a tragic revelation perceived but kept secret by a Reachmen witch.

title: The Prayers of Baranat
topic_desc: A traditional Dunmer myth recounting the tale of Baranat, a frail adventurer who undertakes the rescue of Lady Genevrah from the legendary Coribael brothers. Blessed by the Tribunal and aided by successive apparitions of Saints Veloth, Nerevar, Roris, and Olms, Baranat receives divine gifts of speed, strength, endurance, and cunning to slay each brother through unarmed combat. After defeating the eldest, Airen, using the Redguard Cycle of Blood technique, Baranat discovers his reward is hollow: the lady is ill-tempered and the inherited estate is blighted and ruined. Saint Delyn delivers the moral, cautioning that one should learn what they are truly fighting for before entering battle. The story serves as both Temple hagiography and wry cautionary tale.
topic_desc_basic: A traditional Dunmer myth about Baranat, a frail adventurer who rescues Lady Genevrah from the Coribael brothers with divine aid from Tribunal saints. After defeating each brother using miraculous gifts, Baranat discovers his prize is a ruined estate and an ill-tempered bride, illustrating the moral to learn what you fight for before fighting.

title: The Ransom of Zarek
topic_desc: The Ransom of Zarek is the opening volume of the Ancient Tales of the Dwemer, a fictitious scholarly translation attributed to the persona Marobar Sul. The narrative follows a student named Zarek who escapes three boastful Nord kidnappers by exploiting their vanity, luring them into fatal athletic contests involving swimming and running. A publisher's note exposes the work as a fraud: scholars agree that the Interregnum-era playwright Gor Felim invented the Marobar Sul identity to lend false authenticity to his adapted stage comedies. The text's depiction of the Dwemer bears no resemblance to the actual enigmatic race, and no record confirms Sul ever existed. The tale is widely studied as an example of literary forgery rather than genuine cultural history.
topic_desc_basic: The Ransom of Zarek is the first volume of the Ancient Tales of the Dwemer, attributed to the translator Marobar Sul. It recounts how a student named Zarek escapes boastful Nord kidnappers by tricking them into fatal athletic competitions. A publisher's note reveals the work is a fraud, actually written by the Interregnum playwright Gor Felim under a false identity to sell adapted comedies.
aliases: Ancient Tales of the Dwemer Part I

title: The Rear Guard
topic_desc: A tale by Tenace Mourl recounting the siege of Cascabel Hall, where the Bosmer mercenary Menegur served as rear-guard for the King of Solitude's retreating army. Stranded without food, Menegur survived by donning netch leather armor and raiding the surrounding enemy-held orchards. The narrative frames a practical lesson on netch leather's defensive properties: its velvety texture and residual nematocysts allow a wearer to absorb and divert blows by moving with the strike rather than against it, using an opponent's momentum to throw them off balance—a technique taught by the Dunmer armor specialist Aerin. The story concludes with Menegur exploiting an obscure 3E 246 Imperial decree to claim the county he defended, though this legal maneuver's historicity remains unverified.
topic_desc_basic: A story by Tenace Mourl about the Bosmer mercenary Menegur, who defended Cascabel Hall alone while starving. Wearing netch leather armor, he survived close-quarters raids for food by letting the membranous material divert enemy blows. The tale illustrates netch armor's unique defensive properties and concludes with Menegur claiming the castle through an obscure Imperial property law.

title: The Seed
topic_desc: Part II of Marobar Sul's fictional series Ancient Tales of the Dwemer, this allegorical tale recounts the deforestation of a settlement called Lorikh by the woodsman Juhnin, who harvests the sacred Hist for resin armor and massacres the Argonian populace. A surviving Argonian gives the orphan Kamdida a seed; planted at Juhnin's cottage, it engulfs him in an inescapable, self-healing tree, restoring partial vitality to the barren land. A publisher's note exposes the narrative as appropriated Argonian slave folklore originally set in Sadrith Mora, with Sul replacing Dunmer perpetrators with Dwemer and dismissing Temple Zero's speculative Lorkhan connections.
topic_desc_basic: Part II of Marobar Sul's fictional Ancient Tales of the Dwemer. It tells an allegorical story of a woodsman who destroys sacred Hist trees and Argonians for resin armor, only to be trapped by a vengeful seed. A publisher's note reveals the tale is actually appropriated Argonian slave folklore.

title: The Third Door
topic_desc: Annanar Orme's epic poem recounting the legend of Ellabeth, a master axewoman trained in Tel Aruhn. After her romantic rejection by rival Nienolas Ulwarth in favor of Lorinthyrae, Ellabeth devises a cruel revenge inspired by Mephala and Sheogorath. She imprisons Lorinthyrae in a room with three doors, falsely claiming they conceal Nienolas, a demon, and freedom. Though Ellabeth relents and opens the true exit, Lorinthyrae opens the first door seeking Nienolas, only to discover his dismembered remains. The tale also surveys diverse axe-fighting styles across Tamriel, including Orcish barbed axes, Winterhold long-axes, and hollow-bladed Elven weapons, framing Ellabeth's prowess within a broader martial tradition.
topic_desc_basic: A legendary epic by Annanar Orme about the axewoman Ellabeth. After her love is rejected by Nienolas, she takes revenge on his beloved Lorinthyrae with a deceptive three-door trap, concealing his dismembered body behind one. The poem also catalogs various axe-fighting traditions across Tamriel.

title: The Wraith's Wedding Dowry
topic_desc: A narrative by Voltha gra-Yamwort, translated by Apthorne, recounting the reformed Orc thief Kepkajna gra-Minfang, called the Wraith. On her wedding day to an Imperial jailer in Dagon Fel, her dowry gift is stolen by her former gang to curse the union. Relying on evasion techniques learned from her mentor Khargol, she retrieves the chest from the Shrine of Malacath without donning the armor within, preserving her gown instead. The tale serves as an illustrative tract on unarmored combat, detailing footwork, ducking, and erratic rhythm to evade armed attackers.
topic_desc_basic: A tale by Voltha gra-Yamwort of the Orc thief Kepkajna gra-Minfang, whose former gang steals her wedding dowry. She recovers it through skilled evasion rather than brute force, illustrating the principles of unarmored combat against armed foes.

title: Trap
topic_desc: An anonymous first-person account by a starving thief who stole gold from a hooded stranger in a southern Vvardenfell tavern. What follows is a harrowing pursuit through the night by multiple figures—a gold-masked man, a veiled woman, a dark knight, and others—who methodically drive the narrator from every hiding place into a crumbling rural manor. There, an aged vampire of the Berne bloodline seizes him. The pursuers are revealed not as hunters but as harriers, herding the narrator into the predator's lair for sport. Granted a perverse mercy, the narrator is kept alive as cattle alongside other captives. The text serves as both a warning and a testament to sanity, written from the vampires' cellar. Its reliability as a factual record is uncertain; the narrator admits fragmented memory and extreme distress, though the depiction of Berne hunting practices is internally consistent with other accounts.
topic_desc_basic: A cautionary tale by an anonymous thief. After stealing gold from a stranger in a Vvardenfell tavern, he was relentlessly pursued through the night by several figures who drove him into a ruined manor. There, an ancient vampire of the Berne bloodline claimed him. Kept alive as captive cattle, the narrator writes to warn others that some fates are worse than starvation.

title: Vernaccus and Bourlor
topic_desc: A legendary tale by Tavi Dromio, framed as a tavern story offering consolation about posthumous influence. It recounts the Colovian West rampage of Vernaccus, a lesser daedra taunted by his rival Horavatha. The Kynareth-blessed archer Bourlor confronts Vernaccus, who flees before the shot lands. Molag Bal twists this cowardice into a triumph over divine blessings, proclaiming Vernaccus 'He Who Cannot Be Touched,' and shrines arise in remote Morrowind and Skyrim. Passersby inevitably stone these shrines, and during one such assault, a rusted arrowhead—Bourlor's original bolt, lodged in the shrine's Evensacon-sourced door—works loose and fatally impales Vernaccus. Bourlor died believing he missed, yet his arrow ultimately found its mark.
topic_desc_basic: A legendary tale by Tavi Dromio about the lesser daedra Vernaccus and the Kynareth-blessed archer Bourlor. When Bourlor confronted the rampaging daedra, Vernaccus fled before the arrow flew. Molag Bal spun this cowardice into a false legend of invulnerability, but passersby stoning Vernaccus's shrines ultimately caused Bourlor's rusted arrowhead—lodged in a door—to strike the killing blow.

title: Words and Philosophy
topic_desc: A three-part interview with Lady Allena Benoch, a Bosmer master swordswoman and head of the Emperor's personal guard. Benoch recounts her transition from a tribal Jaqspur archer to a disciplined blade-wielder under the Redguard tutor Warday A'kor, emphasizing a pivotal moment where formal technique saved her life in darkness. She addresses rumors surrounding her career—confirming her duel to claim the Valenwood Fighter's Guild and her defense of Queen Akorithi, while denying responsibility for the Guild's broader disintegration. She refuses to confirm or deny the rumor that the Imperial Guard assassinated Archbishop Calaxes, the Emperor's bastard, citing the secrecy of her duties. Benoch laments the decline of the philosopher-swordsman ideal from eras past, contrasting historical Redguard swordsingers with modern crude fighters, and offers blunt practical advice for facing spellcasters.
topic_desc_basic: An interview with Lady Allena Benoch, a Bosmer master swordswoman and commander of the Emperor's personal guard. She recounts her journey from tribal archer to disciplined blade-wielder, addresses rumors of her storied career, and laments the decline of the philosopher-swordsman ideal from past eras.

title: The Warrior's Charge
topic_desc: An old Redguard poem recounting a mythic confrontation among the constellations, rooted in Yokudan star-lore. The narrative follows the Warrior as he sails his charges through the Serpent's snare. The Lord of Runes abandons his ship to wake the coiled snake and claim its scales, while the Lady East screams at a worm revealed by her sky-lit eye. The mailed Steed rides toward the bright scales, leaving the Warrior's care. When the Serpent rises to strike, the Warrior slays it with his blade, ending the charges' wandering. The poem personifies the celestial figures as active participants in a cosmic struggle rather than passive sky-marks, reflecting a cultural tradition that views the heavens as a realm of ongoing conflict and heroic deed.
topic_desc_basic: An old Redguard poem rooted in Yokudan tradition that recounts a mythic battle among the constellations. It describes the Warrior sailing charges through the Serpent's snare, the interventions of the Lord of Runes, the Lady, and the Steed, and the Warrior ultimately slaying the Serpent with his blade.

title: Arcana Restored
topic_desc: A handbook on restoring depleted magical items by Wapna Neustra, Praeceptor Emeritus of the Imperial College. The text outlines a hazardous ritual requiring a Mana Fountain primed with pure gold to rectify magical humors and coax pure principles from raw power. Neustra emphasizes strict adherence to her manual for the necessary incantations, warning that errors risk discorporation. She defensively dismisses rival scholars Kharneson and Rattor as envious frauds whose competing manuals are steeped in error. The author also cautions that the process inflicts painful injuries known as manacaust, advising practitioners to seek immediate healing afterward and explicitly rejecting rivals' claims that enduring such agony enhances the restored item's potency.
topic_desc_basic: A handbook by Wapna Neustra, Praeceptor Emeritus of the Imperial College, detailing a hazardous ritual for restoring depleted magical items. The process requires a gold-primed Mana Fountain and exact incantations, carrying risks of severe injury and discorporation. Neustra vehemently dismisses rival scholars Kharneson and Rattor while advising immediate healing after the painful manacaust.

title: Arkay the Enemy
topic_desc: A manifesto authored by "KW," the King of Worms, addressing his undead followers. The text claims Mannimarco ascended from mortality to godhood through will, drawing a deliberate parallel with Arkay, whom he names his enemy. It identifies Arkay's Blessing and Arkay's Law as the primary obstacles to necromantic dominance over souls. The tract outlines strategic roles: scholars must undermine Arkay's priests and subvert rulers, priests must conceal undead and recruit vampires and liches, and hidden agents must await the signal to destroy Arkay's temples and erase his name. The work functions as propaganda, promising inevitable victory while inciting a covert war against the divine order.
topic_desc_basic: A manifesto by Mannimarco, the King of Worms, urging his followers to destroy Arkay's influence. It identifies Arkay's Blessing and Law as the chief obstacles to raising the dead and commands scholars, priests, and hidden agents to undermine Arkay's priesthood, recruit undead, and prepare to overthrow his temples entirely.

title: Biography of Barenziah v I
topic_desc: The first volume of an official Imperial biography of Queen Barenziah, authored by Stern Gamboge, Imperial Scribe. It narrates her birth to the rulers of Mournhold, the destruction of her city during the conflicts preceding the Armistice with Tiber Septim, and her subsequent fostering under General Symmachus's arrangement with Count Sven of Darkmoor in Skyrim. Raised to embody Imperial virtues, Barenziah is depicted as an innocent who is deceived by a stable-boy named Straw into believing her guardian intends to sell her into concubinage. The account, framed as factual Imperial record, functions as propaganda by emphasizing Imperial benevolence and civilizing influence while portraying pre-Armistice Morrowind as decadent and the young Barenziah as trusting and naive.
topic_desc_basic: This Imperial-sponsored biography by Stern Gamboge covers Queen Barenziah's early life. It describes her birth in Mournhold, the city's destruction during Tiber Septim's conquest, and her fostering in Skyrim. Raised with Imperial values, the young princess is tricked by a stable-boy into fleeing her guardian's household.

title: Biography of Barenziah v II
topic_desc: This volume by Imperial Scribe Stern Gamboge continues the official biography of Queen Barenziah, covering her youth at Count Sven's Darkmoor estate, her flight with the stable boy Straw, and her time in Rifton. The narrative presents a heavily Imperial-sanitized account, depicting Barenziah as a pious, loyal subject who voluntarily betrayed her companions' planned theft of the Imperial Commandant's residence to protect the Empire. The Commandant is revealed as General Symmachus, who had been searching for her. Rather than punishing her, he informs her of her destined restoration as Queen of Mournhold. She is subsequently taken to the Imperial City, where she befriends Tiber Septim and his heirs before returning to Mournhold at eighteen. The work functions as Imperial propaganda, emphasizing Imperial benevolence and Barenziah's unwavering loyalty while omitting the controversial details found in the uncensored version of her memoirs.
topic_desc_basic: This volume of the official Imperial biography covers Queen Barenziah's youth, her deception by the stable boy Straw, and her time in Rifton. It portrays her as a loyal Imperial subject who willingly foiled her companions' theft plot, leading to her discovery by General Symmachus and her relocation to the Imperial City before reclaiming her throne in Mournhold.

title: Biography of Barenziah v III
topic_desc: The third volume of the official biography of Queen Barenziah, written by Imperial Scribe Stern Gamboge. It covers her marriage to General Symmachus, the birth of Helseth and Morgiah, and the theft of the Staff of Chaos by the Nightingale. The account details how Barenziah discovered the Emperor was the impostor Jagar Tharn, her covert collaboration with King Eadwyre and the spirit of Ria Silmane, and her role in aiding the Champion who ultimately ended the Imperial Simulacrum. Following Symmachus's death in the Mournhold insurrection, Barenziah fled to Wayrest, married Eadwyre, and currently rules alongside him. The narrative presents a loyalist perspective, portraying Barenziah as a cunning and heroic figure while omitting the scandalous elements found in the unauthorized biography.
topic_desc_basic: An official biography by Imperial Scribe Stern Gamboge covering Queen Barenziah's marriage to General Symmachus, the Jagar Tharn imposture, and her covert role in ending the Imperial Simulacrum. It recounts her flight to Wayrest after Symmachus fell and her subsequent marriage to King Eadwyre, presenting a loyalist account of these events.

title: Blasphemous Revenants
topic_desc: This polemical treatise argues that ancestral summoning is righteous only when performed by a blood-bound Dunmer in service to the Tribunal Temple, while any necromantic conjuration by foreign sorcerers constitutes an abominable theft that traps spirits in profane slavery. The author insists that necromancers must be exterminated and extends this condemnation to vampires, characterizing them as arrogant Western demons infesting Daedric shrines, abandoned strongholds, and Dwemer ruins. Declaring that the Great Houses and Temple have historically kept Morrowind pure, the text demands that both vampires and their mortal cattle be purged by fire and stake. The work serves as zealous Temple doctrine, blending cultural reverence for honored ancestors with xenophobic calls for violence against outsiders and the undead.
topic_desc_basic: A Temple polemic condemning necromancy as blasphemous slavery of ancestral spirits, asserting that only righteous Dunmer bound to the Temple may summon the dead. It demands the extermination of foreign sorcerers and vampires alike, framing both as profane invaders defiling Morrowind.

title: Confessions of a Skooma-Eater
topic_desc: Tilse Sendas's memoir chronicling her descent into skooma addiction and subsequent recovery. It directly challenges the widespread Khajiit assertion that skooma dependence is permanent, arguing instead that freedom comes through understanding and accepting one's desire rather than through magical or alchemical cures. Sendas contends that self-despising traps the addict, and that overcoming shame makes redemption possible. Her further suggestion that addiction does not necessarily signify moral weakness, and that renunciation is a choice rather than an obligation, has provoked significant outrage among conservative Dunmer, who view the work as an affront to social decency.
topic_desc_basic: A memoir by the Dunmer Tilse Sendas recounting her skooma addiction and recovery. It challenges the common belief that skooma dependency is incurable, arguing that self-knowledge and acceptance offer a path to freedom. Her claim that addiction is not necessarily a moral failing has provoked strong opposition from conservative Dunmer society.

title: Corpse Preparation v I
topic_desc: The first volume of a necromancer's instructional treatise on acquiring corpses across the provinces of Tamriel. Written from an openly necromantic perspective, the anonymous author surveys each region's legal, cultural, and environmental obstacles to obtaining bodies. Cyrodiil permits limited use of executed criminals; Morrowind's slavery institution offers cover despite Temple prohibition; Elsweyr's deserts preserve corpses well; Hammerfell's Arkay worship blocks most acquisition; and Orsinium presents a hoped-for diplomatic opportunity. The author displays clear bias, dismissing non-necromantic cultures as backwards and unenlightened, and acknowledges that some practitioners resort to murder when other sources fail. The text also notes that animal corpses produce poor servants compared to sentient beings, whose intelligence in life determines their usefulness when raised. The Sload are referenced as Tamriel's most famous necromancers, with uncertain practices in their homeland of Thras. The work serves as both practical manual and ideological justification for the necromantic arts.
topic_desc_basic: A necromancer's instructional text surveying each Tamrielic province for the ease or difficulty of obtaining corpses for study. The author discusses legal avenues in Cyrodiil, the cover provided by Morrowind slavery, desert preservation in Elsweyr, Arkay's prohibitions in Hammerfell, and Sload practices. The perspective is openly partisan toward the necromantic arts.
aliases: On the Preparation of the Corpse Volume One

title: Corpse Preparation v II
topic_desc: This necromantic treatise, the second volume in a series on corpse preparation, addresses the creation and maintenance of skeletal servants. The author stresses that completeness of the skeleton is paramount before attempting reanimation, as missing crucial bones yields frustrating results. While the reanimating magic assembles bones automatically, the practitioner is advised to reinforce the servant's joints using leather straps or, for greater durability, metal spikes. The text cautions that over-tight binding restricts movement and renders the servant useless, recommending that novices err toward tightness since bindings can be loosened later. Finally, the author notes that skeletal undead are particularly susceptible to irreparable damage, making careful preparation essential. The writer scorns inexperienced necromancers who reanimate incomplete skeletons, arguing that the difficulty of obtaining corpses makes such waste intolerable.
topic_desc_basic: The second volume of a necromantic series on corpse preparation, this text instructs practitioners on raising skeletal servants. It advises ensuring the skeleton is complete before reanimation and recommends reinforcing joints with leather straps or metal spikes. It warns that over-tight binding limits mobility and that skeletons are easily damaged beyond reanimation, making careful preparation essential to avoid wasting corpses.
aliases: On the Preparation of the Corpse Volume Two

title: Corpse Preparation v III
topic_desc: The third volume of a necromancer's instructional treatise on preparing corpses for animation as undead servants. Written from the perspective of a practitioner instructing apprentices, it covers techniques for stripping flesh using coastal scavengers such as mudcrabs, raising and re-raising decayed zombie servants through bone-binding and catgut sewing, and the superior method of mummification. The author describes soaking corpses in salt or natron for at least one month, wrapping them in linen, and performing rituals to imbue the desiccated body with strength and independence. The text treats necromancy as a practical craft and addresses climate-specific preservation concerns, referencing Argonia and Thras. As instructional writing by an self-identified necromancer, it presents the Art as legitimate scholarly work rather than forbidden practice, reflecting an in-world viewpoint at odds with Temple doctrine.
topic_desc_basic: An instructional necromancy text covering preparation of fresh and decayed corpses for animation. It describes using mudcrabs to strip flesh, raising zombie servants, and mummifying corpses through salt soaking and linen wrapping. The author writes as a practitioner teaching apprentices, treating necromancy as a legitimate craft despite its condemnation by Temple authorities.
aliases: On the Preparation of the Corpse Volume 3

title: Darkest Darkness
topic_desc: A treatise on the summoning, binding, and classification of Daedra from a Tribunal Temple perspective. It distinguishes between short-term conjuration and long-term pacts, and categorizes Daedric Lords as Good or Bad based on their submission to Almsivi. The Good Daedra—Boethiah, Azura, and Mephala—command hungers, winged twilights, and spider Daedra respectively, though spider Daedra are noted as dangerously unmanageable. The Bad Daedra—Mehrunes Dagon, Malacath, Sheogorath, and Molag Bal—oversee scamps, clannfears, dremora, ogrim, golden saints, and daedroths. Atronaches are described as unaligned elemental Daedra serving by whim. The text reflects Temple doctrine, framing Daedra as subordinate spirits and labeling uncooperative entities as treacherous rebels.
topic_desc_basic: A Tribunal Temple treatise classifying Daedra. It explains summoning and binding practices, and divides Daedric Lords into Good Daedra, who submit to Almsivi, and Bad Daedra, who defy them. It catalogues the lesser Daedra serving each lord, such as dremora, winged twilights, and golden saints, and describes unaligned elemental Atronachs.

title: Diary of a Lost Sailor
topic_desc: A personal journal chronicling a shipwrecked sailor's desperate twenty-five-day ordeal inland after a storm near Ebonheart. The narrator leaves their unarmed crew on the shore to seek passage, but is repeatedly misled by locals and grows steadily weaker from starvation. Upon reaching a sizable town, likely Mournhold, a resident offers help but leads the sailor into the city's extensive underground tunnels and sewers, where an insult results in a beating and imprisonment in a pit. The final entry records a creature being thrown into the pit, with the sailor expecting death. The diary serves as an unreliable but vivid account of a foreigner's disorientation and the perils lurking beneath the city.
topic_desc_basic: A journal detailing a shipwrecked sailor's twenty-five-day struggle after a storm near Ebonheart. Leaving his crew on the shore to find passage, the narrator is repeatedly misled by locals and nearly starves. Reaching a sizable town, he is lured underground into its sewers, beaten, and trapped in a pit. His final entry records a creature being thrown in after him, ending his tale.

title: Fellowship of the Temple
topic_desc: Archcanon Tholer Saryoni authored this evangelical guidebook to introduce outsiders to the Tribunal Temple and encourage their conversion. It presents orthodox Temple doctrine, asserting that Almalexia, Vivec, and Sotha Sil were mortal guardians who achieved divine substance through extraordinary discipline and virtue, subsequently defeating the Nords and Dwarves. The text outlines the faith's expectations: adherents require strong willpower and personality, study Restoration, Alchemy, Mysticism, and Conjuration, and fight with staves and hammers. It prescribes fourfold duties to Faith, Family, Masters, and goodness, and recommends further study of sacred texts and pilgrimage for spiritual advancement.
topic_desc_basic: Archcanon Tholer Saryoni wrote this guidebook to introduce outsiders to the Tribunal Temple. It outlines orthodox doctrine regarding the Tribunal's divine ascension, the expected magical studies and martial practices of members, and the fourfold duties of the faithful to faith, family, masters, and virtue.

title: Fighters Guild Charter
topic_desc: The Imperial Charter of the Guild of Fighters is the official founding document governing the Fighters Guild across the Empire. It outlines the Guild's purpose: employing mercenaries and facilitating contracts for citizens, such as pest removal, dangerous deliveries, and beast collection. The charter derives its authority from Section 4 of the Guilds Act, confirmed under Potentate Versidue-Shaie in 2E 321. It establishes strict internal rules, mandating expulsion for members who strike or steal from one another, and provides a dispute resolution hierarchy for citizens. Membership requires strength, health, proficiency with long blades, axes, blunt weapons, and shields, and competence with heavy armor. An attachment details Vvardenfell District chapters: independent guildhalls operate in Ald'ruhn and Balmora, while the Sadrith Mora and Vivec chapters lease their facilities from the Telvanni Council and the Tribunal Temple, respectively.
topic_desc_basic: The Imperial Charter of the Guild of Fighters is the founding document of the Fighters Guild, established under the Guilds Act by Potentate Versidue-Shaie in 2E 321. It defines the Guild's role in employing mercenaries and offering citizen contracts for creature removal and escort duties. It mandates expulsion for inter-member violence or theft and requires prospective members to demonstrate martial proficiency and heavy armor competence.
aliases: Imperial Charter of the Guild of Fighters

title: Fragment: On Artaeum
topic_desc: Taurce il-Anselma's treatise surveys the Isle of Artaeum, home of the Psijic Order, Tamriel's oldest monastic order. The text traces Psijic history from the First Era, when they already counseled kings and practiced the Elder Way—a philosophy binding nature to individual will, distinct in origin from magicka. The author notes Artaeum's unexplained disappearance at the Second Era's dawn and its return five centuries later, after which the relocated inhabitants refused to explain their absence or the fate of Ritemaster Iachesis. Now led by Loremaster Celarus, the Order's political influence fluctuates; recent emperors distrust them enough to bar their ambassadors. The island itself is said to shift geographically, and the author describes its idyllic landscapes and the Ceporah Tower, a pre-Elven relic used in Psijic rites, from a rare personal visit.
topic_desc_basic: Taurce il-Anselma's work describes the Isle of Artaeum, home of the ancient Psijic Order. It records the island's mysterious five-century disappearance at the dawn of the Second Era, its equally unexplained return, and the Psijics' fluctuating political influence across Tamriel. The author notes recent imperial suspicion toward the Order and describes the island's elusive geography and idyllic landscapes from a rare personal visit.

title: Frontier, Conquest...
topic_desc: Frontier, Conquest, and Accommodation: A Social History of Cyrodiil, published by the University of Gwylim Press in 3E 344, challenges the conventional narrative that human settlement of Tamriel began with Nord military expansion under Ysgramor. Drawing on archaeological evidence dating Nedic settlements to ME 800–1000, the work argues that humans from Atmora had migrated to Tamriel for centuries before Ysgramor, living peacefully alongside Elven populations in High Rock, Hammerfell, Cyrodiil, and possibly Morrowind. The Nords are characterized as the only Nedic people who failed to accommodate the Elves, establishing a militaristic frontier in Skyrim rather than merging with the Elder Race. The text treats the twelve pre-Harald Nord kings as historically uncertain and positions the Song of Return as a partial account rather than definitive history. As a scholarly work, it advances a revisionist interpretation of Tamriel's social history, emphasizing accommodation over conquest in most regions.
topic_desc_basic: A scholarly work published by the University of Gwylim Press in 3E 344. It argues that humans settled Tamriel centuries before the Nord conquests, living peacefully alongside Elves in most regions. Only in Skyrim did accommodation fail, leading to the militaristic frontier tradition associated with Ysgramor.

title: Grasping Fortune
topic_desc: Grasping Fortune is a recruitment tract and guide to House Hlaalu's philosophy authored by Councilor Dram Bero. The work presents Hlaalu as the most progressive Great House, crediting its embrace of Imperial law and custom for its rise to dominance. Bero critiques rival Houses—Redoran's martial debt, Telvanni's inflexibility and infighting, Indoril's dependence on charity, and Dres's tendency toward enmity—as evidence that tradition cannot withstand historical progress. The text advocates seizing opportunity and balancing profit against the long-term value of reputation, arguing that theft and murder ultimately harm commerce. It outlines practical skills for Hlaalu success: mercantile agility, persuasive speech, property security through locks and traps, and, when forced to fight, the use of light armor, short blades, and marksman weapons. The tract concludes by directing prospective members to the Balmora Council Manor, emphasizing that the House above all prizes initiative and ambition.
topic_desc_basic: A guide and recruitment tract for House Hlaalu by Councilor Dram Bero. It presents the House as progressive for embracing Imperial custom, critiques rival Houses as backward or self-defeating, and advises balancing profit with reputation. It recommends mercantile skill, persuasive speech, and light, agile combat, directing prospective members to Balmora.

title: Guide to Ald'ruhn
topic_desc: This travel guide surveys Ald'ruhn, the district seat of House Redoran and one of Vvardenfell's largest settlements. It describes three principal districts: the Redoran-style town with its organic architecture, the remarkable manor and council district of Ald'ruhn-under-Skar sheltered beneath an ancient giant crab's carapace, and the Imperial Buckmoth Fort to the south. The author catalogs services, names the six Redoran councilors residing under Skar, identifies guild and Temple stewards, and outlines road, silt strider, and Mages Guild transport routes. Written in practical, advisory prose for travelers, it reflects an Imperial administrative perspective on a major Dunmer stronghold. The heading 'Principle Districts' appears to be a scribal error for 'Principal Districts.'
topic_desc_basic: A practical travel guide to Ald'ruhn, the House Redoran district seat on Vvardenfell. It describes the town's three districts, the Redoran village, the council manors built beneath a giant crab shell known as Ald'ruhn-under-Skar, and the Imperial Buckmoth Fort, along with available services, notable residents, and transportation routes by road, silt strider, and Mages Guild teleportation.

title: Guide to Balmora
topic_desc: This practical guide surveys Balmora, the district seat of House Hlaalu and Vvardenfell's second largest settlement. It details the city's four districts: the affluent High Town on the western hill, the Commercial District west of the Odai River, the commoner Labor Town to the east, and the southeastern Fort Moonmoth housing the Imperial garrison and cult. The text catalogs available services, from Hlaalu Council Manor and the Tribunal Temple to the Fighters, Mages, and Morag Tong guildhalls, noting that outlanders must venture to Fort Moonmoth for Imperial provisions. It identifies ranking local figures, including guild stewards and Hlaalu representatives, while cautiously framing the Thieves Guild presence as unconfirmed rumor. Concluding with transportation, it outlines roads, silt strider routes, Mages Guild teleportation, and the perilous Foyada Mamaea trail to Ghostgate.
topic_desc_basic: A concise travel guide to Balmora, the House Hlaalu district seat and Vvardenfell's second largest city. It describes the four urban districts, available guild and temple services, prominent local figures, and regional transportation routes including silt striders and roads.

title: Guide to Sadrith Mora
topic_desc: A practical guidebook detailing the geography, services, and social customs of Sadrith Mora, the district seat of House Telvanni. Written for outlanders, it emphasizes that the island town is officially open only to Telvanni retainers. Outsiders are directed to the Gateway Inn or the Imperial garrison at Wolverine Hall for lodging and services. The guide describes the Great Market and its small slave market, the Telvanni Council Hall suspended on giant mushroom stalks, and Tel Naga, the wizard tower of Councilor Neloth. It identifies specific service locations for Imperial guilds, the Thieves Guild, and the Tribunal Temple, and explains the role of the Telvanni Mouths who speak for their absent mage-lords. Transportation options via ship and Mages Guild teleportation are also outlined.
topic_desc_basic: A traveler's guide to Sadrith Mora, the island district seat of House Telvanni. It advises outsiders to confine themselves to the Gateway Inn or Wolverine Hall, as the town is otherwise restricted to Telvanni retainers. The text describes key sites like the Telvanni Council Hall, Master Neloth's tower of Tel Naga, and the Great Market, while listing available services and transport options.

title: Guide to Vvardenfell
topic_desc: A comprehensive geographical survey of Vvardenfell District, cataloging its nine distinct regions based on Ashlander land classifications. The text presents an Imperial administrative perspective, detailing the island's recent opening to settlement and trade. It describes the temperate Ascadian Isles and the agrarian Bitter Coast, the arid Ashlands and volcanic Molag Amur, the rugged Azura's Coast and remote Sheogorad archipelago, the pastoral Grazelands, the western West Gash highlands, and the blighted Red Mountain encircled by the Ghostfence. The account emphasizes Imperial infrastructure, Great House seats, and Temple garrisons while noting Ashlander nomadic presence. As an Imperial reference, it naturally foregrounds colonial governance and trade while treating native traditions primarily as useful classification frameworks.
topic_desc_basic: A geographical survey of Vvardenfell detailing its nine regions, from the fertile Ascadian Isles to the blighted Red Mountain. Written from an Imperial perspective, it describes major settlements, Great House seats, and the nomadic Ashlander tribes, emphasizing the district's recent opening to Imperial settlement and trade.

title: Homilies of Blessed Almalexia
topic_desc: A collection of didactic fables attributed to the Tribunal god Almalexia, intended for the moral instruction of the young. Each homily employs Vvardenfell's native creatures to illustrate a virtue or warning, frequently featuring the young Sotha Sil or Lord Vivec as figures of wisdom and authority. The tales emphasize empathy, humility, vigilance against gradual corruption, and the perils of arrogance and thoughtless companionship. As Temple-sanctioned teachings, the work serves a doctrinal and propagandistic role, presenting the Tribunal as the ultimate arbiters of righteousness and shaping devotees' conduct through accessible parables rather than abstract theology.
topic_desc_basic: A collection of moral fables attributed to the god Almalexia, used to teach Temple youth. The stories feature Vvardenfell creatures and depict Sotha Sil and Vivec imparting lessons on empathy, humility, and vigilance, serving as accessible doctrinal instruction.

title: Honor Among Thieves
topic_desc: Written by the self-styled Arnie the Scrib, this tract serves as a recruitment manual for the Thieves Guild. It outlines the Guild's preferred skills—stealth, security, light armor, and marksman—and emphasizes mutual support, including information sharing and discounted bribery of guards, as the foundation of its titular honor. The text functions partly as propaganda, sharply contrasting the Guild's non-lethal ethos with the native Camonna Tong, which Arnie characterizes as violently xenophobic and murderous. It advises prospective thieves to seek contacts at cornerclubs and tradehouses in Balmora, Ald'ruhn, Sadrith Mora, and Vivec's Foreign Quarter.
topic_desc_basic: Arnie the Scrib authored this recruitment pamphlet for the Thieves Guild. It outlines preferred thieving skills, stresses mutual support and non-lethal business, and warns against the violently xenophobic Camonna Tong. Prospective members are directed to cornerclubs in Balmora, Ald'ruhn, Sadrith Mora, and Vivec.

title: Invocation of Azura
topic_desc: In this personal testament, the priestess Sigillah Parate recounts three centuries of Daedric worship across four cults. She describes Molag Bal's reliance on treachery, Boethiah's appetite for cultist bloodshed, and Nocturnal's deliberate unfathomability, ultimately finding Azura alone genuinely values her followers' sincere love and emotional engagement. The text details each Prince's invocation day and conditions, including Azura's caution during thunderstorms belonging to Sheogorath. As memoir and devotional argument, it reflects one priestess's subjective spiritual journey rather than objective doctrine.
topic_desc_basic: A devotional memoir by the priestess Sigillah Parate comparing her worship of four Daedric Princes. She ultimately favors Azura, claiming this Princess uniquely values genuine love from her followers, unlike the cruelty, bloodlust, or impenetrable mystery characterizing Molag Bal, Boethiah, and Nocturnal.

title: Legions of the Dead
topic_desc: This scholarly treatise categorizes undead into three types: spirit, flesh, and fleshless revenants. It details their vulnerabilities, noting spirits require enchanted or silver weapons, while bonewalkers—the Dunmer term for zombies—and common skeletons succumb to ordinary arms. The bonelord is highlighted as a dangerous fleshless exception needing enchanted arms. The text claims vampires were hunted to extinction in Morrowind by Ordinators and Buoyant Armigers but acknowledges recent sightings, suggesting infiltration or awakening. A final note distinguishes ash vampires as living, non-undead entities unaffected by anti-undead magic, citing Tribunal Temple warriors as the source for this claim.
topic_desc_basic: A treatise classifying undead into spirit, flesh, and fleshless types. It outlines their combat vulnerabilities, such as spirits requiring enchanted or silver weapons, and notes regional terminology like bonewalkers for zombies. It claims vampires were once eradicated from Morrowind by Temple forces but have recently reappeared, and clarifies that ash vampires are not undead.

title: Lives of the Saints
topic_desc: This Tribunal Temple hagiography presents twelve Dunmer saints as moral exemplars, each paired with a virtue and a craft patronage. The text exhorts the faithful to emulate figures ranging from Saint Veloth the Pilgrim, who led the Dunmer from Summerset Isles, to Saint Olms the Just, credited as founder of the Ordinators. The narrative is explicitly doctrinal, characterizing the Dwemer as evil and House Dagoth as traitorous, framing Nerevar's death as martyrdom, and presenting Tribunal theology as established truth. Several accounts blend legend with political purpose, particularly Saint Roris's martyrdom serving as the rallying cry of the Arnesian War. The work reflects Temple orthodoxy rather than dispassionate history.
topic_desc_basic: A Tribunal Temple hagiography profiling twelve Dunmer saints, each paired with a virtue and a trade patronage. The text presents figures such as Saint Veloth, Saint Nerevar, and Saint Olms as moral models for the faithful, reflecting Temple doctrine and legend rather than neutral history.

title: Mixed Unit Tactics v1
topic_desc: A military treatise by the Imperial observer Codus Callonus, arguing that the Imperial Legions should study Khajiiti warfare. Stationed at Fort Sphinxmoth during the Five Years War of 3E 396, Callonus describes a northern skirmish where Khajiiti forces lured Bosmer archers into split detachments by felling trees, provoking the Bosmer's religious prohibition against harming the forest. The Khajiit deployed multiple morphologies in concert: Cathay-raht and Senche-raht served as ground forces and shield-bearers, Ohmes and Ohmes-raht emerged from concealed tunnels to ambush descending Bosmer infantry, and the arboreal Dagi and Dagi-raht silently climbed into high branches to attack the remaining archers with fire. Callonus expresses skepticism regarding a Bosmer survivor's claim that the small Alfiq Khajiit cast spells, dismissing it as unreliable. The author notes this mixed-unit tactic succeeded twice before a larger Bosmer force with native animal allies prevailed, a confrontation he promises to address in a second volume.
topic_desc_basic: A military treatise by the Imperial observer Codus Callonus, arguing the Legions should study Khajiiti warfare. It details a Five Years War skirmish where Khajiit forces used multiple morphologies in concert—ground troops, concealed tunnel ambushers, and arboreal Dagi attackers—to defeat Bosmer archers.
