In the tale, three beasts journey toward the sky, but when the Adversary demands one sacrifice themselves, only the angry Bear is left to survive, condemned to remain alone in fury until the end of time.

title: Tanna
topic_desc: Tanna is a plant whose leaves are harvested for smoking or raw consumption, growing in the dry regions of southern Morrowind.
topic_desc_basic: Tanna is a leafy plant growing in the dry regions of southern Morrowind, especially Shipal-Shin and the Coronati Basin. Its leaves are commonly smoked in pipes like hackle-lo and can also be eaten raw.

title: Tantha Egg
topic_desc: Tantha eggs are the eggs of gold tanthas. In alchemy, they are recognized as an ingredient with distinct properties, valued by practitioners for their esoteric characteristics. As a natural product of the gold tantha, these eggs are typically sourced from the creature's habitat by hunters and alchemists familiar with the species.
topic_desc_basic: Tantha eggs are laid by gold tanthas and are used as an alchemical ingredient.

title: Taragetis Blossom
topic_desc: The Taragetis blossom is a small yellow flower harvested from the taragetis plant. The flora grows predominantly in Vorndgad Forest, with smaller populations found in Midkarth and Lorchwuir Heath in Skyrim. Alchemists and hunters value the blossom for its alchemical properties, and it is commonly gathered from these western Skyrim regions.
topic_desc_basic: A small yellow flower taken from the taragetis plant, which grows mainly in Vorndgad Forest and occasionally in Midkarth and Lorchwuir Heath in Skyrim.

title: Tawny Funnel Cap
topic_desc: Tawny Funnel Caps are a variety of mushroom found growing in the Vorndgad Forest, the Grey Plains, and the Druadach Highlands of Skyrim. As a fungal ingredient, they are of interest to practitioners of alchemy for their inherent properties, and they are commonly gathered by hunters and foragers traversing these regions.
topic_desc_basic: Tawny Funnel Caps are a type of mushroom that grows in the Vorndgad Forest, the Grey Plains, and the Druadach Highlands of Skyrim.

title: Teachings of the Master-Student
topic_desc: A martial treatise by Taren Omathan advocating a holistic discipline uniting body, mind, and spirit. It prescribes thrice-daily stretching, meditation, and prayer to maintain limberness across all three. The combat philosophy emphasizes redirection over blocking, fluidity over mechanical execution, and using an opponent's strength against them. It identifies vital targets—throat, solar plexus, groin, eyes, nose, temple—while forbidding knee and elbow strikes in honorable combat. Omathan teaches that every movement contains its own counter, and that true mastery lies in restraint, balance, and avoiding conflict entirely.
topic_desc_basic: A martial treatise by Taren Omathan offering instruction in unarmed combat and personal discipline. It teaches that physical effectiveness depends on equally rigorous mental and spiritual conditioning, advocating thrice-daily stretching, meditation, and prayer.

title: Tektite
topic_desc: Tektite is a rare mineral ingredient of uncertain natural origin, valued by alchemists and hunters for its esoteric properties. It is not found in common leveled lists or typical wildlife, making it exceptionally scarce. Its specific alchemical effects remain a subject for specialist study rather than general knowledge, and it holds no widespread culinary or common medicinal use.
topic_desc_basic: Tektite is a rare mineral ingredient. It is not found on common creatures or in typical supplies, making it exceptionally scarce and difficult to obtain.

title: Teleportation Praxis, Vol. I
topic_desc: Voganna Plotinus's scholarly work examining the historical methods and challenges of teleportation, from Oblivion traversal to arcane engines, arguing that early successes were rare and impractical before modern praxis.
topic_desc_basic: A scholarly volume by Voganna Plotinus surveying the history and difficulties of teleportation magic, covering early methods such as traversing Oblivion and constructing arcane engines.

title: Teleportation Praxis, Vol. II
topic_desc: Voganna Plotinus's scholarly treatise on teleportation examines two historical methods predating the Celaudine era. The first, the Dawn Magics, draws on primordial forces; the eastern mage Barilzar famously wielded them to bypass standard teleportation limits before vanishing in the Second Interregnum. Imperial authorities now prohibit such study following subsequent disasters, and Plotinus dismisses claimed Merethic-era elven connections as archaeologically unsupported. The second method, Intervention, first appears in First Interregnum hagiographies and became common by Reman's reign. Plotinus questions whether these spells are truly divine, noting they draw on personal magicka and function for secular casters, yet their precise effects remain unreplicated without a faith component, suggesting a link to the caster's psyche or desire for sanctuary.
topic_desc_basic: A scholarly work by Voganna Plotinus examining historical teleportation methods, specifically the prohibited Dawn Magics and the commonly known Intervention spells.

title: Teleportation Praxis, Vol. III
topic_desc: Voganna Plotinus's scholarly work examining the historical development of the Celaudine method, the foundational technique of modern mark-and-recall teleportation. The text details the discovery by Breton mage Celaud Mabeurre in 2E 662 at the College of Gwylim, whose lifelong experimentation yielded the stable spiritual anchor approach after decades of fatal arcane mishaps at the institution. Plotinus recounts how Celaud's assistant spent two decades refining the spells into practical use, and how the resulting magic faced centuries of suspicion. During the Interregnum, commoners feared teleportation stole souls or produced doppelgangers, while High Rock nobility viewed it as a threat to serfdom and imprisonment, leading to the persecution of early practitioners. Only with the Septim-era Mages Guild's renewal of trans-provincial scholarship did Celaudine teleportation overcome its controversial origins.
topic_desc_basic: A scholarly volume by Voganna Plotinus detailing the Celaudine method of teleportation, the modern mark-and-recall technique invented by Breton mage Celaud Mabeurre in 2E 662, and the centuries of popular suspicion and noble persecution it faced before becoming accepted practice.

title: Temarin Bugloss Flower
topic_desc: The temarin bugloss flower is an alchemical ingredient harvested from the temarin bugloss plant, a flora species native to the Padomaic Isles. As a regional specialty of those remote islands, the flower is seldom encountered in mainland Tamrielic markets and typically reaches alchemists only through specialized import channels or chance findings among randomized ingredient supplies. Its properties make it a subject of interest for practitioners seeking region-specific reagents, though its distant origin renders consistent acquisition difficult.
topic_desc_basic: The temarin bugloss flower is an ingredient taken from the temarin bugloss plant, which grows native to the Padomaic Isles.

title: Temple Dome
topic_desc: Temple Domes are a yellow-tinted fungus common throughout central Morrowind. They are notable for usually emitting some light. In alchemical practice, the fungus is recognized for its distinct properties and is utilized by practitioners in the region. The ingredient is commonly sourced from the wilds of central Morrowind and appears in regional supply lists, including those associated with Mournhold, Narsis, and the Velothi lands.
topic_desc_basic: Temple Domes are a yellow-tinted, light-emitting fungus common throughout central Morrowind.

title: Temple Zero - A Warning
topic_desc: A polemical tract circulating in Imperial scholarly circles that denounces the Temple Zero Society as a threat to both intellectual discourse and Imperial stability. The anonymous author accuses the Society of concealing its true nature behind a respectable historiographical facade, alleging that its members are not mere Numidianist theorists but open Arcturianists and adherents of Marukhati heresies. The author further claims, contrary to the Society's own founding minutes, that the organization predates the Third Empire entirely and carries the hallmarks of Sethite mystery-cults, Nocturnalite occluded harmonics, and Eastern Psijjic nihilist teachings. The tract defends Imperial censorship of forbidden mysteries and condemns the Society's populism in promoting public education as seditious. Its significance lies in documenting the factional anxieties surrounding the Temple Zero Society's growing prominence in the capital following the Miracle of Peace and the legitimization of historical Numidianism.
topic_desc_basic: A polemical tract denouncing the Temple Zero Society, a scholarly collective prominent in the Imperial capital. The work accuses the Society of masking seditious Arcturianist and Marukhati heresies behind a respectable historiographical facade, and claims the organization predates the Third Empire. It defends Imperial censorship and condemns the Society's calls for public education as a threat to Imperial stability.

title: The 1,000 Spirits of Old Cyrod
topic_desc: Umalchio Tricho's guide to Cyrodiilic religious practice, published with Imperial Seminary patronage for provincial immigrants. It contrasts the formulaic piety of Colovian colonists with the Nibenay's extravagant devotion to thousands of spirits. The work surveys the Great Faiths and their charismatic sub-cults honoring facets of the Divines; regional hero-gods and the vast hagiography of Imperial saints; institutionalized Daedric worship, noting the censure of Dagon cults after the Simulacrum; and the Nedic-derived Totem Societies of the rural east, whose animal spirits manifest the collective power of their communities. Tricho dismisses rumored Tiger Society worship as grotesque and doubtful.
topic_desc_basic: A guide by Umalchio Tricho explaining Cyrodiilic religion to provincial newcomers. It surveys the diverse cults, saints, Daedric worship, and totem societies practiced in the Nibenay and Heartlands, where thousands of spirits are honored.

title: The Adabal-a
topic_desc: The Adabal-a is traditionally attributed to Morihaus, the winged-bull demigod and consort of Alessia the Slave Queen, though this authorship cannot be historically verified. It is among the oldest surviving written accounts from the early First Era. The text recounts three episodes central to the Alessian Rebellion: the death of Pelinal Whitestrake in the blood-floored throne room of White-Gold, where his severed head warns Morihaus that Umaril yet lives and will return; Alessia's youth in enslavement at Sard, detailing the brutal conditions of Ayleid dominion over the peoples of the Niben; and Morihaus's explanation of the many names by which Alessia was known, from Al-Esh to Paravant to Paravania. The work is a vital, if uncertain, primary source for the founding of the First Empire of Cyrodiil.
topic_desc_basic: The Adabal-a is an ancient text traditionally attributed to Morihaus, consort of Alessia the Slave Queen. It is among the oldest surviving written accounts from the early First Era. The work describes key events of the Alessian Rebellion, including Pelinal Whitestrake's death, Alessia's enslavement under the Ayleids, and the origins of her many names.

title: The Alik'r
topic_desc: A travelogue and philosophical meditation by the author Enric Milres, chronicling a two-year sojourn in the Alik'r Desert of Hammerfell. Inspired by the Redguard poet Weltan, Milres abandoned urban life to experience the desert directly, finding that political boundaries dissolve beneath the shifting sands and that inhabitants view themselves as part of the landscape rather than separate from it. The work characterizes the Redguards' relationship with the desert as a perpetual, sacred struggle befitting their warrior nature, and describes the land's stones as burning with the deep power of Tamriel itself. Returning to Sentinel during a war with Daggerfall, Milres contrasts the tragedy of petty political conflicts with the eternal, formless permanence of the desert, finding lasting inspiration in its changeless yet ever-changing nature.
topic_desc_basic: A book by Enric Milres describing his two years in the Alik'r Desert. Inspired by the Redguard poet Weltan, the author explores the desert's eternal landscape and the Redguard people's sacred, perpetual struggle with their harsh homeland.

title: The Ancestor Moth Cult
topic_desc: This work, promulgated under the Imperial Geographical Society, surveys the origins and practices of the Cult of the Ancestor Moth. It traces the tradition from early Cyro-Nordic export of gypsy moth silks inscribed with genealogies to the Nibenese synthesis where ancestor and moth became synonymous. The Cult captures the singing spirits of forebears in special silk-gathering rituals; garments woven from this material reproduce an ancestral chorus when they move. Higher-order monks forgo enchanted vestments entirely, wearing living ancestor-moths on their skin. They attract the moths using ground bark-dust and sub-vocalized mantras, a constant discipline maintaining cosmic balance; any spoken interruption causes the moths to burst away before returning when the chant resumes. The text is a significant record of Nibenese sacred custom and the order's distinctive spiritual discipline.
topic_desc_basic: This Imperial Geographical Society publication examines the Cult of the Ancestor Moth, a Nibenese order that weaves the captured singing spirits of ancestors into silk garments. Higher-order monks wear living moths directly, maintaining them through constant sub-vocalized mantras and bark-dust.

title: The Arrowshot Woman
topic_desc: The Arrowshot Woman is an anonymous work recounting a humorous urban legend set in the Elsweyr city-state of Riverhold. The narrator insists on the truth of a story heard from a friend of a witness. In the tale, a traveler named Terron encounters a woman in a locked carriage who believes she has been shot in the head and is holding her brains in. A healer and knight force open the carriage door, only to discover that an exploding jar of barley dough, propelled by the summer heat, had struck the woman; she had mistaken the dough for her own brains. The work exemplifies the circulation of farcical, secondhand anecdotes across Tamriel.
topic_desc_basic: The Arrowshot Woman is an anonymous book recounting a popular urban legend. Set in the Elsweyr city-state of Riverhold, the humorous tale describes a woman who mistakes an exploding jar of barley dough for an arrow wound, believing she is holding her own brains in.

title: The Assassination of Pelagius I
topic_desc: A scholarly work by Horatio Gargonath examining the unresolved murder of Emperor Pelagius I at the Temple of the One. The book outlines Pelagius's brief three-year reign following Tiber Septim's death and confirms the Dark Brotherhood as the assassins. Gargonath surveys the enduring mystery of who hired them, noting theories ranging from Daedric cultists to Pelagius's cousin Kintyra, who succeeded him as she was his heir. The author includes a pilgrim's firsthand account of a black-clad assassin in the temple that night and recounts popular rumors of a beggar who vanished after claiming to know the truth. The work ultimately underscores that the patron behind the assassination remains unidentified.
topic_desc_basic: A book by Horatio Gargonath investigating the unsolved assassination of Emperor Pelagius I. It confirms the Dark Brotherhood carried out the killing at the Temple of the One but explores why the client who hired them remains unknown.

title: The Asylum Ball
topic_desc: Waughin Jarth's work recounts an apocryphal family story concerning the mad Emperor Pelagius III. After learning that commoners had come to gawk at him, Pelagius arranged a grand ball at his asylum in Torval. Empress Regent Katariah financed the lavish preparations, but the Emperor's guest list—filtered through advisors who distinguished the living, the dead, and the imaginary—ensured no one attended. The Emperor sat alone for hours while an orchestra played to an empty room before suffering a severe breakdown. He was subsequently transferred to a secure facility in Black Marsh, where he died shortly after. Years later, a warder clearing the quarters of a kleptomaniac duchess discovered hidden stacks of the ball's engraved invitations, signed in the Emperor's handwriting, suggesting the invitations were stolen before they could be delivered. The tale illustrates the tragic intersection of Imperial dignity and Pelagius's profound madness.
topic_desc_basic: A book by Waughin Jarth recounting an apocryphal tale of the mad Emperor Pelagius III throwing a lavish ball at his asylum in Torval. No guests attended, and the event ended in the Emperor's severe breakdown.

title: The Battle of Sancre Tor
topic_desc: This historical account details General Talos's 2E 852 winter assault on Sancre Tor, where allied Nord and Breton forces occupied the impregnable Jerall Mountain citadel. Facing a small, ill-supplied Cyrodilic army, the defenders sallied forth, expecting an easy victory. However, Talos had left a weak force as a diversion and scaled the supposedly unscalable rear heights. A Breton turncoat sorcerer reportedly revealed a hidden trail and the secret of the citadel's illusory lake entrance. Talos captured the Nord-Breton leadership, compelling surrender. The Nords, distrustful of their Breton commanders, swore loyalty to Talos; the Breton battlemages were executed. This victory shattered the invasion, swelled Talos's army with hardened Nord veterans, and proved crucial for consolidating the Empire. The author credits Talos's resolve to a divine vision of the Amulet of Kings but insists this does not diminish admiration for his tactical genius against impossible odds.
topic_desc_basic: A historical work recounting General Talos's 2E 852 victory at Sancre Tor. It describes how Talos used a diversion and a hidden trail to capture the impregnable mountain citadel from its Nord-Breton defenders, a triumph that provided veteran troops for his future campaigns.

title: The Belharzareta I
topic_desc: The opening volume of a biographical work recounting the early life of Belharza, son of blessed Al-Esh. It describes his birth as the unhappy product of a convenient marriage and his removal to Skyrim at his Nord warlord father's request. Rather than earning martial honor, Belharza spends eight isolated years in a cold fortress, kept hidden as a potential claimant to the Ruby Throne. The narrative emphasizes his ignorance of his royal Cyrodiilic blood, his dreams of bleached towers and a faceless, glowing woman, and his father's cruel lies that his mother was a camp follower, extinguishing the boy's belief in his heritage and resigning him to a thane's daughter in the marshes of Hjaal.
topic_desc_basic: A historical account of Belharza, son of Al-Esh, covering his childhood. It relates how his Nord father took him to Skyrim and kept him isolated in a fortress, hiding his imperial royal blood and lying about his mother to prevent him from claiming the Ruby Throne.

title: The Belharzareta II
topic_desc: The Belharzareta II is the second volume of a legendary account chronicling the life of Belharza, the Man-Bull of early Alessian history. This installment depicts Belharza's youth as a captive of a Nord warlord. On his ninth name-day, Belharza demands freedom, enraging his captor. Before the warlord can execute him, Morihaus intervenes, slaying the Nord. Though Morihaus acknowledges Belharza is not his own son, he recognizes the boy's royal Alessian heritage and grants him bull's horns, transforming him into the Man-Bull. Morihaus then directs Belharza to seek his half-siblings in the high places of Ald Cyrod to claim his birthright. The narrative serves as a foundational myth explaining Belharza's taurine aspect and his rise as a leader of the early Alessian order.
topic_desc_basic: The second volume of the Belharzareta, a legendary account of Belharza the Man-Bull. It tells of his youth as a captive of a Nord warlord and his liberation by Morihaus, who grants him bull's horns and urges him to claim his Alessian birthright.

title: The Belharzareta III
topic_desc: The Belharzareta III is the third volume of a biographical work chronicling the life of Belharza, the Man-Bull and son of Morihaus. This installment covers his journey through the Colovian highlands, where he visited and secured the fealty of sixteen mountain clans, training them into a legion at the site later known as Sancre Tor. It then recounts his march on the Imperial City at age twenty-three to confront three rival pretenders who had divided the capital after Alessia's death. Rather than a direct assault, Belharza lured his enemies into a trap under White-Gold Tower and defeated all three in single combat, claiming the throne with the Chim-el Adabal. The narrative presents Belharza as a cunning unifier despite his self-admitted lack of wit, emphasizing his martial legitimacy and divine right as Alessia's heir.
topic_desc_basic: The Belharzareta III is a historical account of Belharza the Man-Bull's rise to power, detailing his unification of the Colovian mountain clans and his defeat of three rival pretenders to claim the Imperial City and the throne of Alessia.

title: The Belharzareta IV
topic_desc: The Belharzareta IV is the fourth volume of a historical chronicle treating the reign of Belharza, the Man-Bull king of Cyrodiil and successor to Al-Esh. The narrative portrays Belharza as a warrior-king who refused marriage, declaring himself wedded to the empire itself, knowing that taking a wife would cost him the Amulet of Kings and the Ruby Throne. The text details the pressures he faced from tribal wise women, western warlords, and courtiers urging him to restore a natural order, and his administrative labors: integrating Colovian city-states, managing Ayleid vassals, and defending against external threats from western elves and northern men. The volume also highlights his intimate partnership with the battlemage Hathna, a Nibenese tribesman, and the public's tolerant reception of rumors surrounding their bond. The work offers a romanticized but politically detailed portrait of early Cyrodiilic statecraft.
topic_desc_basic: The Belharzareta IV chronicles the reign of Belharza, the Man-Bull king of early Cyrodiil and successor to Al-Esh. The volume recounts his refusal to take a wife, declaring the empire itself his bride, and the resulting tensions with vassals who urged him to restore what they considered the natural order of rule.

title: The Belharzareta V
topic_desc: The fifth volume of The Belharzareta, subtitled Belharza the Godmaker, chronicles the latter reign of the Emperor Belharza. It recounts the assassination of his trusted advisor Hathna by Ayleid sorcery, Belharza's subsequent descent into wrath and despair, and the near-collapse of the Alessian Empire. The work details how the Imga prophet Marukh roused the grieving Man-Bull with sermons on the One and the inherent wickedness of mer, leading Belharza to embrace the Marukhati faith. The volume culminates with Belharza's dramatic proclamation that Cyrodiil's next ruler should be determined by Virtue rather than blood, an act that formally intertwines imperial succession with Marukhati doctrine and signals the rising influence of the Selective.
topic_desc_basic: A historical account covering the later reign of the Emperor Belharza, detailing his grief over the murder of his advisor Hathna, his embrace of the Imga prophet Marukh, and his decree that imperial succession be determined by Virtue rather than lineage.

title: The Bird-Goblins
topic_desc: The Bird-Goblins is a song warning of fearsome creatures bearing both goblin and avian traits. The verses describe them as tall, pale-faced, clever, and cruel, with feathers and claws, dwelling among trees and underground. The song distinguishes these beings from common green goblins of the sewers, calling them Sons of Hadhuul. Its later verses reference Colovia and the Wild Elves of ald-Cyrod, casting the Bird-Goblins as a persistent presence in the region. The song serves as a cautionary verse, urging listeners to flee upon sighting one. The identity of Hadhuul and the precise nature of the Bird-Goblins remain matters of regional folklore rather than documented natural history.
topic_desc_basic: The Bird-Goblins is a song warning of fearsome creatures with goblin and bird-like features—tall, pale-faced, feathered, and clawed. The verses distinguish them from common sewer goblins, calling them Sons of Hadhuul, and associate them with Colovia and the Wild Elves of ald-Cyrod. The song urges listeners to make haste upon sighting one.

title: The Blessed Life of St. Reman
topic_desc: A hagiographic account of the Reman dynasty, covering the death of Reman Cyrodiil and the miraculous rise of Reman II. It relates that after Reman I was interred in the Imperial City, the Akaviri Potentate Tsamien-Varyel submitted to the Elder Council and the Ruby Throne. The Divines then sent the aged Sed-Yenna an egg of Reman's seed, but its loss in the Niben heralded eighteen years of civil war. A river-dragon later delivered the infant Reman II to the farmer Theiden, who raised him across war-torn Nibenay. Compelled by ancestral calling, Reman II journeyed to the Imperial City, was recognized by the Potentate, and within half a year forcibly reunified the two Cyrodiils from Sutch to Gemha.
topic_desc_basic: A hagiographic work recounting the death of Emperor Reman Cyrodiil and the miraculous birth and rise of Reman II, who reunified the two Cyrodiils after an eighteen-year civil war.

record_links.display_name: The Blessed Life of St. Reman

title: The Blessings of Sheogorath
topic_desc: A devotional text honoring Sheogorath, composed as a litany of thirteen blessings. The work reframes states of mental affliction and compulsion as sacred gifts, maintaining that without the Madgod, thought would be rigid and emotion transitory. It bestows blessing upon the mad, phobic, obsessed, addicted, murderous, fire-loving, artistic, musical, sleepless, paranoid, visionary, and pain-loving, assigning each a redemptive virtue. The litany concludes by venerating Sheogorath himself, who deceives the foolish, punishes the wrongdoer, tortures the unmindful, and yet loves the imperfect. The text serves as significant evidence of how the Prince's followers theologize madness, recasting suffering and instability as proof of divine favor.
topic_desc_basic: A devotional text listing thirteen blessings that honor Sheogorath. It treats madness, obsession, and compulsion as sacred gifts from the Madgod, concluding with praise for his deceit, punishment, and love of imperfection.

title: The Blood-Money Siege
topic_desc: A Colovian legendary account recounting how Rein Manellis, the Beggar-King of Brumath, lost his siege-wealth from Kvatch in the river Scahat. Unable to repay his debt to Heimth, the Coin-King of Skingrad, Rein Manellis deceived him into besieging Chorral for the supposed stolen gold. The conflict culminated in a champion's duel beneath Chorral's sacred oak, where Skingrad's champion Batûn Half-Giant was defeated by Hermwnthe-of-Thistles but secretly poisoned the tree with the blood of Artheim the King Betrayed—one of the Twelve Dishonorable Acts by a Half-Man for an otherwise virtuous Colovian ruler. The siege ended in defeat and tribute for the aggressors, and Chorral's subsequent prosperity was cut short by the delayed Nibeth poison. The tale serves as a moral exemplar on greed, deception, and Colovian martial virtue.
topic_desc_basic: A Colovian legendary tale about the Beggar-King of Brumath who tricked the King of Skingrad into besieging Chorral over a disputed debt, ending in defeat and the secret poisoning of Chorral's sacred oak.

title: The Book of Lamentations
topic_desc: A compilation of mourning verses and inscriptions drawn from across Tamriel's cultures. It includes the Lament for Nerevar, an inscription at a Nord Tongue's grave, a Redguard proverb on death and renewal, a Chimeri lament for failing Veloth's path, an Ashlander's despair after Peakstar's failure and plea for the Nerevarine, and a Khajiit mother's farewell to a dying kitten. The work gathers expressions of grief, cultural loss, and mortality into a single meditation on lamentation.
topic_desc_basic: A collection of mourning verses and inscriptions from various Tamrielic cultures, including laments for Nerevar and Veloth, an Ashlander's plea for the Nerevarine, and other expressions of grief and loss.

title: The Cabin in the Woods
topic_desc: A ghost story attributed to Mogen Son of Molag, chronicling a soldier's harrowing journey through a pine forest. Over three nights, the soldier is stalked by a sobbing, axe-wielding ghostly woman. After barricading himself in an abandoned cabin, he destroys the apparition with a firebolt scroll, only to hear the sobbing resume as he finally exits the woods. The tale serves as a chilling reminder that some hauntings cannot be permanently laid to rest.
topic_desc_basic: A ghost story by Mogen Son of Molag about a soldier who encounters a sobbing, axe-wielding spirit while traveling through a pine forest.

title: The Cavern Door
topic_desc: An adventure tale of unknown authorship recounting the experiences of a man named Haldin. While preparing to enter a cavern, Haldin is ambushed by Vermai—sensory-driven creatures with poor eyesight but keen olfactory hunting. The narrative details his sequential use of a paralysis scroll, a frost-enchanted blade, a silver dagger, and a bonemold bow to survive the encounter, culminating in a desperate flight across grasslands to a lake where the Vermai's aversion to water proves decisive. Haldin's limited knowledge of the creatures derives secondhand from his brother Heldin, a seasoned adventurer. The tale emphasizes practical monster lore—Vermai scent-based tracking and water hostility—alongside the expendable nature of scroll magic and the volatile behavior of enchantments released into water. The work circulates in collections across eastern Morrowind, including Telvanni and Imperial settlements.
topic_desc_basic: An adventure tale of unknown authorship following a man named Haldin, who is ambushed by Vermai creatures near a cavern entrance. The story recounts his survival through magic scrolls, enchanted weapons, and a desperate flight to water, which the Vermai despise. The narrative conveys practical lore about Vermai behavior and the perils of adventuring.

title: The Collected Ysmritis
topic_desc: A compilation of five tales concerning the Ysmirs, or Dragons of the North—heroic Nords exalted by Shor. The work observes that these mythic figures share a great thirst for elf-killing, though whether the title precedes the slaughter or vice-versa remains ambiguous. Unlike Cyrodiilic saints or Dunmer ancestors, the Ysmiris drift timelessly, untethered from causality. The collection includes excerpts from the Songs of the Return exalting Ysgramor and his axe Wuuthrad; an oar-song of the reaver Bomundl and his unclaimed hoard; the seventy-six oaths sworn upon High King Harald Hairy-Breeks' breeches; a song of High King Wulfharth, whose thu'um drove the Alessians from Skyrim and who became Shor's literal tongue; and a neo-Nordic song of Talos, the dragon-headed scion who shattered the elven bastions of Morrowind and the Aldmeri Dominion.
topic_desc_basic: A collection of tales about the Ysmirs, or Dragons of the North—heroic Nords exalted by the dead god Shor. The Ysmiris are famous for their great success at elf-killing, and include legendary figures such as Ysgramor, High King Wulfharth, and Tiber Septim.

title: The Coronation of Eplear
topic_desc: Harman Maurus's collated translation of annotations from the Song of Eplear, a lengthy First Era Bosmeri epic amalgamating older poems. The Song chronicles King Eplear's unification of the Bosmer tribes—a seminal military feat founding the Camoran Dynasty and Valenwood—yet curiously remains less renowned than lesser Bosmeri epics. The verse resists direct translation; Maurus instead renders the surrounding scholarly notes. This section details Eplear's coronation atop the walking graht-oak Falinesti. Amid heavy poetic imagery and probable exaggeration, the account describes Boiche tribes and other ancient peoples—giants, bird-men, satyrs, centaurs—offering gifts which Eplear redistributes to all Bosmer. Y'ffre's priests crown him with a golden ape skull, after which he slays a great sky-bird to forge a new bow. Despite its embellishments, the work remains a vital, if enigmatic, window into early First Era Valenwood.
topic_desc_basic: A translation of annotations from the Song of Eplear, a First Era Bosmeri epic. Compiled by Harman Maurus, it details the coronation of King Eplear, who unified the Bosmer tribes to found the Camoran Dynasty and the kingdom of Valenwood.

title: The Dangers of Reach-Magicks
topic_desc: A treatise by Edwistair Admand examining the ritualistic spellcraft of the Reachmen. Admand argues that Reach-Magic, which likely incorporates Orcish shamanism and Direnni spellcraft, is fundamentally reckless and dangerous. He describes a practice where casters seal prepared spells internally—sometimes for years—before releasing them, causing severe harm to the host. He also attributes environmental blights and curses to Reach-Magic, contrasting its uncontrolled manipulation of forces with the Mages Guild's sanctioned methods. Rejecting comparisons to Mysticism, Admand contends that while Mysticism studies magicks gone wrong, Reach-Magic relies on magicks gone horribly right. He notes Empress Morihatha Septim outlawed the practice, ultimately dismissing it as hazardous and unreliable.
topic_desc_basic: A treatise by Edwistair Admand warning against the ritualistic spellcraft of the Reachmen. It describes their practice of internally sealing spells for later release and blames their uncontrolled magicks for environmental blights, arguing the craft is dangerously harmful to both caster and surroundings.

title: The Danstrar Serpent
topic_desc: A skaldic epic recounting the founding of the Corpse-Hold of Danstrar. It chronicles King Bergryf of Gorvik, a Nord of the Sightless clan bearing a third eye, who slew the great water-serpent Thirst during the reign of High King Snorik. After his navigator Jhugyr consulted sea-hags and learned the beast was a child of Orkey that could be killed by skinning, Bergryf sacrificed five waves of his fleet to breach its armor. A vajrar of Tongues then Shouted the serpent ashore, where the common folk butchered it for meat. Bergryf declared the creature's fallen skull Danstrar, establishing his new kingdom on the Northshore.
topic_desc_basic: A bardic song recounting how King Bergryf of Gorvik slew the water-serpent Thirst and founded the Corpse-Hold of Danstrar from the beast's skull on the Northshore.

title: The Death of Artheim
topic_desc: A Colovian mythic-historical narrative recounting the treacherous death of King Artheim of Kvatch and the ensuing cycle of vengeance. The work exemplifies traditional Colovian storytelling, framing regional history through heroic lineage and martial pride while portraying the Nibenease as deceitful outsiders who wield secret poisons and value royal blood for their rituals. The tale catalogs the Forty-Eight Futile Charges of the Inner City and the Eight Inconclusive Pilgrimages to Sancre Tor, embedding cultural memory of Colovian military futility and inter-kingdom blood feud. Its extensive roll of assembled heroes and strange beings reflects the mythic depth of the Colovian tradition, culminating in the mustering of a great siege against Kvatch.
topic_desc_basic: A Colovian mythic narrative about King Artheim of Kvatch, who is treacherously slain by Rein Manellis at the Imperial City. The tale details the ensuing blood feud and the mustering of a great host of heroes to besiege Kvatch.

title: The Divadamakalluh
topic_desc: An abridged Yokudan epic recounting the trial and restoration of the hero Divad. Cursed by swine-demons at the siege of Usthûk, Divad wanders the Alik'r and endures a three-day ordeal where the interventions of Morwha, Zeht, and Tava sustain him while he purges both plague and venom through inner resolve. Ruptga proclaims him Emperor, and Divad returns to slay the usurper Ko-okso and reclaim his spear. The work explores Yokudan ideals of warrior ferocity and royal dignity, and Divad's emergence as the Emperor Unknowable and Lord of the North Wave.
topic_desc_basic: An abridged Yokudan epic about the hero Divad, who is cursed by swine-demons at Usthûk, endures a three-day ordeal in the desert, and emerges healed through inner resolve. Ruptga proclaims him Emperor, and he returns to defeat the usurper Ko-okso.

title: The Dreadful Theft
topic_desc: The Dreadful Theft of the Sun's Dusk Ale is a memoir by the Breton Rascien Wickersly recounting his time in the Valenwood city of Greenheart. The work details a dispute between the Bosmer brewer Foroch and a band of Imga led by the self-styled Duke Boff over stolen kegs of Sun's Dusk ale. Wickersly mediates the conflict, discovering that the Imga find the prized brew repulsive while Bosmer consider it exquisite. He leverages this sensory divide to negotiate the ale's return, convincing Foroch to formally acknowledge the theft and grant the Imga unlimited access to a beverage they despise. The narrative provides insight into Valenwood's inter-species tensions, the unusual brewing methods permitted under the Green Pact, and the cultural gulf separating Bosmer and Imga.
topic_desc_basic: A book by the Breton Rascien Wickersly about mediating a dispute between a Bosmer brewer and Imga over stolen ale in Valenwood.

title: The Dwarven Firmament
topic_desc: A scholarly work by Amiel Callonus introducing Dwemer astronomy, serving as a companion to Ffoulke's Firmament. The author surveys ruins from Stros M'Kai to the Telvanni Isles, noting that while the Dwemer precisely tracked stellar movements, much of their knowledge is lost. Because the Dwemer rejected magic, they reinterpreted the constellations through a technological lens: the Mage became the Mechanist, governing steam power, with charges renamed the Automaton, Warmachine, and Laboratory. Other constellations received distinct forms: the Steed appears as a scarab beetle, possibly reflecting Rourken mechanical constructs; the Warrior wears Dwemer armor; the Thief holds lockpicks and a key; and the Shadow is a wraith-like figure with a runic eye. The Serpent remained visually unchanged but was always listed separately. Ongoing research continues into the constellation runes, including an untranscribed Serpent rune.
topic_desc_basic: A book by Amiel Callonus explaining Dwemer astronomy. It details how the Dwemer reinterpreted the thirteen constellations through a technological rather than magical framework, renaming the Mage as the Mechanist and depicting the Steed as a scarab beetle.

title: The Eastern Quarantine
topic_desc: A recent historical treatise by Caius Invictus examining the Imperial quarantine of Vvardenfell in 3E 426. The work traces the crisis to a Grand Council dispute over flin import tariffs, which exacerbated tensions between the pro-Imperial Hlaalu and the traditionalist Redoran. A subsequent tax revolt in Balmora required Legion intervention, and a series of unsolved public murders of Imperial and Hlaalu figures fueled fears of a broader conspiracy. In response, Legion District Commander Varus Vanitius ordered a sweeping quarantine and punitive expedition across Vvardenfell. Invictus details how this overreach collapsed under logistical impossibility, lack of reinforcement from the Lord Marshall, and unified opposition from House Hlaalu, the Tribunal Temple, and the East Empire Company. The failed quarantine damaged the Legion's local standing, isolated Vanitius politically, and raised serious doubts about Imperial capacity to manage the district's worsening blight crisis.
topic_desc_basic: A historical work by Caius Invictus detailing the failed Imperial quarantine of Vvardenfell in 3E 426. Triggered by trade disputes, a Balmora tax riot, and unsolved murders of Imperial and Hlaalu figures, Legion Commander Varus Vanitius ordered a heavy-handed island-wide lockdown. The quarantine collapsed due to poor logistics and opposition from Dunmer factions and the East Empire Company, ultimately weakening Imperial authority in the district.

title: The Ebon Arm
topic_desc: A devotional narrative by Witten Rol depicting Reymon Ebonarm, the God of War, intervening in a bloody but baseless conflict. The work describes Ebonarm's dramatic arrival on the battlefield in ebony armor, riding his golden stallion War Master and accompanied by two ravens. His fused ebony blade and arm, wounds from primordial battles, command immediate awe. By compelling both warring leaders to hear each other's grievances, Ebonarm reveals the war's futility without favoring either side, securing a peaceful resolution. The text serves as a significant theological account of Ebonarm's role as a protector of warriors and a peacemaker, emphasizing his capacity to end strife honorably.
topic_desc_basic: A book by Witten Rol recounting the appearance of Reymon Ebonarm, the God of War, on a battlefield. The narrative describes how Ebonarm's imposing presence and fused ebony blade compel two warring factions to lay down their arms after realizing their conflict is baseless, portraying him as both a warrior's protector and a bringer of peace.

title: The Epic of the Grey Falcon
topic_desc: A Second Era tale of survival recovered and translated by Royal Archaeologist Anido Jhone from an ancient tome, likely originating after the Knahaten Flu. It recounts the destruction of the Summerset Isle warship Grey Falcon by a mage-captained pirate vessel. Only the sailor Darik Seaspit and the Khajiit mercenary Helnor Snarlsbane escape in a lifeboat, only to discover the food stores were removed by a navy inspector. Faced with starvation, the two agree that cannibalism is the only means of survival for one to reach port. Six weeks later, Helnor alone arrives at Corwich in High Rock. Brought before an inquest, he explains their mutual decision and reveals that he survived because Darik was a vegetarian. Jhone admits to an informal translation, emphasizing the story's universal message over rigid fidelity.
topic_desc_basic: A Second Era tale translated by Royal Archaeologist Anido Jhone. It recounts the destruction of the Summerset warship Grey Falcon by pirates and the ordeal of two survivors adrift without food, culminating in a darkly humorous inquest in High Rock over how the sole survivor, a Khajiit mercenary, resorted to cannibalism to live.

record_links.display_name: The Epic of the Grey Falcon

title: The Faerie
topic_desc: A scholarly work by Szun Triop examining the diverse beings collectively called Faerie, who have inhabited Tamriel since before recorded history. The text surveys their many names—Fey, Illyadi, Sprites, Pixies, and Sylphim—and their fundamentally unpredictable natures. Its central focus is the Faerie Chain theory proposed by the scholar Ahrtabazus at the Crystal Tower, which arranges Fey variants hierarchically from minor glimmering sparks like Pixies and Whilloki to godlike beings such as Gheateus and Sygria, with sentient landscape features and humanoids in between. Ahrtabazus controversially placed elves on this chain, provoking fierce opposition, yet his framework has since gained wider acceptance in modified form. Triop notes that the chain does not imply command structure, as Faerie act on whim rather than higher purpose, and cautions that the theory rests on coincidental evidence and may be flawed.
topic_desc_basic: A book by Szun Triop discussing the various types of Faerie and their unpredictable natures. It is best known for presenting Ahrtabazus's Faerie Chain theory, which arranges Fey beings hierarchically from minor sprites to godlike entities and controversially includes elves within this order.

title: The Failure of the Empire
topic_desc: A polemical tract arguing that the Septim Empire is in terminal decline and must be overthrown. The anonymous author, claiming insider experience, asserts that the Empire has rotted since Tiber Septim's death under weak rulers, culminating in Uriel Septim VII. The work condemns Imperial corruption, the Jagar Tharn interregnum, Dunmer slavery, and the Blades as a repressive spy network, while accusing the Legions of thuggery and civilian murder. Citing riots in Cyrodiil as proof of failure, the author urges citizens to overthrow the Empire and seize control of Tamriel themselves.
topic_desc_basic: A seditious book arguing that the Septim Empire is collapsing from corruption and weak leadership, and urging citizens to overthrow it.

title: The Fall of the Usurper
topic_desc: Palaux Illthre's historical treatise examines Baron Othrok of Dwynnen's role in the Camoran Usurper's defeat at the Battle of Firewaves in 3E 267. The work critically assesses why High Rock hesitated to resist the invasion: the Iliac Bay's major powers lacked capable leadership, the so-called Eight Traitors secretly allied with the Usurper, and the Breton populace initially sympathized with the conqueror due to their disdain for the Nord Emperor Cephorus II. Illthre argues that Othrok and allied rulers of Ykalon, Phrygias, and Kambria shifted this perception by exposing the Usurper's atrocities, enabling the formation of a massive coastal navy. The author also demystifies the Usurper's legendary all-daedric horde, proposing it was largely composed of conquered Redguards and Wood Elves, and thoughtfully weighs the interplay of regional politics, weather, and divine mythos in the victory.
topic_desc_basic: A scholarly history by Palaux Illthre analyzing Baron Othrok of Dwynnen's role in defeating the Camoran Usurper in 3E 267. It examines High Rock's delayed resistance, the political impact of Emperor Cephorus II's Nord heritage on Breton loyalties, and the formation of the coalition that won the Battle of Firewaves.

title: The Fate of House Dwemer
topic_desc: A work extolling the destruction of House Dwemer at the Battle of Red Mountain. The author presents Dwemer ruins and salvaged war trophies—scavenged from destroyed Dwemeri homunculi—as proof of divine retribution against heresy. The text frames their annihilation as the inevitable fate of unbelievers and a testament to the enduring glory and faith of the Dunmer people, guided by their ancestors and the Tribunal. It serves as a pious reminder of orthodox victory rather than a historical inquiry into the Dwemer disappearance.
topic_desc_basic: A work presenting the destruction of House Dwemer at the Battle of Red Mountain as divine retribution against heretics, using salvaged war trophies as evidence of orthodox Dunmer triumph.

title: The Fate of the Snow Elves
topic_desc: A scholarly work by the Nord pilgrim Keviskar, examining the absence of any physical trace of Snow Elf civilization. After twenty years of travel and research yielded no ruins, artifacts, or scrolls, Keviskar dismisses prevailing theories—that Snow Elf remnants lie on unreachable mountain peaks, deep within ice caverns, or that Rieklings are their degenerate descendants. He argues instead that Nord ancestors systematically destroyed Snow Elf cities, settlements, and cultural artifacts millennia ago, erasing them so thoroughly that only folklore and children's songs survive. The text challenges Nord selective historiography, which celebrates ancestral conquests while ignoring the cultures they obliterated.
topic_desc_basic: A book by the Nord pilgrim Keviskar investigating why no physical evidence of Snow Elf civilization survives. He concludes that Nord ancestors destroyed their cities and culture so completely that only folklore remains.

record_links.display_name: The Fate of the Snow Elves

title: The Fifth Ami-El
topic_desc: The Fifth Ami-El is the concluding volume of a mythic cycle recounting the deeds of Amet, a horned figure who reclaims the Empire of Cyrod from the minotaur usurper Asterion. The narrative follows Amet eastward to the Valley of Horns, where minotaurs hold court under Asterion's rule. Armed with a knife fashioned from her own severed horn, Amet slays the gate-guard Tull-Am, disguises herself in his skin, and confronts Asterion, who claims invulnerability through the blood of Esha. She kills him with the horn-knife—kin-bone to Asterion—and the minotaurs, recognizing Empire in Amet, disperse into the wilds and forget the tongues of men. Amet is then crowned Emperor Ami-El the One-Horned in the City of Cyrod, ruling for over a century. The work frames the transfer of imperial authority from beast to man as both violent and divinely sanctioned.
topic_desc_basic: The Fifth Ami-El is the final volume of a legendary cycle about Amet, a horned figure who slays the minotaur usurper Asterion and reclaims the Empire of Cyrod. Crowned Emperor Ami-El the One-Horned, she rules for over a century. The tale concerns the violent transfer of imperial power from minotaurs to men.

title: The First Ami-El
topic_desc: A surviving but historically dubious account of Ami-El, Cyrodiil's forgotten third Emperor, valued primarily as a curiosity of Nibenese thinking. The text recounts the birth of the horned child Amet to Emperor Belharza and his Nibenese bride Llesa, who died when the divine blood of Morihaus manifested as bull horns in the womb. Grieving, Belharza cast the child into a lake rather than bear the omen of blood; the river carried the infant to humble Nibenese fisher-folk who raised her as Amet. The work reflects a distinctly Nibenese cultural lens on the early First Empire, emphasizing river piety and divine manifestation, though its claims are contested and contradicted by other sources.
topic_desc_basic: A dubious but surviving account of Ami-El, Cyrodiil's forgotten third Emperor. The text narrates the birth and river-exile of the horned child Amet, daughter of Emperor Belharza, and is valued mainly as a curiosity of Nibenese thought rather than reliable history.

title: The Formalities of Mirth
topic_desc: The Formalities of Mirth, written by Draler Ilvi, examines laughter from a rigid Dunmer perspective, treating public mirth as a vulgar outlander custom and an act of impiety linked to the House of Troubles—associating Molag Bal, Sheogorath, Malacath, and Mehrunes Dagon with mirth, mania, ridicule, and disorder. Ilvi argues that while gravity unites the Dunmer, diplomatic necessity sometimes requires participating in foreign levity. To mitigate this spiritual transgression, he prescribes preemptive penitence through prayer to Saint Aralor and financial amends to the Temple proportional to the duration and frequency of the laughter. He concludes that such controlled impiety remains a practical diplomatic tool, paraphrasing the warrior poet's pragmatic view of deceptive courtesy.
topic_desc_basic: The Formalities of Mirth by Draler Ilvi is a Dunmer treatise that regards public laughter as vulgar and impious, associating it with the House of Troubles, while offering spiritual precautions for Dunmer who must engage in the custom for diplomatic purposes.

title: The Four's Homily
topic_desc: The Four's Homily, also known as The Hungry Nix-Hound, is an Ashlands fable recounting a nix-hound's ascent of a barren hill to reach succulent ash yams. Four companions attempt the climb, but each fails due to a fundamental flaw: the guar succumbs to laziness, the scrib to rigid clinging, and the cliffracer to flighty rootlessness. Only the nix-hound succeeds, overcoming hunger through stoicism, unstable slopes through quickness and cleverness, and fierce winds through the wisdom of forging its own footholds. The homily serves as an allegorical justification for the nix-hound's survival traits while explaining the behaviors of other Ashlands creatures—the alit's scavenging, the cliffracer's wandering, and the scrib's reclusive nature—as the consequences of their failures.
topic_desc_basic: The Four's Homily, also called The Hungry Nix-Hound, is an Ashlands fable about a nix-hound climbing a hill for ash yams. It explains the nix-hound's success through stoicism, quickness, cleverness, and wisdom, while attributing the behaviors of other creatures—such as the alit's scavenging and the cliffracer's wandering—to their failures.

title: The Fourth Ami-El
topic_desc: The fourth volume of the Ami-El series, this work recounts the episode of the Dmath, an otherworldly creature appearing as a loathsome ape, which enters the chamber of the slumbering Emperor Amet. The Dmath warns Amet of his impending death fighting the undefeated Asterion the White and offers aid in exchange for the hearts of his descendants to instruct them. Claiming to speak the word of Aleshut, the beast promises that Amet's empire will encompass the world if granted the Emperor's voice. Upon demanding proof, Amet receives a prophetic song hailing Ami-El and listing the realms and cities of Cyrod, including Sancre Tor and eight city islands, foretelling a reign of silk, iron, and moth-light, but one built upon kindred blood and partnership with the beast.
topic_desc_basic: The fourth volume of the Ami-El series, recounting the encounter between Emperor Amet and an otherworldly ape-like creature called a Dmath, who offers the Emperor otherworldly aid and prophesies a vast Cyrodic dominion in exchange for instructing his descendants.

title: The Friend of Giants
topic_desc: An old Nord tale recounting the mythic kinship between men and giants in Atmora under Shor, Kyne, and Shor's brother Hirtyk-Tsun, the Bear. Hirtyk-Tsun taught men to hunt for glory, but some men turned against giants, slaying them as beasts. This first breaking of kinship was partially mended through sacrifice and mutual mercy, and giants fought alongside Shor at the last great battle against elven demons. After Shor's death, further betrayals drove Hirtyk-Tsun to abandon fickle men and dwell among the giants, who venerate him still. The accompanying translator's note flags the text as unusual for identifying Tsun as Shor's brother, for suggesting Tsun did not die alongside Shor, and for the name Hirtyk-Tsun, which may simply mean Tsun the Bear but bears a striking resemblance to the hunting god Hircine of High Rock.
topic_desc_basic: An old Nord tale about the ancient kinship between men and giants in Atmora. It tells of Hirtyk-Tsun, brother of Shor, who taught men to hunt for glory but was grieved when some men turned against giants. The story explains the first breaking of that kinship and Tsun's eventual departure to live among the giants.

title: The Gift Of Consolation
topic_desc: An ancient, brittle scroll preserving a poem attributed to Vivec. The verse addresses an unnamed, absent recipient, declaring the transformation of their word into a symbol for the dead, their sword into a quill and thought, and their love into a defense against the horizon. Scholars identify this final declaration as an allegorical expression of Vivec's intention to construct the Great Ghostfence, framing the monumental barrier as an act of enduring love and consolation for the lost.
topic_desc_basic: An ancient poem attributed to Vivec. It addresses an absent figure, transforming their word, sword, and love into symbolic forms. Scholars interpret its declaration of love as a defense against the horizon as an allegory for Vivec's intention to build the Great Ghostfence.

title: The Gospel of Saint Aralor
topic_desc: A hagiographical account of Saint Aralor the Penitent, a notorious brigand lord of uncertain lineage who plagued Morrowind's borderlands before the razing of Mournhold. After a mine collapse trapped him and his treacherous followers abandoned him, a female voice—understood as a manifestation of the Tribunal—confronted his despair. She freed him on the condition that he undertake lifelong penance, visiting the holy places of ALMSIVI to work off his sins through visible contrition and suffering. Aralor subsequently shed his worldly possessions and endured lifelong hardship and mockery as a penitent pilgrim. The text emphasizes that the soul is renewed by suffering and the abandonment of worldly things. It concludes with the devotional assertion that his spirit watches over and protects true pilgrims, establishing the work's significance as a Temple text reinforcing the virtues of pilgrimage, penitence, and devotion to the Tribunal.
topic_desc_basic: A Temple text recounting the life of Saint Aralor the Penitent, a former brigand who turned to lifelong pilgrimage and suffering after a divine encounter freed him from a collapsed mine. The work teaches that the soul is renewed through penance and the shedding of worldly goods, and holds that his spirit protects true pilgrims.

title: The Gospel of Saint Delyn
topic_desc: A hagiographic account of Saint Delyn the Wise, depicting his role as a prophet who heralded the coming of the Tribunal and rebuked Azura.
topic_desc_basic: A religious text recounting how the mystic Delyn rejected Azura after the Battle of Red Mountain and became a prophet of ALMSIVI.

title: The Gospel of Saint Felms
topic_desc: A hagiographic account of Saint Felms the Bold, detailing his miraculous transformation from a voiceless standard-bearer into an instrument of ALMSIVI's wrath against the Nord occupation of Resdayn.
topic_desc_basic: A religious text recounting the story of Saint Felms the Bold, a voiceless youth who became a champion of the Tribunal and drove the Nords from Resdayn.

title: The Gospel of Saint Llothis
topic_desc: The Gospel of Saint Llothis recounts the post-Red Mountain mission of Llothis the Pious, a veteran of the First Council who served alongside the Tribunal before their apotheosis. Sent by ALMSIVI to restore order to Morrowind, Llothis discovers his home village subjugated by Naheb, a false mystic claiming a divine mandate from Seht. Llothis challenges Naheb to a contest of prayer, exposing his sorcery and defeating him through genuine Tribunal blessing rather than arcane artifice. Refusing lordship, Llothis ordains a truthful local as priestess and departs, dedicating his life to founding temples and establishing faithful clergy across Morrowind to preserve authentic Tribunal worship.
topic_desc_basic: The Gospel of Saint Llothis is a Temple text chronicling the deeds of Saint Llothis the Pious. It describes his mission to restore true ALMSIVI worship after the Battle of Red Mountain by defeating the false mystic Naheb and establishing faithful priesthoods across Morrowind.

title: The Gospel of Saint Meris
topic_desc: A hagiographic account of the Dunmer saint Meris, detailing her healing miracles, her devotion to ALMSIVI, and her role in ending a generations-long war between House Ra'Athim and House Oroynyon.
topic_desc_basic: A Tribunal Temple text recounting the life and miracles of Saint Meris the Peacemaker, who ended a war between two Great Houses through healing and devotion to ALMSIVI.

title: The Gospel of Saint Nerevar
topic_desc: The Gospel of Saint Nerevar is a hagiographic account of Nerevar the Captain during the War of the First Council. It depicts the march of Indoril and Redoran armies toward Red Mountain and Nerevar's confrontation with Mephala at Marandus, where the Daedra accepted blood sacrifice from the debauched Lord Hlervu after he drove a pious farmer to suicide. Nerevar slew Hlervu and denounced Mephala and Boethiah for failing the Velothi covenant, prompting Mephala's withdrawal and proclamation of rebirth. The work frames this episode as the moment the old Daedric ways ended, replaced by the coming of ALMSIVI. It concludes with Nerevar's death at Red Mountain, his prophecy of the Tribunal's dawn, and his body being carried to Necrom and restored as a bonewalker through ALMSIVI's divinity, leading to the mass conversion of Houses Indoril and Redoran. The narrative serves as a Temple-sanctioned justification for the Tribunal's supplanting of the Anticipations.
topic_desc_basic: The Gospel of Saint Nerevar is a religious text venerating Nerevar the Captain. It recounts his march to Red Mountain, his denunciation of the Daedra Mephala at Marandus for failing the Velothi, and his death and restoration as a bonewalker by the Tribunal, events that justified the Temple's shift from Daedric worship to ALMSIVI.

title: The Gospel of Saint Olms
topic_desc: A hagiographic account of Saint Olms the Just, detailing his spiritual trial between devotion to Boethiah and loyalty to the Chimer people during the march to Red Mountain.
topic_desc_basic: A Temple text recounting the story of Saint Olms the Just, a Redoran warrior caught between service to Boethiah and devotion to Almalexia during the war against the Dwemer.

title: The Gospel of Saint Rilms
topic_desc: A hagiographic account of Saint Rilms the Barefooted, a Redoran nobleborn mer whose miraculous healing touch was suppressed by her father through Daedrically consecrated shoes. Abducted and raised by the Mephala-worshiping thief Salothas, Rilms eventually reclaimed the enchanted footwear, which compelled her northward to the ruins of her family estate. There, she encountered a suffering girl and surrendered the shoes, embracing barefooted compassion. The gospel reflects on the tension between Tribunal veneration and older Daedric cults, framing Rilms's destiny as a journey from miraculous birth through Daedric manipulation to voluntary renunciation.
topic_desc_basic: A hagiographic work recounting the life of Saint Rilms the Barefooted, a Redoran-born mer whose healing touch was suppressed by enchanted shoes, and who ultimately renounced them to embrace a path of compassion.

title: The Gospel of Saint Roris
topic_desc: A hagiographic account of Saint Roris the Martyr, detailing his capture and execution by Argonians and the miraculous manifestations of the Tribunal's power at his death.
topic_desc_basic: A Temple text recounting the martyrdom of Saint Roris, a Dunmer monk who was captured and mutilated by Argonians in the Arnesian Jungle but whose unwavering faith in ALMSIVI produced miracles that converted countless souls.

title: The Gospel of Saint Seryn
topic_desc: The Gospel of Saint Seryn is a Temple hagiography recounting the life of Seryn the Merciful, a dreugher's daughter born near Veranis shortly after Vivec defeated the Akaviri Horde. Almalexia granted the pious girl the power to absorb others' diseases into her own body and then heal herself. Word of her miracles spread across Morrowind, drawing afflicted pilgrims from all Great Houses. The Temple initially sent a skeptical priest, Orolas, to investigate; after Seryn healed his own hidden affliction, the Temple endorsed her work and directed the incurable to her. Seryn absorbed countless plagues until old age, when she mistakenly touched a corpse brought to her and died. The Temple thereafter received a portion of the mercy the Triunes had formerly granted her. The text venerates self-sacrifice, Tribunal piety, and compassion for the diseased and outcast.
topic_desc_basic: The Gospel of Saint Seryn is a Temple hagiography of Seryn the Merciful, a girl born near Veranis after Vivec's defeat of the Akaviri. Almalexia granted her the power to absorb others' diseases and heal herself, and she spent her life curing the afflicted from across Morrowind until her death in old age.

title: The Gospel of Saint Veloth, v 1
topic_desc: A theological work presenting Saint Veloth's early life and the beginning of the Aldmeri Exodus through a framework of Light and Darkness. It recounts Veloth rejecting his elders' stagnant veneration of ancestral Light, instead looking inward and to the nurturing Shadows to find a path forward. When the champion Trinimac attempts to block Veloth's discovered Door, he falls into it and is swallowed, emerging as a new being—Malacath—who despairs and is dispersed with his followers. Veloth teaches his people circumspection rather than heedless advance, and seizes the wind to carry the faithful over the waters to their new journey. The text frames the Velothi departure as a progression away from lost origin toward self-reliant purpose, guided by inward vision and the lessons of others' mistakes.
topic_desc_basic: A religious text recounting Saint Veloth's rejection of Aldmeri stagnation, the transformation of Trinimac into Malacath, and the beginning of the Velothi Exodus.

record_links.display_name: The Gospel of Saint Veloth, v 1

title: The Gospel of Saint Veloth, v 2
topic_desc: The second volume of a hagiographic work detailing Saint Veloth's exodus, presenting his encounters with obstacles and Mistakes as allegorical Doors and Corners that impart doctrinal lessons. It recounts Veloth overcoming the feathered sorcerers of the marble wheel by conjuring a hearth, dispersing a disorienting fog by looking inward to separate Light from Darkness, and glimpsing new truths at the Door of Resolution. The narrative culminates at the Corner of Termination, where Mehrunes Dagon slays Veloth. In his burial chamber, Veloth recognizes the Daedra and his Ancestors, then inverts the room to step through the Waiting Door. The text frames these events as instructional parables for the Velothi, advocating self-reliance, the application of past wisdom, and forward progression guided by Ancestors and ALMSIVI.
