title: The Grand Alliance I
topic_desc: A historical work by Andreil of Falkreath examining the formation of the Grand Alliance, a coalition of the kingdoms of Solitude, Falkreath, and the Reach that became a dominant political force during the Imperial Simulacrum. The text contrasts the widespread provincial dissolution under Jagar Tharn's treachery with Western Skyrim's relative stability. It attributes the alliance's origins to the childhood fostership and bond between Prince Vorngyd of the Reach and Prince Eyrfin of Solitude, whose friendship resolved longstanding trade disputes between their realms. Andreil notes scholarly debate over whether Tharnite conspiracy simply failed to penetrate Markarth Side's court or if Lady Hania, a cousin of the true Imperial line, actively steered the kingdoms toward unification. The volume also references the assassination of Queen Hellne and catastrophic events elsewhere in Skyrim, which are treated in subsequent volumes.
topic_desc_basic: A historical account by Andreil of Falkreath detailing the formation of the Grand Alliance between the western Skyrim kingdoms of Solitude, Falkreath, and the Reach during the Imperial Simulacrum, a coalition that shielded the region from the era's widespread political collapse.

title: The Grand Alliance II
topic_desc: Andreil of Falkreath's historical work examines the formation of the Grand Alliance between the Nordic kings of Haafinheim, Falkreath, and the Reach prior to the War of the Bend'r-Mahk. Challenging the view that Nordic egos alone provoked the conflict, the author argues that King Bjeld of Falkreath orchestrated the 3E 396 mutual defense pact out of strategic necessity, anticipating inevitable war as Imperial law deteriorated during the Simulacrum. The account details how early cooperation against Reachmen banditry collapsed following cross-border raids, leading to full-scale war. Though initially disastrous for the Nords, the narrative highlights the front-line leadership of Kings Vorngyd and Eyrfin, suggesting their shared combat experience during the eventual turnaround may have fractured their lifelong friendship.
topic_desc_basic: A historical account by Andreil of Falkreath detailing how King Bjeld of Falkreath orchestrated a mutual defense pact between the Nordic kings of Haafinheim, Falkreath, and the Reach in 3E 396, forming the Grand Alliance on the eve of the War of the Bend'r-Mahk.

title: The Grand Alliance III
topic_desc: The Grand Alliance, Volume III by Andreil of Falkreath is a historical account of the latter phase of the War of the Bend'r-Mahk, covering the decisive Nordic turn in 3E 398 and the war's final years. The work examines the alliance of Kings Eyrfin of Haafingar, Vorngyd of Markarth, and Bjeld of Falkreath, focusing on Vorngyd's controversial decision to field eastern Skyrim volunteer warbands alongside allied forces. Andreil details the battlefield effectiveness but devastating brutality of these eastern clans—particularly Clan Fire-Hand under Jarl Jona 'the Ansei-Ender'—and the resulting political friction among the allied kings. The volume recounts Vorngyd's death at the Battle of Vorngyd's Stand, the Fire-Hands' seizure of eastern Dragonstar and lordship over Karthwasten, and Bjeld's occupation and temple-pillaging at Elinhir. The narrative reflects a western Nordic perspective on the war's conduct and its enduring resentments.
topic_desc_basic: The Grand Alliance, Volume III by Andreil of Falkreath chronicles the latter years of the War of the Bend'r-Mahk from 3E 398. It details the Grand Alliance of three Nordic kings—Eyrfin, Vorngyd, and Bjeld—and their controversial use of eastern volunteer warbands, culminating in King Vorngyd's death in battle and the Nordic occupation of Elinhir.

title: The Grand Alliance IV
topic_desc: Andreil of Falkreath's historical work, the final volume in The Grand Alliance series, chronicles the aftermath of the War of the Bend'r-mahk and the fraying of the victorious Nordic coalition. It details how the Treaty of Chorrol formalized territorial gains—awarding the Karthwasten Cession to the Reach and confirming Falkreath's occupation of Elinhir—while the Dragonstar question remained unsettled. The narrative traces the alliance's deterioration: Solitude's withdrawal following the Snowline incident and King Eyrfin's death, contrasted with the enduring Markarth-Falkreath partnership under Kings Barda and Grovald. The volume provides a Falkreath-sympathetic perspective on the ongoing western Skyrim borderlands, noting Karthwasten's pacification after Jarl Jona's expulsion and emerging Reachman tensions in the Sundered Hills.
topic_desc_basic: The final volume of Andreil of Falkreath's history covering the War of the Bend'r-mahk's aftermath. It recounts the Treaty of Chorrol's territorial settlements and the gradual dissolution of the victorious Nordic alliance, with Solitude withdrawing while Markarth and Falkreath maintain their partnership.

title: The Healer's Tale
topic_desc: An anonymous healer's essay advocating compassion and emotional care in medical practice, illustrated by a darkly humorous anecdote about delivering a terminal diagnosis to a young patient at the Temple of Stendarr in the Iliac Bay. The author argues that healers must serve as counselors and comforters, not merely as curatives, claiming that kind words and sympathy often benefit patients more than spells. The work uses the tale of distracting a dying youth with a personal revelation about the temple's proselytizer to argue that considering patients' feelings, rather than rushing to heal and dismiss them, would create a healthier society.
topic_desc_basic: A short essay by an anonymous healer at the Temple of Stendarr in the Iliac Bay. It argues that healers should offer emotional comfort and compassion rather than simply casting curative spells, using a humorous anecdote about delivering bad news to illustrate the point.

title: The Holy Brothers of Marukh
topic_desc: The sole surviving fragment of a chronicle from a First Era sect of the Alessian Order, Volume IV recounts the Cleansing of the Fane. Dated 1E 393 in the Alessian reckoning, it records a solar eclipse followed by a demonic incursion from the Elvish temple Malada. Abbot Cosmas led the brothers against the High Fane with holy fire, destroying the demons and burning the temple's relics and books. The chronicle was likely kept at the sect's Lake Canulus monastic complex before its destruction during the War of Righteousness in 1E 2321 dispersed the archives.
topic_desc_basic: A surviving fragment of an Alessian Order chronicle describing Abbot Cosmas leading the sect to destroy demons and burn Elvish relics at the temple Malada in the First Era.

title: The Homily of the Pilgrim
topic_desc: A didactic parable about a pilgrim who systematically removes the sources of his pain—his toes, his hand, his wife, and finally his heart—only to die from the final excision. The homily teaches that pain is an inescapable and necessary part of existence, and that one should endure suffering with patience and humility rather than destroy what causes it. The tale's cultural context, with its mention of mushroom groves and House Heads, situates it firmly in Dunmer society, serving as a cautionary moral lesson against the destructive avoidance of suffering.
topic_desc_basic: A moral parable about a pilgrim who dies after cutting off each source of his pain, including his own heart. The work teaches that pain is necessary to life and should be met with patience and humility.

title: The Hoom, Habitat and Habits
topic_desc: A naturalist treatise by Menulus Flavis, an Imperial scholar whose family fortune originated in the decorated shell trade. Motivated by personal curiosity, Flavis traveled to Blacklight and bribed Dunmer farmers for information. The work documents the Hoom, a large crustacean native to the Velothi Mountains, describing its four-stage life cycle: aquatic larvae called Grulbs, amphibious Hoomcrabs resembling Mudcrabs, dormant attachment to adult males, and herbivorous adulthood lasting fifty to sixty years. Flavis catalogs Hoom products central to Dunmer society: shells used for instruments, bonemold armor, tools, and shelter; treated wool for construction insulation; saliva with restorative properties; and dung-based cement. He notes the cultural significance of tuned herds singing at dusk and references the scholar Adrys on shell acoustics. The work stands as a rare Imperial account of a creature deeply intertwined with Morrowind's arts, architecture, and daily life.
topic_desc_basic: A scholarly work by Menulus Flavis documenting the Hoom, a large crustacean native to the Velothi Mountains between Morrowind and Skyrim. The book describes the creature's four-stage life cycle and the many Dunmer uses for Hoom shells, wool, and other products in construction, armor, instruments, and medicine.

title: The Hounds of Hircine
topic_desc: The Hounds of Hircine, subtitled Call of the Wolf, is a first-person account by Matinus Byrne, a Cyrodilic noble who abandoned city life to trace his Nord heritage. The narrative follows Byrne from Skyrim to Morrowind, where he encounters and joins bands of Nord hunters devoted to Hircine, the Daedric Prince called the Hunter. The work details their organization under Pack Fathers and Pack Brothers, their reverence for lycanthropes, and initiation rites including the Chamber of the Wolf, a Dwemer ruin housing a captive werewolf used to test prospective leaders. The publisher's note disclaims factual accuracy, noting Byrne was rumored dead in the Skyrim wilderness. The manuscript offers rare, if unverified, insight into Hircine cult practices on Vvardenfell.
topic_desc_basic: The Hounds of Hircine is a first-person narrative by Matinus Byrne recounting his time among bands of Nord hunters devoted to Hircine, the Daedric Prince of the Hunt. The work describes their wilderness lifestyle, reverence for lycanthropes, and initiation rites on Vvardenfell. Its publisher disclaims factual accuracy.

title: The Hsaarik Elegy, Book One
topic_desc: A Nordic saga composed by Goderlog the Song-Maiden that memorializes the fallen of the Companions at Hsaarik. The elegy recounts a calamitous maritime disaster in which the vessel Harakk foundered upon a shore, detailing each Companion's death in succession. Oyvind perishes first, cast overboard by a rock; Geir is smashed against the ship's boards after the wind steals his warning of the reef; Vigdis, a mother who lost her children to starvation the prior winter, drowns at peace; and Yngol, a great smith of divine lineage, is pulled beneath the waves by his own heavy mail. The work emphasizes the tragedy of lost potential, noting each fallen's former 'knowing'—a name or distinction now rendered meaningless or painful by death, and attributing their demise to the caprice of Orkey and the sea.
topic_desc_basic: A Nordic saga by Goderlog the Song-Maiden that memorializes the Companions who died in a shipwreck at Hsaarik. It recounts the successive drownings of the fallen, including the smith Yngol, emphasizing the tragedy of their lost lives and names.

title: The Hsaarik Elegy, Book Three
topic_desc: The Hsaarik Elegy, Book Three is the final part of a poetic saga by Goderlog the Song-Maiden, chronicling the deaths of Nordic warriors during an ancient battle. This volume memorializes the fifty-first through the last of the fallen on the conflict's first day. Each entry records the grim manner of death—such as Idunn's merciful throat-crushing or Kynmud's violent disintegration after screaming her foes apart—and grants the deceased a new knowing-name, like Haafin or Ottra. Trygve, the final casualty, dies overlooked after the fighting ceases, nursing his gut wound as if it were the child he left behind at Jylkurfyk. The elegy preserves the memory and transformed identities of these warriors, marking Kynmud as the one-hundredth death since Atmora and the first of her kind upon Mereth.
topic_desc_basic: The Hsaarik Elegy, Book Three is the concluding volume of Goderlog the Song-Maiden's Nordic saga, chronicling the deaths and name-transformations of warriors slain during an ancient battle in Mereth.

title: The Hsaarik Elegy, Book Two
topic_desc: The second installment of a Nordic elegiac saga by Goderlog the Song-Maiden, chronicling individual deaths among Ysgramor's companions during the campaign about Saarthal.
topic_desc_basic: A Nordic saga by Goderlog the Song-Maiden memorializing warriors who fell during Ysgramor's campaign around Saarthal. It catalogs individual deaths—some in battle against the Snow Elves, others from age or cold—assigning each fallen companion a 'knowing,' a single word serving as a conceptual epitaph. The work forms part of a longer elegiac sequence.

title: The Image and the Divine
topic_desc: A theological treatise by Primate Dalus addressing the difficulty mortals face in perceiving the true nature of the Divines.
topic_desc_basic: A book by Primate Dalus about how mortals perceive the Divines.

title: The Imperial Kitchen I
topic_desc: A culinary treatise celebrating the hearty, unpretentious cuisine of Colovia as the sustenance that fueled the Imperial Legions' conquests. The work details regional recipes including Highlands Grouts porridge made from tough ironrye grain, Sarchal's traditional Lyco Stew using nightshade-family lycovine, Durenta with Fish and Eggs prepared from Redguard-introduced durata kernels, the festive Grandpa Goat in Garlic Sauce attributed to Saint Potri, and the mandrake-laced Colovian Battlewine once served to warriors before combat. Through these dishes, the author argues that Colovian fare, though less refined than Nibenese cooking, possesses enduring cultural and practical significance.
topic_desc_basic: A cookbook cataloging traditional Colovian dishes such as ironrye porridge, lyco stew, and festive goat recipes, presenting the region's simple, hearty cuisine as the practical fare that sustained the Imperial Legions.

title: The Imperial Kitchen II
topic_desc: The Imperial Kitchen II is a culinary treatise contrasting the perceived extravagance of Nibenese cuisine with the everyday fare of the common people. The work catalogs regional recipes and ingredients from the Heartlands and the Niben river valleys, including pauper's poppad marrow, garlicked snails, glazed prawns, and brandied plums. It details the preparation of mokre, a ubiquitous fermented fish sauce, and distinguishes Imperial rice varieties, noting that red rice is reserved for the Emperor's court. The text also observes that Cyrodiilic brandy, though famous for export, is largely inaccessible to common Imperials, who substitute cheaper provincial spirits or illegal pomace distillations. A second version of the text, attributed to Arruntius Horatia, includes additional recipes for Imperial desserts and veal.
topic_desc_basic: The Imperial Kitchen II is a cookbook examining the everyday cuisine of the Nibenay and eastern Heartlands rather than courtly decadence. It records common regional recipes, such as garlicked snails and glazed prawns, and details staple ingredients like mokre fish sauce and the various rice varieties cultivated across Cyrodiil.

title: The Imperial Navy
topic_desc: Bacola Gloriosus's treatise defends the Imperial Navy against critics who question its expense, arguing that the service is essential for defending Tamriel's vast coastline and enforcing maritime law. Gloriosus highlights anti-smuggling patrols off northern Morrowind, where the Navy's adoption of shallow-draft vessels has forced ebony and Dwemer artifact thieves into the treacherous Inner Sea, and notes the mixed results of anti-slavery operations south of Black Marsh, where interdiction has inadvertently increased the black market value of slaves. The work details naval composition and tactics, describing crews of archers, soldiers, officers, and spellcasters who use Alteration to control winds and Restoration to treat casualties. Gloriosus emphasizes the economic efficiency of capturing enemy vessels rather than destroying them, allowing the Empire to seize cargo, commission ships, and salvage materials at minimal cost.
topic_desc_basic: A book by Bacola Gloriosus arguing for the importance of the Imperial Navy, detailing its role in coastal defense, anti-smuggling patrols, and law enforcement across Tamriel's waters.

title: The Jewel Dragon's Glass Wife
topic_desc: A folktale ascribed to the recorder Yolanda Greatwood, recounting the tale of a Jewel Dragon — a creature with gemstone anatomy that consumes gold and breathes noxious smoke that devours the life-force of living things. The dragon demands a wife from a cowardly Lord, who yields his only daughter: a being with glass skin and a heart of pure gold. The narrative follows her servitude, her absorption of the dragon's smoke, and the intervention of a grieving mother-spirit whose children the dragon has slain. Through this spirit's passage through the wife's golden heart, the dragon perishes and the shattered wife is reborn as a spirit-being. The tale frames a moral cosmology of greed, sacrifice, and selflessness using allegorical terms for soul and life-force.
topic_desc_basic: A folktale recorded by Yolanda Greatwood about a Jewel Dragon that claims a cowardly Lord's glass-skinned daughter as its wife. The story follows her captivity and eventual transformation into a spirit-being after the dragon's death, exploring themes of greed, sacrifice, and selflessness.

title: The Kendhall Book of Riddles
topic_desc: The Kendhall Book of Riddles is a weighty tome compiled by Kendhall containing hundreds of riddles and their answers. The work presents each riddle as a descriptive verse requiring the reader to deduce a common subject from metaphorical clues, such as a horse, bell tower, tree, or teeth. Its significance lies in its extensive collection of these enigmatic puzzles, serving as a scholarly or recreational exercise in interpretation and lateral thought across Tamriel.
topic_desc_basic: The Kendhall Book of Riddles by Kendhall is a large collection of hundreds of riddles and their answers, presenting each puzzle as a descriptive verse whose subject must be deduced from metaphorical clues.

title: The Knights of the Nine
topic_desc: A historical study by Karoline of Solitude chronicling the rise and dissolution of the original Knights of the Nine. Founded by Sir Amiel Lannus in 3E 111 to recover Pelinal Whitestrake's Crusader's Relics, the order achieved widespread fame after reclaiming the Cuirass from the Wyrm of Elynglenn and establishing their priory in the West Weald. Their unity shattered during the War of the Red Diamond; members split along familial loyalties, with Sir Berich Vlindrel departing with the Sword and Greaves to support Cephorus. Berich likely orchestrated the order's official dissolution in 3E 131. The work traces the subsequent loss of the Relics: the Gauntlets remain immovable in Chorrol's Chapel of Stendarr after Sir Casimir's crime, while the Cuirass and Amiel's fate remain unknown after a final sighting in 3E 150.
topic_desc_basic: A historical work by Karoline of Solitude recounting the original Knights of the Nine. Founded in 3E 111 to recover Pelinal Whitestrake's Crusader's Relics, the renowned Cyrodiilic order was destroyed by divisions during the War of the Red Diamond and officially dissolved in 3E 131.

title: The Language of Birds
topic_desc: A marginal text recovered from the Piukanda scrolls, likely an Ayleid children's fable that scholars consider the closest surviving approximation of an Ayleid creation myth. It recounts the origin of the Ayleidoon as speechless bird people inhabiting an eightfold island, living under starlit benevolence without arts or crafts. Besieged by the loathsome people of Man from the surrounding jungle, the birds were transformed when a western seeker called the Pilot Torval arrived and gifted them language. The fable presents language as the source of all civilization, art, architecture, and power, enabling the newly articulate birds to defeat their enemies, master the beasts, and build Ayleidoon. The Marukhati Selectives destroyed most Ayleid mythic traditions, leaving this allegorical account as a rare, if enigmatic, window into their cultural origins.
topic_desc_basic: An Ayleid children's fable found in the Piukanda scrolls, regarded as the closest surviving account of Ayleid origins. It tells how speechless bird people, besieged by the people of Man, were given language by the Pilot Torval, transforming them into the powerful Ayleidoon civilization.

title: The Lantern Thief
topic_desc: A short narrative by Mavon Romaris advocating the study of practical Illusion magic for survival in the Telvanni homeland. The story follows Fathis, a Dunmer who learns a basic light spell from the veteran adventurer Gilvas Rathon in Llothanis. Returning home, Fathis encounters the Bloody Moth, a terrifying northeastern legend said to be drawn to household lanterns. By casting the light spell directly at the creature to disorient it, Fathis extinguishes his lanterns and hides, surviving the encounter. The work illustrates how even rudimentary Illusion spells can provide common folk a crucial means of evasion against otherwise lethal threats in dangerous regions.
topic_desc_basic: A story by Mavon Romaris about a Dunmer who survives an encounter with the legendary Bloody Moth by using a practical Illusion light spell taught by a veteran adventurer, illustrating the survival value of basic magic in the Telvanni lands.

title: The Last Dart of the Scholar
topic_desc: A fable by Astochus Enrinus recounting a scholar's encounter with a Dark Brotherhood assassin in the Royal Palace of Mournhold. When cornered by the killer, who carried only five darts, the scholar goaded the assassin's pride by demanding a series of escalating marksmanship trials. After the assassin expended all five darts proving his skill, the unarmed killer was slain by the scholar's common dagger. The tale extols intellect and composure over brute confidence, illustrating how arrogance can leave even a master assassin vulnerable.
topic_desc_basic: A fable by Astochus Enrinus about a scholar in Mournhold's Royal Palace who outsmarts a Dark Brotherhood assassin. By goading the killer into a series of marksmanship trials, the scholar tricks him into expending all his darts, leaving the assassin defenseless against a concealed dagger.

title: The Last Story of Sirof the Oak
topic_desc: A Nordic fable recounting the final tale of Sirof, a figure of the Merethic Era, who instructs his three children in proper Nordic traditions before their divine marriage to Mara. Set during the Companions' colonization of Skyrim following the sack of Saarthal, the story emphasizes adherence to ancestral customs over elven influences and explains the origin of certain stars as the progeny of Sirof's children. The narrative frames matrimony as a sacred bond with distinct roles—feast-spouse, sword-spouse, and breath-spouse—ordained by the goddess, reflecting early Nordic cultural values regarding duty, hospitality, and the cosmic significance of marriage.
topic_desc_basic: A Nordic fable about Sirof, an early settler of Skyrim, who tells his three children of their impending divine marriage to Mara. The story explains the origin of stars as the descendants of this union and emphasizes maintaining proper Nordic traditions.

record_links.display_name: The Last Story of Sirof the Oak

title: The Legend of Lovers Lament
topic_desc: A romantic tragedy by Croll Baumoval recounting the legend of Lord Gerthland and Lady Madylina, betrothed lovers separated when Gerthland died in battle. Spurned by Madylina, the manor's sorcerer Hergen cursed their souls, forbidding them rest unless she consents to be his consort in death. Unable to touch, the lovers' ghosts meet briefly each night on the shores of the lake now known as Lover's Lament, leaving behind crimson and white roses that the water reclaims at dawn. Hergen is said to still wander Gerthland Manor, awaiting her capitulation.
topic_desc_basic: A romantic tragedy by Croll Baumoval about the ghosts of betrothed lovers, Lord Gerthland and Lady Madylina, who meet nightly by a haunted lake. A spurned sorcerer's curse prevents their souls from resting unless Madylina agrees to become his consort in death.

title: The Legend of Red Eagle
topic_desc: A Reach legend of the hero Faolan and his war against the First Empire.
topic_desc_basic: An ancient tale recounting the Reachman hero Faolan, called Red Eagle, and his resistance against Empress Hestra's First Empire invasion around 1E 1030. It describes his pact with a Hagraven for power and his oath to one day return when his blade is brought back to his tomb and the Reach is freed.

title: The Legend of the Krately House
topic_desc: A play by Baloth-Kul concerning the infamous haunted Krately House in Cheydinhal. The drama follows two thieves, Theophon and Nirim, who burglarize the abandoned residence only to discover its ghostly inhabitants reliving the night of their gruesome murder. The ghosts interact with the living intruders, and the work builds tension through the revelation that the unseen creature that killed the family may still lurk within the house. The narrative also references rumors that Dominitia Krately was a witch who abandoned her coven for marriage, prompting them to send the lethal creature. The play is recognized for its suspenseful theatrical structure and its exploration of ghostly interaction with the living.
topic_desc_basic: A play by Baloth-Kul about the haunted Krately House in Cheydinhal. It depicts two thieves burglarizing the home and encountering the ghosts of the murdered Krately family as they relive the night of their deaths.

record_links.display_name: The Legend of the Krately House

title: The Legendary City Sancre Tor
topic_desc: Matera Chapel's historical study chronicles the rise and fall of Sancre Tor, the ancient holy city founded by Alessia in the Jerall Mountains. The work examines the settlement's strategic vulnerability to Nordic occupation despite its magical defenses, the relocation of religious authority to the Imperial City, and the city's destruction during General Talos's siege in 2E 852. Chapel disputes claims of divine protection, attributing the citadel's falls to betrayed enchantments. The account also details the Reman emperors' funerary precincts, the Amulet of Kings' placement in Reman III's tomb, and Talos's recovery of the artifact, linking it to the Third Era imperial renaissance. Sancre Tor now lies in ruin.
topic_desc_basic: Matera Chapel's historical study chronicles the rise and fall of Sancre Tor, the ancient holy city founded by Alessia in the Jerall Mountains. It details the city's strategic vulnerability, its destruction during General Talos's 2E 852 siege, and his recovery of the Amulet of Kings from Reman III's tomb.

title: The Light and The Dark
topic_desc: A philosophical work by Irek Unterge presenting a cosmology in which two primordial, antithetical forces—the Light and the Dark—chose Tamriel as their battleground before the gods existed. The narrator contends that these opposites are neither good nor evil themselves, but their conflict generates the impersonal energies from which life and magic arise. The book claims the et'Ada drew upon these energies to shape the gods, who now mostly align with the Light. It argues that mortals influence this eternal struggle through their actions, since slaying creatures aligned with one force marginally empowers the other. The author warns that forgetting the Dark's constant threat invites catastrophe, and calls for vigilance against those it perverts.
topic_desc_basic: A book by Irek Unterge outlining a cosmology where two primordial opposites, the Light and the Dark, chose Tamriel as their battleground. It claims their conflict generates all life and magic, and that mortal actions can marginally strengthen one force over the other.

title: The Lily of Dibella
topic_desc: The Lily of Dibella is a popular tale among Nordic followers of Dibella, composed during the later years of the First Empire of Man (1E 200–1E 400) and translated into modern Tamrielic by the Hall of Culture in Winterhold in 3E 289. The narrative recounts a contest of beauty between Dibella—portrayed as the Pulchrimancer of Creation and Bed-Wife of Shor—and a Snow Elf dwelling upon Mount Kilkreath. Dibella cultivates a previously unknown lily and, through the aid of Sister Hawk (Kyne), summons a vast horde of moths whose silkworms weave her a dress of surpassing beauty, humiliating the elf. The tale articulates a distinctly Nordic theology: that true beauty is earned through labor and devotion rather than superficial adornment, and it reflects Nordic cultural attitudes toward elves and the pantheon's familial structure.
topic_desc_basic: The Lily of Dibella is a popular Nordic tale of the goddess Dibella, composed during the later First Empire of Man and translated into modern Tamrielic in 3E 289 by the Hall of Culture in Winterhold. It recounts Dibella's contest of beauty against a Snow Elf and teaches that true Nordic beauty is earned through honest toil rather than superficial decoration.

title: The Line of Emperors I
topic_desc: A scholarly work by Jaume Abtacil, written under the patronage of Emperor Pelagius IV, examining the early emperors of Cyrodiil. The first volume covers the First Empire's founding by Alessia, whose obscure ancestry and contested moment of ascendancy the author subjects to critical scrutiny, favoring the Taking of the Citadel as the true beginning of her reign. Abtacil attributes the scarcity of reliable sources to Marukhati archive destruction and the War of Righteousness. He profiles Belharza, the Man-Bull and son of Morihaus, whose soldierly rule secured the fledgling empire's borders despite a succession crisis over maternal lineage. The volume concludes with the obscure Ami-El, who enacted the Alessian Doctrines and furthered Marukhati influence, deepening the cultural divergence between Nibenay and Colovia. The work is significant for its critical approach to early Imperial historiography.
topic_desc_basic: A historical work by Jaume Abtacil, written under Emperor Pelagius IV, chronicling the early emperors of Cyrodiil. The first volume covers Alessia, Belharza the Man-Bull, and the obscure Ami-El, examining their lives and the challenges of reconstructing the First Empire's history due to Marukhati archive destruction and the War of Righteousness.

title: The Line of Emperors II
topic_desc: Jaume Abtacil IV's scholarly inquiry into the Alessian emperors from Gorieus to Herda. It examines Gorieus' disputed five-hundred-year reign and the decadence of the Woven City, attributing such accounts to either a Goriathite dynasty or the emperor's mastery of Ayleid sorcery. It praises Empress Hestra the Builder for reuniting Cyrodiil, constructing the Hestra-Ways, and founding the Imperial Arena with Gaiden Shinji, though the Middle Dawn obscures her later life and possible Oblivion colonies. The obscure Shor-El, possibly a Nordic usurper, presided over diminished borders, while Empress Herda, the last known Alessian ruler, briefly restored Colovian-Nibenese unity before the line's extinction precipitated the First Interregnum.
topic_desc_basic: A scholarly history by Jaume Abtacil IV covering the late Alessian emperors of Cyrodiil from Gorieus to Herda.

title: The Line of Emperors III
topic_desc: A historical work by Jaume Abtacil covering the Remanite emperors from Reman I to Kastav.
topic_desc_basic: Jaume Abtacil's historical study of the Remanite emperors, covering the reigns of Reman I, Brazollus Dor, and Kastav.

title: The Line of Emperors IV
topic_desc: Jaume Abtacil's historical work, the fourth volume in his comprehensive inquiry into the Cyrodiilic succession, covers the late First Era Reman emperors from Reman II through Reman III. The account presents a staunchly Imperial perspective, celebrating Reman II for quelling Nordic and Argonian uprisings using Tsaesci warriors and launching the eighty-year war against Morrowind, while omitting the details of the expunged predecessor between them. Reman III is portrayed as a merciful martyr undermined by treachery, including that of his consort Empress Tavia, whose imprisonment in Black Marsh is justified as necessary. The work frames his assassination and the death of his heir as the tragedy that initiated the chaotic Second Era, dismissively characterizing the Akaviri Potentate rule as an inadequate substitute and the subsequent Interregnum as a period of illegitimate pretenders and despair.
topic_desc_basic: A scholarly history by Jaume Abtacil covering the late First Era Reman emperors, from Reman II through Reman III, and the onset of the Second Era's Interregnum.

title: The Line of Emperors IX
topic_desc: The ninth volume of Tyr Ymanwe's comprehensive inquiry into the Septim succession, commissioned by Emperor Pelagius IV. The work chronicles the reigns of Cephorus II through Morihatha, emphasizing the restoration of the true Septim bloodline after the Lariat dynasty, the resurgence of imperial ambition under Uriel V, and the delicate recovery of imperial authority from the Elder Council by Uriel VI and Morihatha. Ymanwe frames these emperors as a revitalization of the empire, portraying Uriel V's disastrous Akaviri campaign as a triumphant validation of the dynasty's Talosic will, and Morihatha's assassination as the tragic cost of her deliberate reforms. The account concludes with dutiful praise for Pelagius IV's continuation of this imperial renaissance.
topic_desc_basic: The ninth volume of Tyr Ymanwe's history of the Septim emperors, covering the reigns from Cephorus II to Morihatha and commissioned by Emperor Pelagius IV.

title: The Line of Emperors IX: Add.
topic_desc: This addendum to Tyr Ymanwe's comprehensive inquiry into the Septim succession covers the reigns of Pelagius IV and Uriel VII. Written after twenty years of Uriel VII's rule, the text presents a highly favorable imperial perspective. It credits Pelagius IV, who ascended in 3E 339 following Morihatha's death, with continuing his aunt's pacification efforts through infrastructure and military expansion, though it acknowledges some criticism regarding the durability of this peace. The section on Uriel VII, the twenty-first Septim Emperor who took the White-Gold Throne in 3E 368, is an unfinished preliminary draft. It effusively praises the Emperor as a synthesis of his predecessors' virtues—Morihatha's diplomacy, Uriel VI's political acumen, and Uriel V's military foresight—and celebrates the first decade of his reign as a safeguard for Tamriel's future.
topic_desc_basic: An addendum to Tyr Ymanwe's history of the Septim Emperors, covering the reigns of Pelagius IV and the early rule of Uriel VII from a loyalist imperial perspective.

record_links.display_name: The Line of Emperors IX: Add.

title: The Line of Emperors V
topic_desc: The Line of Emperors V, by Jaume Abtacil, is the fifth volume of a comprehensive inquiry into the Cyrodiilic line of succession. Covering the period from Cuhlecain to Kintyra I, the work presents a fiercely pro-Imperial and hagiographic account of the early Septim dynasty. It details Cuhlecain's designation as Emperor Zero at Tiber Septim's request, Tiber's Atmoran origins and divine ascension, Pelagius I's establishment of Talos worship, and Kintyra I's cultural patronage. The author dismisses contrary accounts as treasonous or fanciful, attributing Cuhlecain's death and Tiber's throat wound to conspiracy while celebrating Tiber's conquests and the Armistice as righteous victories. The text serves as significant evidence of orthodox Imperial historiography.
topic_desc_basic: The Line of Emperors V is a scholarly volume by Jaume Abtacil chronicling the early Septim Emperors from Cuhlecain through Kintyra I. It presents a highly favorable Imperial account of Tiber Septim's rise and divine nature, the assassination of Pelagius I, and Kintyra I's reign.

title: The Line of Emperors VI
topic_desc: A scholarly volume by Jaume Abtacil covering the Septim emperors from Uriel I through Antiochus, offering a strongly pro-Imperial interpretation of their reigns.
topic_desc_basic: A book by Jaume Abtacil chronicling the Septim Emperors from Uriel I to Antiochus, emphasizing their lawful virtue and Imperial purpose.

title: The Line of Emperors VII
topic_desc: A historical work covering the Septim succession from Kintyra II through Magnus I.
topic_desc_basic: A volume of Jaume Abtacil's historical inquiry into the Septim emperors, covering Kintyra II, Uriel III, Cephorus I, and Magnus I.

title: The Line of Emperors VIII
topic_desc: The eighth volume of Tyr Ymanwe's comprehensive inquiry into the succession of Cyrodiil's emperors, commissioned by Emperor Pelagius IV. This installment covers the reigns of Pelagius III, Katariah I, Cassynder, and Uriel IV. Ymanwe presents a distinctly critical Imperial perspective, characterizing Pelagius III's line as a withered branch that produced no good fruit. He openly questions the legitimacy of Katariah's regency, dismissing the popular memory of her reign as joyful and attributing its stability to her diplomatic skills and the preceding era's turmoil. He condemns her as a foreign Dunmer unsuited to Imperial morals and dismisses Montalius's account of her death. Cassynder's brief rule is portrayed as a heavy burden on his half-elven health, while Uriel IV is labeled an illicit steward-Emperor whose lack of Septim blood and reliance on a mere adoption technicality alienated the Elder Council and undermined Imperial virtue.
topic_desc_basic: A scholarly history covering the Septim Emperors from Pelagius III to Uriel IV, examining the controversial succession and legitimacy of Katariah I, Cassynder, and Uriel IV.

title: The Liturgy of Affliction
topic_desc: The Liturgy of Affliction is a memoir transcribed by Anias Gae from the writings of Vexis Velruan, a former temple healer expelled for unorthodox attempts to cure Red Fever. The work chronicles Velruan's discovery that channeling destruction magic through his own body deepened his understanding of magicka's raw forces. He became addicted to the practice, suffering catastrophic physical ruin—loss of sight, shattered limbs, charred flesh—yet claimed to surpass guild grand masters in understanding. The memoir frames pain as the gods' greatest gift to mortals rather than something to be feared, and concludes with praise to Sheogorath, casting Velruan's destruction as madness-blessed revelation rather than mere tragedy.
topic_desc_basic: The Liturgy of Affliction is a memoir by Vexis Velruan, transcribed by Anias Gae. Velruan, a former temple healer expelled for unorthodox methods, recounts his addiction to channeling destruction magic through his own body. The text venerates pain as a divine gift and ends with praise to Sheogorath.

title: The Mabrigash's Wishes
topic_desc: A dramatic work recounting the encounter between a House Dunmer named Nilaer Teddlu and a mabrigash of the Thirr River. Nilaer demands the mabrigash grant his wish for an ideal woman, but she punishes his crude specificity by summoning an infant, a toothless crone, and finally a vampire who desires to kiss his neck all night. The tale serves as a cautionary Ashlander folk narrative about the perils of making careless wishes, while also reflecting cultural hostility between Ashlander and settled House Dunmer society.
topic_desc_basic: A dramatic Ashlander folk tale about a House Dunmer who demands a mabrigash of the Thirr River grant his wish for an ideal woman, only to be punished with increasingly monstrous results.

title: The Magicka of a Moons Dancer
topic_desc: A Khajiiti instructional text adapted from a lecture by a Dagi-Raht master at the Temple of Two-Moons Dance in Torval. It outlines the Moons Dance martial tradition, which posits four interdependent masteries: breath, body, technique, and magicka. Unlike Altmer casting, which separates magicka from the physical form, Moons Dancers channel animus energy through movement, breath, and physical conditioning, making their spells an extension of martial technique. The work emphasizes that neglecting any single mastery weakens the whole, and describes advanced applications such as life-force manipulation, environmental alteration, and the ritualized use of moon sugar to ingest lunar animus.
topic_desc_basic: A Khajiiti primer on the Moons Dance martial tradition, adapted from a Dagi-Raht master's lecture in Torval. It teaches that magicka must be channeled through breath, body, and technique rather than cast as pure thought, emphasizing the unity of physical and magical training.

record_links.display_name: The Magicka of a Moons Dancer

title: The Malahk: Scourge of the East
topic_desc: A treatise by Laurina Macurio on the Malahk Orcs and their highland home of Malahk-Bazul between Nibenay and western Morrowind. The author characterizes the Malahk as merciless raiders who appease the Daedric god-king Mauloch and fight among their own clans in abandoned forts and caves. Their persistent assaults forced the Empire to abandon the mountain extension of Cheydinhal's Blue Road, transferring its defense to House Redoran and diverting Imperial commerce through Hlaalu territory. The Malahk exploited the subsequent withdrawal, capturing undermanned Imperial forts to intensify raids against Redoran. Macurio notes that Redoran now manages the threat through well-guarded trade and champion duels with Malahk warchiefs. While some eccentric scholars speculate the Malahk possess a sophisticated culture where violence serves as rites of passage, Macurio dismisses this, portraying the Orcs as brutal barbarians.
topic_desc_basic: A book by Laurina Macurio describing the Malahk Orcs of Malahk-Bazul, a remote highland valley between Nibenay and western Morrowind. The work portrays these Mauloch-worshipping Orcs as ferocious raiders whose attacks forced Imperial withdrawal from the region's mountain trade route.

record_links.display_name: The Malahk: Scourge of the East

title: The Middle Dawn
topic_desc: This text examines the Dragon Break of 1E 1200–2208, a catastrophic temporal disruption initiated by the Maruhkati Selective. This fanatical Alessian sect sought to sever the acknowledged connection between Akatosh and the Elven god Auriel. When invented rituals failed, the sect's secret masters channeled the Aurbis to mythically excise the offending aspects of the Dragon God. A tower manifested, splitting into eight pieces and shattering linear time, returning the non-linearity of the Dawn Era. The work highlights the period's inherent unreliability: surviving accounts contradict each other on events, the sun's color, and divine presence, and the Elder Council's figure of one thousand and eight years is considered arbitrary. Whether the Selective succeeded remains unknown, as the War of Righteousness destroyed surviving records a century later.
topic_desc_basic: A scholarly overview of the Dragon Break of 1E 1200–2208, when the Maruhkati Selective shattered linear time by attempting to separate Akatosh from the Elven god Auriel. The text explains why surviving records of this millennium-long disruption are deeply contradictory.

title: The Million Lessons of Shor
topic_desc: A Nordic polemic asserting that a Chimer woman's fabricated tale of divine abduction by Ayem, dreugh, and other entities concealed her pregnancy by Shor, and that her bastard child was raised as a king among the Chimer god-kings in Mournhold.
topic_desc_basic: A Nordic book claiming a Chimer woman invented an elaborate tale of supernatural abduction to conceal her pregnancy by Shor, and that her child was raised as a king among the Chimer.

title: The Necklace
topic_desc: A short story by Ormax Endre about a thief, a dragon, and a stolen ornament.
topic_desc_basic: A short story by Ormax Endre about a thief who steals a dragonscale necklace from a dragon named Garryk.

title: The Origin of the Ash Yam
topic_desc: A treatise by Cantur Caelmoryn challenging the assumption that the ash yam is merely a yam cultivated in Morrowind's ashy soils, instead arguing the name is cultural. Caelmoryn documents over fifteen crossbreedable varieties, some containing a compound that causes severe illness and serves as a Redoran political toxin. He observes a Redoran pre-meal ritual where ancestral ash is ingested to neutralize this poison, and confirms through personal experimentation that consuming ash salts or fine clay before dining prevents the yam's ill effects.
topic_desc_basic: A study by Cantur Caelmoryn on the ash yam. It reveals that some varieties are poisonous and explains that the Dunmer ritual of ingesting ancestral ash before meals neutralizes the toxin, with clay serving as an alternative remedy.

record_links.display_name: The Origin of the Ash Yam

title: The Pilgrim and the Soldier I
topic_desc: The opening installment of a literary series recounting the encounter between a Nibenese pilgrim and a Colovian soldier on the road to Sancre Tor, contrasting their motives and cultural origins while meditating on solitude and the demands of the pilgrimage.
topic_desc_basic: The first part of a literary work describing the meeting of two travelers on the road to Sancre Tor: a Nibenese merchant's son turned pilgrim seeking spiritual truth, and a scarred Colovian veteran seeking to atone for past deeds. They share a meal and resolve to journey together, though the road demands solitude.

record_links.display_name: The Pilgrim and the Soldier I

title: The Pilgrim and the Soldier II
topic_desc: The second installment of The Pilgrim and the Soldier, titled The Road, follows two travelers—a martial soldier wielding an iron hammer and a devout pilgrim employing whispered abjurations—journeying together toward Sancre Tor. The narrative emphasizes the perilous nature of the route, depicting it as a barren, malevolent path haunted by evil spirits, beasts, and bandits. While the siblings in fate rely on complementary strengths to survive, the prose stresses that the road itself offers no solace, negating the comfort of their companionship with its bitter cold. The work presents a meditation on the harshness of the pilgrimage to the ancient Colovian fortress, contrasting physical and spiritual fortitude against an inhospitable landscape that remains indifferent to mortal solidarity.
topic_desc_basic: The second part of The Pilgrim and the Soldier, titled The Road, depicting the journey of a soldier and a pilgrim traveling the perilous, haunted route to Sancre Tor.

record_links.display_name: The Pilgrim and the Soldier II

title: The Pilgrim and the Soldier III
topic_desc: The third part of the series depicting a nighttime conversation between a pilgrim and a soldier resting on the road to Sancre Tor. The pilgrim recounts the Nibenese view of the fortress as a hidden city shrouded by deep water and secret arts, where bells once rang for Reman, Al-Esh, Pelinal, and Morihaus before a faithless age silenced the spirits. The soldier describes the Colovian perspective of Sancre Tor as a great necropolis holding a thousand dancing kings and their scions, lamenting that the Empire's total subsumption of the world has left him a sullied weapon seeking cleansing at the site. The work contrasts these cultural visions of a sacred past against a diminished present, concluding with the image of Sancre Tor looming indifferent to the travelers' desires, as the merciless road knows not who treads it.
topic_desc_basic: The third part of a series recording a conversation between a pilgrim and a soldier on the road to Sancre Tor, contrasting the Nibenese view of the fortress as a hidden, silenced holy site with the Colovian view of it as a great necropolis of fallen kings.

record_links.display_name: The Pilgrim and the Soldier III

title: The Pilgrim and the Soldier IV
topic_desc: The fourth and final part of the poetic series, subtitled *The Valley*. It depicts the pilgrim succumbing to infected wounds and fever on the road to Sancre Tor, while the soldier watches helplessly, unable to cure him. After his death, she continues alone, her bloodied hammer at her side, toward the hidden city. The work frames the road to Sancre Tor as a merciless, solitary path that demands abandonment of love and hope, emphasizing that such journeys must ultimately be walked alone.
topic_desc_basic: The final part of a poetic series about two travelers on the road to Sancre Tor. It recounts the pilgrim's death from infected wounds and the soldier's solitary continuation toward the hidden city, portraying the road as a merciless path that must be walked alone.

record_links.display_name: The Pilgrim and the Soldier IV

title: The Port of Anvil
topic_desc: Calixta Avidrian's historical work chronicles Anvil, largest and most prosperous city of West Colovia, from its origins as a fishing village under the minor House of Olo through its rise as the Abecean's foremost trade port. The narrative traces Bendu Olo's alliance forged after the Slug-Famine of 1E 2200, the All Flags Navy campaign against Thras, and the Oloman dynasty's ascent over the fallen Shore-Kings of Mischarstette. Avidrian details Anvil's decline following Reman III's death, its submission to Tiber Septim under terms of elective monarchy and service as the West Navy's home port, the Camoran Usurper's devastation in 3E 249, and Commodore Fasil Conomorus's reconstruction of the sacked city with Castle Goldstone. The work presents Anvil as a testament to resilience and Cyrodiilic diplomacy.
topic_desc_basic: Calixta Avidrian's history chronicles Anvil, the largest and most prosperous city of West Colovia. The work traces the city's rise from a fishing village to a major Abecean trade port, covering the Oloman dynasty, the All Flags Navy, submission to Tiber Septim, the Camoran Usurper's sack, and Commodore Conomorus's rebuilding of the city.

title: The Purpose of the Corkbulb
topic_desc: A botanical treatise by Cantur Caelmoryn correcting widespread misconceptions about the corkbulb root. Caelmoryn refutes the assumption that Dunmer use corkbulb as a timber substitute due to a lack of trees, noting Morrowind's adequate woodlands and the plant's preference for warmer temperate regions near forests. He details the taproot's specific uses: the stiff outer layer is stripped, soaked, and woven into baskets or mats, and possibly used in bonemold sculpting; the hard inner core is carved into pegs, bowls, or arrows, though it may sprout if sun-exposed; and the softer tendrils are consumed in teas and dishes. He also notes these tendrils physically anchor the large bulb, preventing it from dislodging and rolling away.
topic_desc_basic: A scholarly work by Cantur Caelmoryn examining the corkbulb plant. It corrects the misconception that the root serves as a wood substitute, instead detailing its varied Dunmeri uses: woven outer layers for baskets, carved inner cores for tools, and flavorful tendrils for food and tea.

title: The Real Meaning of Life
topic_desc: A parable by Atrius Novolus recounting the tale of a notorious Altmer vampire in High Rock who called himself Emperor. Having succumbed to porphyric hemophilia and terrorized the province for decades, he experienced a crisis of purpose while hunting in Shornhelm. Observing two children at play, he recognized the innocence his existence had forsaken. When a mugger threatened them, he slew the attacker, sacrificing himself to the arriving guards rather than flee. His final declaration—that the meaning of life is simply to live—was preserved by those guards, though dismissed by the wider populace.
topic_desc_basic: A philosophical tale by Atrius Novolus about a notorious Altmer vampire in High Rock who sacrificed his immortality to save two children, concluding that the meaning of life is to live.

title: The Red Kitchen Reader
topic_desc: The Red Kitchen Reader is a memoir by Simocles Quo, the only Master of Cuisine ever appointed to the Imperial Court, a title bestowed by Emperor Pelagius IV. Quo declined Emperor Uriel VII's invitation to continue in the role owing to age and poor health. The work addresses the recurring question of the finest meal he ever ate, arguing that a meal's memorability depends on setting, company, and circumstance as much as on the food itself. He recounts a near-fatal Merringar fishing expedition off northern Skyrim that made a subsequent shore meal in Solitude unforgettable, and a visit to Falinesti where he joined Imga in harvesting Kollopi from graht-oak branches. The title derives from his childhood discovery in Cheydinhal of a hidden sub-basement kitchen with red walls, where he tasted a roast that ignited his lifelong devotion to fine cuisine. He never relocated the house.
topic_desc_basic: The Red Kitchen Reader is a memoir by Simocles Quo, who served as the sole Master of Cuisine at the Imperial Court under Emperor Pelagius IV. The book recounts memorable meals from his travels across Tamriel and describes the childhood experience in a hidden red-painted kitchen in Cheydinhal that inspired his lifelong passion for fine cuisine.

title: The Refugees
topic_desc: A historical narrative by Geros Albreigh set during the Camoran Usurper's invasion of the Iliac Bay region. The work follows a Redguard youth, Lukar, who fled Hammerfell with his mother after Rihad and Taneth fell, eventually finding refuge in Dwynnen. During the Usurper's final assault, a scout named Orben Elmlock reveals he formerly served Camoran Kaltos alongside Haymon Camoran before the latter's atrocities forced their defection. The account also documents a feverish Bosmer woman, Kaalys, who gives birth amid the siege and flees. Her child is revealed to be named Mankar, an ominous detail given her frantic prophecies of a coming destroyer even as the Usurper himself is slain.
topic_desc_basic: A historical account by Geros Albreigh about refugees displaced by the Camoran Usurper's wars in Hammerfell and High Rock, culminating in the Usurper's defeat at Dwynnen.

title: The Restless North, Book I
topic_desc: Alarne Gold-Quill's historical fiction depicts a Nordic rebellion against the Tsaesci Potentate. It follows Hoari, a Nord woodsmith marching with the Laintar leidang under Thane Rog the Biter, and his Redguard war-wife Demka. The army gathers outside Danstrar where the Potentate's palace still burns, responding to the Tsaesci order dissolving independent Nordic forces. The narrative explores cultural tensions—western Nords doubt Redguard discipline, and Demka openly scorns Nordic clever-men as peddlers of mysticism. The first part concludes as the lawspeaker Pak Stoat-Face arrives to address the rebel camp.
topic_desc_basic: A historical tale by Alarne Gold-Quill about a Nordic rebellion against the Tsaesci Potentate, following a Nord woodsmith and his Redguard war-wife marching to join the rebel gathering at Danstrar.

title: The Restless North, Book II
topic_desc: The Restless North, Book II is the second installment of Alarne Gold-Quill's historical fiction, depicting a Nordic army's encampment on the anniversary of a catastrophic battle against the Tjaski-men. The clever-man Pak Stoat-Face warns the soldiers that the mass death of five hundred years prior has made the night dangerously susceptible to draugr possession. To placate these lingering spirits, he prescribes a protective ritual involving flour lines, meat cairns, and a shared blood-ale pact. The narrative frames this folk magic as a pragmatic necessity for the army of Rog the Biter, which is mustering to resist Tsaesci occupation. The work offers insight into Nordic clever-men as ritual intermediaries and the cultural practices surrounding undeath and mass death.
topic_desc_basic: The Restless North, Book II by Alarne Gold-Quill is a tale of Nords, Tsaesci, and draugr. It depicts a clever-man instructing soldiers to perform protective rituals against undead possession on the anniversary of a great battle.

title: The Restless North, Book III
topic_desc: The Restless North, Book III by Alarne Gold-Quill concludes a fictional tale of Nords and Redguards confronting the undead. It follows Hoari, a Nord carpenter, and his Redguard lover Demka as they march with Thane Rog's leidang toward Danstrar. When clever-men advise blood sacrifice to appease stirring draugr, Demka refuses to wound her sword-hand, insisting that steel is the proper answer to the restless dead. Her pragmatism is vindicated at dawn when a draugr horde overruns the camp; Demka saves Hoari from a strangling corpse, and the two join the Laintar Nords in fighting the swarm. The work contrasts Nord ritual tradition with Redguard martial directness in the face of undeath.
topic_desc_basic: The Restless North, Book III by Alarne Gold-Quill is the final part of a fictional tale about Nords and Redguards facing the undead. It recounts a draugr attack on a Nord camp and contrasts Nord ritual sacrifice with Redguard martial resolve.

title: The Sage
topic_desc: Aegrothius Goth's hagiographic account of Gyron Vardengroet, a Breton mage of extraordinary talent born in Moonguard during a rare lunar eclipse. The work chronicles his rise from a village prodigy through the Mages Guild in Shornhelm and study at the Crystal Tower, where the Elder Esthlainder revealed a divine prophecy naming him a promised champion of magic users. Granted indestructible indigo robes and a magical staff, Gyron assumed the title of the Sage. Devastated by his parents' deaths, he dedicated himself to defeating death, accidentally achieving immortality through botanical experiments. Now residing in a magical fortress in the Kurallian Mountains, the Sage continues aiding worthy mages. The narrative establishes the Sage as Tamriel's legendary counselor to magic users and forms the first part of a trilogy continued in Feyfolken and The Final Lesson.
topic_desc_basic: Aegrothius Goth's book chronicling the life of Gyron Vardengroet, a Breton mage of exceptional talent who rose from a village prodigy to become the Sage, a legendary champion and counselor to magic users across Tamriel. The work details his journey through the Mages Guild and Crystal Tower, his prophesied destiny, and his eventual achievement of immortality.

title: The Saint and the Left Hand
topic_desc: A scholarly treatise by Ianus Gaer-Frae, published by the Gwylim University Press, examining the fundamental antagonism between magic and religion. Gaer-Frae argues that religion presupposes a mutable world governed by conscious, personal agents whose favor can be conciliated, while magic assumes an immutable world governed by impersonal, mechanical laws that can be coerced. The work asserts that even when magic deals with personal agents such as spirits or Daedra, it constrains rather than propitiates them, subordinating all beings to impersonal forces that a skilled practitioner can manipulate through spells and ceremonies.
topic_desc_basic: A scholarly work by Ianus Gaer-Frae examining the conflict between magic and religion. It argues that religion seeks to conciliate conscious, personal powers to alter the world's course, whereas magic relies on coercing impersonal, immutable laws, treating all beings as subject to mechanical forces.

record_links.display_name: The Saint and the Left Hand

title: The Sea of Ghosts
topic_desc: Louis Renoit's treatise investigating the eponymous waters north of Skyrim. Drawing on skjalds from the Bards' College, Renoit cites verses claiming Ysgramor's fleet encountered pale, shimmering forms during their voyage from Atmora. He finds no consistent evidence for such apparitions; most mariners attribute sightings to exhaustion, fog, and aurorae, while others variously blame drowned sailors, restless Atmorans, or submerged Aldmeri dead. Renoit also documents Nordic warding traditions, including prow figureheads to frighten spirits and the custom of naming ships only after a successful maiden voyage to prove the vessel's disinterest to the sea's malignance.
topic_desc_basic: Louis Renoit's book investigating the icy waters north of Skyrim. It examines the mariner's belief in a malign presence within the sea, surveys various folk explanations for the 'ghosts,' and documents Nordic ship-naming and figurehead traditions used to ward off the water's hostile spirits.

title: The Seasons
topic_desc: A poetic work by Horatio Gargonath comprising four verses, each dedicated to a distinct phase of the natural cycle. The verses observe the sensory qualities of the changing landscape, from the blossoming flora and gentle warmth of spring to the languid, fragrant air of summer, the descending colors and migrating birds of autumn, and the serene, ice-shrouded stillness of winter. The composition celebrates the cyclical transformation of the environment, finding unique beauty and tranquility in each seasonal shift. It is found in private libraries and collections across Morrowind.
topic_desc_basic: A book of poetry by Horatio Gargonath. It features four verses celebrating the natural world, with each poem dedicated to the sensory qualities and tranquil beauty of spring, summer, autumn, and winter.

title: The Second Ami-El
topic_desc: A historical account of the succession crisis following the death of Emperor Belharza. The text details how the minotaur king Asterion, Belharza's brother, coveted the Ruby-of-Kings. When Belharza's firstborn, Belmar, claimed the Empire and invoked the divine protection of Aleshut—asserting that no child of the Mother could be harmed by another—Asterion exploited a loophole, goring Belmar with his own horns, which were kin-bone rather than a forged weapon. Asterion's followers then slaughtered Belharza's heirs, burned their remains to prevent any kin-bone weapons from being crafted against him, and retreated to the valley of Horns. The work is significant for its explanation of the minotaur schism and the fall of the early Manan dynasty.
topic_desc_basic: A historical text recounting the succession struggle after Emperor Belharza's death, in which the minotaur king Asterion usurped the Empire by slaying Belharza's heirs using his horns, bypassing the divine protection of Aleshut, and then retreating to the valley of Horns.

title: The Second Book of Lamentations
topic_desc: The Second Book of Lamentations is a Morrowind text memorializing Dunmer suffering during the Second Era invasions of Reman Cyrodiil. It recounts the sack of Ald Roryn and Kragenmoor in Sun's Height 2920, emphasizing Imperial brutality and the desecration of House Redoran holdings. The work frames General Silendai's defense of Castle Vor as a testament to unbreakable Dunmer spirit, attributing his rally and victory to Almalexia's direct intervention. Serving as both mourning liturgy and Tribunal vindication, it asserts that Morrowind's resolve and the Tribunal's destiny outlast any foreign empire.
topic_desc_basic: The Second Book of Lamentations mourns the Dunmer killed during Reman Cyrodiil's 2920 invasion of Morrowind, recording the Imperial sack of Ald Roryn and Kragenmoor and celebrating Almalexia's deliverance of General Silendai at Castle Vor.

title: The Secret Throne of Vampires
topic_desc: A polemical warning about the vampires of Cyrodiil, claiming they are invisible infiltrators who have usurped positions of power as tyrants, magistrates, mages, and plutocrats throughout the Imperial Province. The work alleges these ancient vampires were discovered dormant in the depths of a blackened jungle by the monkey-priests and moth-eaters, who allied with them before a righteous war drove the idolaters out, though some escaped to fester and breed. It asserts that these vampires scheme to command the power of Empire and counsels turning to the Emperor, the warrior orders of the killing princes who follow the word of Reman, the Templars, and the servants of Arkay for protection against the threat.
topic_desc_basic: A warning against the vampires of Cyrodiil, claiming they secretly hold power as invisible infiltrators throughout the Imperial Province and scheme to control the Empire, while urging trust in the Emperor and the servants of Arkay for protection.

title: The Seven Fights I
topic_desc: The Seven Fights of The Aldudagga, shortened from The Aldudaggavelashadingas, is a mythic cycle attributed to Bretonordic skalds. Its first fight, The Eating-Birth of Dagon, recounts the end of a kalpa when Alduin consumes the world. The Leaper Demon King and the Greedy Man confess to hiding portions of previous worlds to gradually overfill Alduin and destroy him. Enraged, Alduin curses the Leaper Demon King, stripping him of his leaping power and renaming him Dagon, banishing him to the void with limited egress until he destroys all stolen kalpic fragments. The Greedy Man traps himself inside his partially consumed mountain. The work presents a mythic origin for the destructive nature of the Daedric Prince Mehrunes Dagon and the concept of kalpic accumulation.
topic_desc_basic: The Seven Fights of The Aldudagga is a Bretonordic mythic cycle. Its first song tells how Alduin the World-Eater cursed a spirit called the Leaper Demon King, transforming him into the destructive Daedric Prince Dagon for hiding pieces of previous worlds to delay the kalpa's end.

title: The Seven Fights II
topic_desc: The second volume of The Seven Fights of the Aldudagga, excerpted from the Bretonordic Songs of Dragon and Dagon. It recounts the fall of Sarthaal, attributing the endless elven horde to Mehrunes Dagon, who pierced the veil through the city's destruction. After the Nord host freezes to death listening to Herkel the Shield-Fed's protracted speech, Dagon gloats but is knocked unconscious by King Ysgrim's hammer, Olendrung. Recognizing that killing the Daedric Prince is futile, Herkel drags the frozen dead and the insensate Dagon back to Sarthaal's ruins. He then prays to Alduin, the world-eating dragon and enemy of men, exploiting the enmity between the two powers. Alduin's intervention projects a glamour of Sarthaal intact and its host arrayed for battle; Dagon, believing he has arrived before the city's fall, retreats to the void. The tale explains the prayer-induced visions of Sarthaal and Herkel's transformation into a Clever Man.
topic_desc_basic: A Nordic legendary account from the Songs of Dragon and Dagon, telling how the warrior Herkel the Fool tricked Mehrunes Dagon into retreating from the ruins of Sarthaal by praying to Alduin for a vision of the city intact, thereby earning the title of Clever Man.

title: The Seven Fights III
topic_desc: A Nordic skaldic tale recounting how a dirtbird and a snow whale journeyed into Coldharbour to confront Molag Bal, attributing the Dirt Patch's skyward displacement to Mehrunes Dagon's meddling with Alduin's sleep. The narrative reflects the broader mythic rivalry between the World-Eater and the Prince of Destruction, framing their cosmic conflict through the strange plight of two unlikely creatures.
topic_desc_basic: A Nordic skaldic tale about a dirtbird and a snow whale traveling to Coldharbour to address the mischief of Mehrunes Dagon.

title: The Seven Fights VI
topic_desc: The sixth installment of The Seven Fights of The Aldudagga, excerpted from the Bretonordic skaldic Songs of Dragon and Dagon. This fragment, titled The 911th Cow, recounts a mythic confrontation between Alduin and Mehrunes Dagon, mediated through a Nord girl named Aless. Terrified that the World-Eater will awaken, Aless paints cows to summon Giants—whom no one fights—to drive the Dragon back to slumber. Dagon, disguised as a Clever Man, exploits her fear on his birthday, magically speeding her labors to draw the Giants down in numbers sufficient to provoke the High King into a ruinous war. The work also etiologizes the Nord tradition of painting cows with swirls to appease Giant-kin, framing it as a survival strategy born from an ancient estrangement between Nords and their ancestral Giant relations.
topic_desc_basic: A Bretonordic myth from The Aldudagga explaining the Nord tradition of painting cows with swirls to appease Giants. It tells of the girl Aless, whom Mehrunes Dagon deceived into summoning a dangerous multitude of Giants by painting herds, supposedly to protect the world from Alduin.

title: The Shoals of Septimia
topic_desc: The Shoals of Septimia is a painting created in 311 by the late Ato artist Claudia Verneti. It depicts the Imperial warship TEM Vasi Hadrach, which ran aground in 289 on the jagged rocks forming the treacherous straits off Septimia during the Akaviri invasion. The artwork reflects a major naval disaster for the Far East Fleet, which lost fifty-one ships over the three-year campaign. Of these, sixteen vessels were destroyed in the dangerous waters immediately off the Septimia landing site. The painting serves as a cultural record of the costly Second Empire military expedition and the maritime perils of the Akaviri coast.
topic_desc_basic: The Shoals of Septimia is a painting by the Ato artist Claudia Verneti. It depicts the Imperial warship TEM Vasi Hadrach, which ran aground off Septimia in 289 during the Akaviri invasion. Sixteen ships of the Far East Fleet were destroyed in those treacherous waters.

title: The Shores of Dwynnen
topic_desc: A wartime memoir by Celimalith Lenwe, a healer aboard the vessel Victory's Hand, recounting the allied assault against the Usurper's Daedric horde on the shores of Dwynnen. The text documents the fleet's bombardment, the crucial landfall aided by a storm, and the horde's subsequent rout. Lenwe displays a distinct Altmeri prejudice, doubting the Bosmer's courage and dismissing rumors that the Bosmer messenger Notorgo summoned the decisive storm from Haven. Despite her skepticism, the memoir acknowledges the combined forces of mer and men in securing the victory and credits the blessing of Syrabane for the ship's survival.
topic_desc_basic: A memoir by the healer Celimalith Lenwe describing the allied naval assault against the Usurper's Daedric horde on the shores of Dwynnen. The account covers the fleet's bombardment, the storm that enabled a crucial landfall, and the eventual rout of the enemy forces.

title: The Siege of Kvatch
topic_desc: A Colovian myth recounting one of the Fifteen Ineffectual Sieges of Kvatch. Kings Cirthes Oath-Oak of Chorral and Rein Manellis of Brumath besiege Kvatch to avenge the murder of Prince Vythu Far-Handed. After nine months, the Shore-King Cioracet arbitrates, demanding each side send a champion to slay the Ayleid king Chir-Al-Al-Boal. Hermwnthe-of-Thistles, leading the assailants, defeats the Kvetchi champion Irroth the Lark, kills the Ayleid king, but is then accused of violating the Law of Three-Days by accepting hospitality before answering a challenge. A subsequent duel ends with Hermwnthe disfiguring Irroth, forcing Kvatch to pay blood-money. The tale emphasizes the complex interplay of knightly oaths, chivalric virtue, and the laws of hospitality.
topic_desc_basic: A Colovian myth describing one of the Fifteen Ineffectual Sieges of Kvatch, resolved when champions dueled over the slaying of an Ayleid king and disputes regarding the laws of hospitality.

title: The Six Truths of Shadow
topic_desc: A mystical treatise by Pergan Asuul outlining six principles of Shadow Magic, presenting shadow as the primordial natural order predating and outlasting light. The work rejects physical sight, warmth, and mortal life as shackles of an oppressive 'Eternal Light' and its divine agents. Asuul reinterprets the Serpent constellation as the true sign of Shadow Magic rather than a void, and the Shadow sign as merely the Serpent's reflection. He describes the Veil as a frame leading to the Plain of Shadows, where consuming one's shadow selves brings wholeness. Citing Azra as his teacher, Asuul criticizes Mannimarco's lichdom as a flawed deception and Azra's own cowardice, advocating instead for retreating into shadow to evade Arkay and empower the Eternal Shadow. Nocturnal, Namira, and Shagrath are named as gods who understand this order.
topic_desc_basic: A treatise by Pergan Asuul on Shadow Magic. It presents six principles rejecting light, warmth, and life as oppressive forces, and teaches that shadow is the primordial natural order. The work reinterprets the Serpent constellation as the true source of Shadow Magic.

title: The Skylamp Night
topic_desc: An account of breaking the siege of Tear during the Arnesian War, dictated by the Dunmer serjo Vaalthys Sur-Enaren to his scribe. The narrative describes the thirty-sixth night of the siege, when starving defenders released weaponized war-netches—called skylamps—bred by Deshaan clan-families and inscribed with sigils by Tear's spellbinders. Set ablaze by flaming arrows, the trained beasts drifted into the Argonian encampment and exploded, sowing fiery chaos. The narrator portrays the ensuing sortie in vivid synesthetic terms, merging sound and color as Dunmer forces clashed with Argonian warriors and shamans. The victory resulted in captured prisoners filling slave pits and impaled Argonian warleaders marking the new border. The work reflects a distinctly Dunmer perspective, celebrating the skylamps as ancestral blessings while recording the Argonian curse "Xuth-taijleel" against them.
topic_desc_basic: A historical account of the siege of Tear during the Arnesian War, narrated by the Dunmer serjo Vaalthys Sur-Enaren. It describes the defenders' use of burning, weaponized war-netches called skylamps to break the Argonian siege and secure a Dunmer victory.

title: The Song of Pelinal, Volume 1
topic_desc: The Song of Pelinal, Volume 1 is the opening fragment of an epic historical cycle transcribed from the Reman Manuscript in the Imperial Library. The text examines the paradox of the legendary crusader Pelinal bearing an Elvish name meaning glorious knight despite being a notorious scourge of that race. It catalogues his many sobriquets—Whitestrake, for his killing-light hand; the Bloody; Insurgent; In Triumph; the Blamer; and the Third—while reflecting on his grim demeanor and white hair. The origin of his final epithet remains disputed: it may indicate he was a divine guiser with prior incarnations, or simply that he was the third vision granted to Perrif, known as Alessia, during her prayers of liberation.
topic_desc_basic: The Song of Pelinal, Volume 1 is the first part of an ancient epic cycle preserved in the Imperial Library. It explores the origins and many titles of the legendary crusader Pelinal, a fierce enemy of the Elves who paradoxically bore an Elvish name.

title: The Song of Pelinal, Volume 2
topic_desc: The second volume of the ancient epic chronicling Pelinal Whitestrake, drawn from the Reman Manuscript in the Imperial Library. This fragment, transcribed by an unknown early Second Era scholar from older fragments of uncertain date, recounts the knight's supernatural arrival. It describes the rebel leader Perrif praying to Kyne for the power to sunder the Ayleidoon masters, equating the desired freedom with the missing god Shezarr. In response, Kyne grants a red diamond symbol that forms into Pelin-El, the Star-Made Knight, clad in armor from a future time. Accompanied by the demiprince Morihaus, Pelinal enters the Cyrod jungles and presents the rebel camp with Ayleid chieftains' remains upon his weapons, declaring an end to their rule.
topic_desc_basic: An epic fragment from the Reman Manuscript recounting Pelinal Whitestrake's arrival during the Alessian Revolt. It describes the rebel leader Perrif praying to Kyne for freedom from the Ayleids, and the goddess sending the Star-Made Knight in otherworldly armor to aid the human uprising.

title: The Song of Pelinal, Volume 3
topic_desc: The third volume of the ancient epic chronicling the Alessian Rebellion, transcribed from the Reman Manuscript in the Imperial Library. It focuses on Pelinal Whitestrake's campaign of single combat against Ayleid sorcerer-kings, detailing his defeats of Haromir, Gordhaur the Shaper, and Hadhuul. The text notes his enigmatic armor, impervious to Ayleid weapons, and recounts his first Madness—a devastating rampage triggered by the death of his companion Huna. The volume culminates at the storming of White-Gold, where the Ayleids summon the Aurorans of Meridia and appoint Umaril the Unfeathered as their champion. Umaril, a golden-hued half-Elf bearing the blood of the ada, is the first to call Pelinal to battle rather than the reverse, possessing immortality that poses an unprecedented threat.
topic_desc_basic: An ancient epic volume chronicling Pelinal Whitestrake's battles against the Ayleid sorcerer-kings during the Alessian Rebellion. It recounts his slaying of several Ayleid lords, his first devastating Madness, and the arrival of the Ayleids' immortal champion, Umaril the Unfeathered, at White-Gold.

title: The Song of Pelinal, Volume 4
topic_desc: The fourth volume of the ancient poetic compilation chronicling the Alessian Rebellion, drawn from the Reman Manuscript housed in the Imperial Library. This fragment, transcribed by an unknown early Second Era scholar from older sources of uncertain date, catalogs Pelinal Whitestrake's martial deeds. It recounts his driving of Ayleid sorcerer armies past the Niben, the liberation of prisoners at the Vahtache, and the recovery of severed hands from the Sedor tribe. The text also describes the first Pogrom, the arrival of Nord allies whom Pelinal angrily rejected as mistaken for Shor, and his battlefield defense of the wounded Morihaus against Umaril's Thundernachs. The fragment culminates at the Council of Skiffs, where Pelinal, furious at the allies' fear and Alessia's counsel of delay, set out alone to assault the Tower of White-Gold.
topic_desc_basic: A volume of the ancient epic chronicling the Alessian Rebellion. This fragment recounts the warrior Pelinal Whitestrake's military campaigns against the Ayleids, his liberation of enslaved humans, and his furious, solitary march to assault the Tower of White-Gold after the allied armies hesitated.

title: The Song of Pelinal, Volume 5
topic_desc: The Song of Pelinal, Volume 5: On His Love of Morihaus
topic_desc_basic: The Song of Pelinal, Volume 5

title: The Song of Pelinal, Volume 6
topic_desc: This volume of the Song of Pelinal, subtitled 'On His Madness,' is preserved in the so-called Reman Manuscript of the Imperial Library, a transcription of older fragments gathered by an unknown early Second Era scholar. No scholarly consensus exists on dating the source fragments. The text examines Pelinal Whitestrake's divine madness during the Alessian revolt against the Ayleids. It records conflicting accounts of his nature—some calling him Padomaic, borne by Sithis; others, like Fifd of New Teed, claiming his star-armor concealed no heart but a diamond-shaped red rage, marking him as a myth-echo. The fragment describes his fits of rampage that devoured whole lands into Void, requiring Alessia's prayers and the Gods' collective intervention to soothe him. The volume is significant for its mythological speculation on Pelinal's nature and its depiction of divine madness as both destructive force and metaphysical condition.
topic_desc_basic: The Song of Pelinal, Volume 6, subtitled 'On His Madness,' is a fragment of the epic cycle preserved in the Reman Manuscript of the Imperial Library.
