It recounts Pelinal Whitestrake's divine madness during the Alessian revolt, describing his uncontrollable rampages that devoured lands into Void and required Alessia's prayers to the Gods to soothe him. The text also speculates on his myth-echo nature.

title: The Song of Pelinal, Volume 7
topic_desc: A fragmentary epic recounting Pelinal Whitestrake's climactic battle against the half-Elf Umaril and his subsequent dismemberment. Recovered from the Alessian monastery at Lake Canulus, the manuscript predates the War of Righteousness, though textual analysis suggests it preserves a mid-sixth-century form of the Song. The text depicts Umaril favoring ranged assault from the white tower, sending soldiers wielding varliance-imbued weapons that finally draw Pelinal's blood. After Umaril reveals himself bathed in Meridian light and claims descent from a god of a previous kalpa, Pelinal defeats and mutilates him. Pelinal's insults against the Ayleid kings provoke a mad assault that cuts him into eight pieces. Morihaus finds the severed head the following morning and speaks with Pelinal, whose regrets remain unrecorded. The fragment preserves obscure mythic references, including the Council of Skiffs and Old Ehlnofey.
topic_desc_basic: An epic fragment covering Pelinal Whitestrake's battle against the half-Elf Umaril, his victory, and his dismemberment by enraged Ayleid kings. Morihaus discovers Pelinal's severed head the next morning.

title: The Song of Pelinal, Volume 8
topic_desc: The Song of Pelinal, Volume 8: On His Revelation at the Death of the Al-Esh is the oldest and most fragmentary existing text of the Pelinal cycle, likely preserving the closest form to the original oral tradition. It recounts Pelinal's apparent presence at the deathbed of Alessia, an event presenting a significant narrative contradiction, as he was slain by Umaril years prior to her death. While some scholars dispute the fragment's inclusion in the Song, most accept its authenticity despite ongoing debate over its meaning. The surviving text features Pelinal speaking of his "other half," the divine joy found in the mortal concept of freedom, and cryptic references to the time before Convention. It concludes with an offer to take the dying Al-Esh "Up" and a disturbing revelation of true faces that "eat one another in amnesia each Age."
topic_desc_basic: The Song of Pelinal, Volume 8 is the oldest and most fragmentary text of the Pelinal cycle. It records Pelinal's apparent presence at the deathbed of Alessia, despite his death years earlier, and contains cryptic dialogue on freedom and divine faces.

title: The Stone of Septimia
topic_desc: The Stone of Septimia is a great violet gemstone seized by Imperial Legions from an ornate Tsaesci riverboat in Septimia's harbor during the 288 Akavir invasion. Uriel V commissioned an amulet to hold it, intending it as regalia for his prospective Akavir Province. Thought lost after the Ionith disaster, it surfaced in 335 on a Bosmer's mantelpiece in Bravil; the retired scout had stolen it from Uriel's quarters. Confiscated by Empress Morihatha, its discovery spurred public calls for a second invasion, which she firmly refused. Kept at White-Gold Tower, Uriel VII later loaned it to the Firewatch College museum's Akavir Invasion collection, where it currently resides.
topic_desc_basic: The Stone of Septimia is a large violet gemstone the Imperial Legions captured from the Tsaesci during Uriel V's Akavir invasion. Long thought lost after the Ionith disaster, it resurfaced in Bravil and was returned to the Empire. Uriel VII currently loans it to the Firewatch College museum in Morrowind.

title: The Story of Lyrisius
topic_desc: Bresne Smythe's legendary account of the First Era hero Lyrisius, who fought the Akaviri slavetraders. After his army was routed, Lyrisius encountered a wyrm that destroyed his Boethiah-gifted shield, Fearstruck. Unable to defeat the beast by arms, he exploited its vanity, climbing upon its back and wounding its vulnerable spot. He coerced the wyrm into destroying the Akaviri army before leaping from its back. Boethiah then transformed him into a raven to escape the creature's wrath. The legend claims the wyrm survives, nursing a grudge against all weapon-bearing mortals. A scholarly note observes that if the tale is factual, the artifact Fearstruck was permanently destroyed, as no other reference to it exists.
topic_desc_basic: A legendary tale by Bresne Smythe about the First Era hero Lyrisius, who outwitted a prideful wyrm into destroying an invading Akaviri army. The story also claims Boethiah transformed Lyrisius into a raven and that his Daedric shield, Fearstruck, was destroyed.

title: The Supposition of Freedom
topic_desc: A philosophical treatise written as a response to Iman Kanten's The Purity of Freedom. The anonymous author challenges Kanten's assertion that freedom operates independently of action and the physical world, arguing instead that mortal freedom is severely constrained by two factors: the binding power of prophecy and the stasis-embodied nature of the Aedra. The work contends that prophecy governs both thought and action, leaving little true autonomy, and questions whether the unchanging Aedra could even impart genuine freedom to their creations. Though it raises profound questions about determinism and divine nature, the author concedes that definitive answers remain elusive, framing the inquiry itself as vital to sentient existence.
topic_desc_basic: A philosophical treatise responding to Iman Kanten's The Purity of Freedom. It argues that mortal freedom is heavily constrained by the power of prophecy and the stasis-embodied nature of the Aedra, challenging the idea that freedom exists independently of action and the physical world.

title: The Tale of Dro'Zira
topic_desc: A transcribed Khajiiti oral tale with commentary by the Imperial scholar Sonia Vette, who overheard a moonsugar-influenced father recounting the legend to his cub. The narrative claims ancient Khajiit served Alkosh as warriors until Lorkhaj, envious of their devotion, granted his roar to Wulfharth. Wulfharth used this power to force Masser and Secunda to fullness, transforming the Khajiiti warriors into the reason-stripped Senche. Only Dro'Zira, an honored ancestor, retained enough memory to answer Wulfharth's summons at Red Mountain. The tale asserts Dro'Zira carried the Ash King into battle and pounced upon Dumac to save Wulfharth's life, earning resurrection from Lorkhaj. It dismisses Nord bards for omitting these deeds and denounces the other transformed Rhojiit as cunning-less creatures. Vette notes the account appears boastful but raises questions about unrecorded Khajiiti roles in widely known events.
topic_desc_basic: A transcribed Khajiiti oral legend with commentary by the scholar Sonia Vette. It recounts the ancestor Dro'Zira's role in the Battle of Red Mountain, claiming he carried Wulfharth into battle and saved him from Dumac, deeds Nord bards allegedly omit. The tale also explains the Senche's origin as Khajiiti warriors stripped of reason by Lorkhaj.

title: The Tale of King Vrage's Sons
topic_desc: An ancient epic poem recounting the saga of King Vrage the Gifted and his three sons, who continued his conquests across Merethland. Vrage, recognizing his limited lifespan, sired three sons with a hill giantess, a daughter of Hircine, and an elven princess. The elven smith Durendaalo forged each a weapon of steel and godsblood ore. After Vrage fell battling the war-elves of Oran the Red, his sons—Hrygg the Strong, Ulfgyir the huntsman, and Vrigyn Half-Blood—avenged him and waged relentless war until their own deaths. They were buried with their weapons at Hryggsholv, Ulfengraf, and Dwimmereld. The poem frames this cycle of vengeance as enduring through generations until the Nords departed Merethland.
topic_desc_basic: An ancient epic poem about King Vrage the Gifted and his three sons, who avenged his death in battle against the war-elves of Merethland and continued his conquests wielding weapons forged of godsblood ore.

record_links.display_name: The Tale of King Vrage's Sons

title: The Talhjolde Companion
topic_desc: A scholarly companion to the Talhjolde, or Song-Stories, published by the Imperial University Press in 3E 421. Curated by the Committee for the Transposition of Indigenous Oral Traditions, it presents academic analyses of six tales linking contemporary Tamrielic culture to Atmoran Nordic roots. The scholars emphasize that these translated songs are neither original Nordic tales nor accurate representations of Atmoran totemic religion. Hakan at-Hatan notes linguistic anachronisms in "Whale's Sorrow" regarding Stuhn and Stendarr. Elvyra Aumilie highlights the distinct Allfather and Fox characters in "Allfather's Riddle." Batul gra-Brok examines the Adversary and non-kalpic end of Nirn in "The Angry Bear." Johannes Silvanus discusses displaced Atmoran archetypes like the Frost Maiden in "Wise Wolf." Basil al-Taneth analyzes forged familiarity in "The Same Question" and its limited post-Atmoran application. Dagny of the Tower traces later southeastern skaldic additions of Orcs to "The Snake of Chaos."
topic_desc_basic: A scholarly companion to the Talhjolde, or Song-Stories, published by the Imperial University Press. It provides academic commentary on six traditional tales, exploring their origins, meanings, and significance as links between contemporary Tamrielic culture and ancient Atmoran Nordic roots.

title: The Talking Guar of Vhul I
topic_desc: A skeptical analysis by Urven Andrelo examining the legend of Mudfoot, a guar near Vhul that supposedly spoke, warned its owner of danger, and entertained townsfolk for years. Andrelo recounts the tale of the farmer Balyn Omathan before promising to refute rational explanations, driven by personal curiosity and his grandfather's alleged witness account lost to the Arnesian War.
topic_desc_basic: Urven Andrelo's skeptical study recounting the legend of Mudfoot, a guar near Vhul that allegedly spoke and entertained townsfolk for years.

record_links.display_name: The Talking Guar of Vhul I

title: The Talking Guar of Vhul II
topic_desc: The second volume of Urven Andrelo's analytical study on the legendary talking guar of Vhul, named Mudfoot. Andrelo systematically dismisses the leading explanations for the phenomenon: that the farmer Balyn Omathan orchestrated a hoax, that a wizard manipulated the beast, or that Daedric trickery was involved. He also refutes the notion that the tale is a mere modern fabrication by presenting archival evidence from the Old Ebonheart tax and census office. An official 3E 358 report from tax collector Goras Indavel, bound by honor-oath, confirms he witnessed the guar speak and recorded Balyn's secondary income as a street performer. While Andrelo establishes the event's historical authenticity, he concludes that the mechanism and purpose behind Mudfoot's speech remain an enduring mystery.
topic_desc_basic: A scholarly analysis by Urven Andrelo investigating the legend of Mudfoot, a guar in Vhul that reportedly spoke. The book uses Imperial tax records to prove the story is not a fabrication and that the guar's owner, Balyn Omathan, actually profited from displaying the creature, though how it spoke remains unexplained.

record_links.display_name: The Talking Guar of Vhul II

title: The Ten Commandments
topic_desc: A doctrinal text of the Nine Divines faith, presented as ten concise commands revealed through Akatosh for impatient mortals. Each of the first nine commandments is attributed to a specific Divine—Stendarr, Arkay, Mara, Zenithar, Talos, Kynareth, Dibella, Julianos, and Akatosh—prescribing virtues such as charity, reverence for the dead, family peace, honest labor, martial courage, respect for nature, love of art, pursuit of truth, and obedience to the Emperor and the Covenants. The tenth command, spoken by the Nine collectively, exhorts mutual goodness. The work frames obedience as the path to divine blessing and comfort, while wickedness brings spiritual burden. However, it emphasizes that the Nine are merciful: sinners may repent, pay fines to the Emperor, perform good works, and redeem their infamy to regain the grace and blessings of the chapels.
topic_desc_basic: A religious text presenting ten commands of the Nine Divines, each attributed to a Divine, prescribing virtues like charity, reverence for the dead, honest labor, and obedience to the Emperor. It teaches that obedience brings blessing, while sinners may repent and perform good works to regain divine grace.

title: The Third Ami-El
topic_desc: A legendary account of Amet, the castaway horned child of Belharza, and the supernatural inheritance of the Empire of Aleshut. On the day of Belharza's death, the river Niben directs Amet to a mourning-ash bull embodying the composite spirits of Morihaus, Belharza, and Asterion. The apparition reveals Amet's true lineage as Belharza's last heir and brands a diamond sign of office into her hand, simultaneously condemning her as a kin-murderer whose birth caused her mother Llesa's death. It charges Amet to defeat her uncle, the white Asterion, who has murdered her siblings and holds court in the valley of Horns. The work frames the succession through the conflicting Nibenese currents of divine right and ancestral curse, leaving Amet stricken with an unquenchable fever from the bull's fiery brand.
topic_desc_basic: A legendary tale of Amet, the horned child of Belharza, who learns of her royal lineage from a mourning bull on the banks of the Niben. The apparition brands her with the diamond sign of the Aleshut Empire and tasks her with defeating her uncle, Asterion.

title: The Travels of Tyal Direnni
topic_desc: A First Era travel account by the Elven diplomat Tyal Direnni, describing his journey through early Alessian Cyrodiil. Direnni observes the human Coloi rulers as proud and hospitable barbarians, notes the restricted but tolerated status of Ayleid scholars within their enclaves, and records details of the wild jungle lowlands, agricultural practices, coastal raiding threats, and the overwhelming spectacle of the Rumaranth citadel. Though colored by Elven bias, the work is treasured as one of the few surviving sources on pre-Marukhati Imperial culture.
topic_desc_basic: A First Era travel account by the Elven diplomat Tyal Direnni describing early Alessian Cyrodiil. Though biased, it is treasured as one of the few surviving sources on pre-Marukhati Imperial culture.

title: The Trials of Saint Alessia
topic_desc: An excerpt from the liturgy of the Re-Kindling of the Dragonfires, this work recounts the covenant between Akatosh and Saint Alessia. It describes how the Dragon God gathered the essence of Oblivion and bound it with his Heart's blood to create the Amulet of Kings, establishing a pact between the King of Spirits and the Queen of Mortals. The text affirms that so long as an heir of their joined blood wears the Amulet and the dragonfires burn, Akatosh's blood holds the Gates of Oblivion closed and the Empire endures. Should the fires fail and no rightful heir wear the Amulet, the text warns that the Demon Lords of Misrule will govern the land. The work is foundational to Imperial religious and political doctrine regarding the Dragonblood and the Empire's divine protection.
topic_desc_basic: A liturgical excerpt recounting the covenant between Akatosh and Saint Alessia. It describes the creation of the Amulet of Kings and establishes that so long as a Dragonblood heir wears it and the dragonfires burn, the Gates of Oblivion remain sealed and the Empire endures.

title: The True Folk
topic_desc: A polemical treatise by Haller arguing that the Orsimer are the truest of mer because they alone remained faithful to Trinimac after Boethiah consumed and transformed him into Malacath. The work recounts the familiar origin myth in which Trinimac's faithful followers bore his corruption upon their bodies, becoming green-skinned and brutish in appearance, while those Altmer who abandoned him retained their golden form. Haller inverts the usual Aldmeri judgment: the Orsimer's ugliness reflects steadfast loyalty, while the unchanged Altmer's beauty masks hollowness and moral failure. The Chimer and later Dunmer are likewise condemned as corrupt celebrants of Boethiah's foulness. The treatise frames Orsimer pariah status as proof of genuine faith and honor rather than shame, and dismisses other mer as shells of falsehood. The work stands as a rare pro-Orsimer theological argument grounded in the Trinimac-Malacath transformation narrative.
topic_desc_basic: A book by Haller arguing that the Orsimer, or Orcs, are the truest of mer. It recounts how those Altmer who stayed faithful to Trinimac after Boethiah transformed him into Malacath bore his corruption upon their bodies, while those who abandoned him kept their golden appearance. Haller contends that Orsimer ugliness reflects loyalty and honor, and that other mer are hollow despite their beauty.

title: The True Houses
topic_desc: A commemorative work celebrating the unity of the Great Houses during the War of the First Council. It recounts how each House contributed its unique strengths to the Resdaynian armies under Hortator Nerevar and the Tribunal: Indoril's faith, Redoran's martial valor, Dres's spiritual fortitude, Telvanni's arcane mastery, and Hlaalu's organizational discipline. The text serves as a patriotic reminder of their shared stand against the Dwemer at Red Mountain, urging readers to set aside contemporary political divisions and remember the foundational alliance that preserved Resdayn.
topic_desc_basic: A book celebrating the Great Houses' alliance during the War of the First Council, praising each House's unique contribution to the war effort against the Dwemer.

title: The Truth of the Bear Clan
topic_desc: A polemical work defending the Bear Clan of the Reach against persistent aspersions. The anonymous author traces the clan's history from the arrival of Clan-Father Rigmad Bearhand, who settled a remote stretch of the Karth-River and drove out local Reachmen. Generations of isolation altered their appearance, sparking false accusations of interbreeding with those same Reachmen; the author attributes their looks to incest instead. The settlement became Karthgad, the Guard of Karth, and earned renown for its ambush tactics against Redguard invaders in the dense Vorndgad Forest. The author rebuts claims of cowardice, insisting the terrain forbade open battle. Now, with the frontier pushed westward, King Barda assigns the clan only dishonorable tasks, and new slanders paint them as greedy criminals. The text stands as a bitter plea for recognition of past glories.
topic_desc_basic: A work defending the Bear Clan of the Reach against accusations of cowardice, interbreeding with Reachmen, and criminality. It recounts their history as frontier defenders at Karthgad and laments their current diminished standing under King Barda.

record_links.display_name: The Truth of the Bear Clan

title: The Unseen People
topic_desc: The Unseen People is an adventure narrative of unknown authorship recounting the journey of Erur Dan, a Bosmer from Dagon Fel in Sheogorad, who ventures into Skyrim's tundra seeking the fabled Falmer. The tale follows his struggle against extreme cold, wolf attacks, and despair, culminating in his arrival at Windhelm. Throughout the journey, unexplained phenomena—ice mysteriously patching his damaged armor, timely good fortune—suggest the presence of an unseen benefactor. The closing passage implies that the unseen people Dan sought do indeed exist. The work blends wilderness survival with speculation on the Falmer's continued existence and touches on themes of determination and providence.
topic_desc_basic: The Unseen People is an adventure tale of unknown authorship following Erur Dan, a Bosmer from Dagon Fel, who braves Skyrim's frozen wilderness in search of the fabled Falmer. The narrative recounts his survival against bitter cold and wolves, his arrival in Windhelm, and hints of unseen supernatural aid throughout his journey.

title: The Uprising in Almalexia
topic_desc: This compilation, edited by Ottrebus Auriil, presents three witness accounts from the Imperial Commission for Post-Simulacrum Restoration archives concerning the 3E 391 peasant uprising in Almalexia. The testimonies—a rickshaw operator who observed foreign agitators inciting the revolt, a household guard who witnessed Lord Symmachus struck down by stones while attempting to pacify the crowd, and a Temple caretaker who saw the dying Symmachus denied an audience by Almalexia—offer conflicting perspectives on the regent's death and the rebellion's origins. The editor notes the likely involvement of Jagar Tharn's spies and disputes the popular claim that Symmachus died by an assassin's poison, while the caretaker's account records Symmachus's final, unheeded call to the Houses to turn against the Empire. The work provides significant, if contradictory, insight into the chaos that precipitated Morrowind's civil war and border conflicts during the Imperial Simulacrum.
topic_desc_basic: A compilation of three witness accounts edited by Ottrebus Auriil from Imperial archives, detailing the 3E 391 peasant uprising in Almalexia, the foreign agitation that fueled it, and the controversial death of Lord Symmachus.

title: The Uprising, part I
topic_desc: A narrative by Cunius Maximus depicting a violent slave uprising on a Dunmer saltrice plantation. The story follows Publicus Larconius, an Imperial enslaved after a shipwreck, and his companions Lakene and Jeroird. Their liberation is facilitated by the Twin Lamps, who secretly provide a key and knife. The freed slaves overwhelm the plantation guards—aided significantly by Jeroird's destructive magic—and execute the manor lord in retribution for their bondage. The work presents the Twin Lamps as active liberators and portrays the institution of Morrowind slavery from the perspective of the enslaved, emphasizing both its brutality and the potential for bloody reprisal.
topic_desc_basic: A story by Cunius Maximus about a violent slave uprising on a Dunmer saltrice plantation, triggered when the abolitionist Twin Lamps secretly provide the means for the slaves' liberation.

title: The Uprising, part II
topic_desc: A fictional narrative by Cunius Maximus, continuing the story of a slave uprising in southern Morrowind. The work follows Glavinis Leranu, a Dunmer plantation guard captain, as he hunts an escaped Argonian slave through the forest. The search party discovers a wounded Dunmer guard instead, who reveals details of a successful slave rebellion at a neighboring plantation. The escaped Argonian, Okaw-Geis, reaches the liberated plantation and warns its leaders, Publicus and Jeroird, that the wounded guard has exposed their identities and uprising to his captors, placing them in imminent danger. The story highlights the precariousness of escaped slaves' freedom and the ever-present threat of Dunmer retaliation.
topic_desc_basic: A story by Cunius Maximus about a slave uprising in southern Morrowind. It follows Dunmer guards hunting an escaped Argonian who warns the freed slaves that their rebellion has been exposed to a nearby plantation master.

title: The War of the Birds
topic_desc: An opera composed by Antho Sarastro in the Imperial tradition, translated from its original Middle-Cyrodiis. The work dramatizes the final days of the Ayleid lord Haromir of Copper and Tea, who opposed the Alessian Rebellion. The narrative portrays Haromir receiving word of his brother Malomir's defeat at the hands of the champion Pelinal and the forces of the Nameless Slave Paravant. It subsequently follows Haromir's march toward Sancre Tor, depicting the Ayleid perspective on the conflict through a lens of loss and defiance. The opera characterizes the Ayleid lords as practitioners of redeeming arts and views the rebellion as a defilement of sacred sites, offering a rare dramatized counterpoint to orthodox Alessian narratives.
topic_desc_basic: An Imperial opera by Antho Sarastro depicting the last days of the Ayleid lord Haromir of Copper and Tea during the Alessian Rebellion. The work dramatizes Haromir's reaction to his brother Malomir's defeat by Pelinal and his subsequent march on Sancre Tor.

title: The Warped West
topic_desc: An autobiographical account by Sonnette Agusere describing her firsthand experience of the Warp in the West. Agusere recounts the fracturing of time when Akatosh faltered as the Brass God activated, causing her to exist simultaneously across six overlapping timelines. She describes the subsequent collapse of these temporal threads into a single reality and the profound disjointment this caused between the affected western provinces and the rest of Tamriel. Beyond the known political and geographical changes, Agusere expresses a lingering dread that the temporal disruption allowed some unseen anomaly to slip into existence undetected.
topic_desc_basic: An autobiographical account by Sonnette Agusere detailing her firsthand experience of the Warp in the West, a temporal fracturing in High Rock and Hammerfell caused by the activation of the Brass God.

title: The Water-getting Girl, Part I
topic_desc: A traditional Kothri folk-story, reputedly Tiber Septim's favorite childhood tale, presented in a drum-accompanied oral performance style. The narrative follows a young girl named Perrif who encounters a talking 'Welcome Stone' near a Topal tributary while fetching water amid tiger-infested jungle. The stone, which absorbs the thoughts of those who touch it, gradually manifests a tiger-like visage reflecting Perrif's fear, before she kicks it into the river. The translator's preface suggests the stone's true identity as Orlyan the Inverse Tiger holds special significance, a notion promised to clarify in the story's second installment. The work preserves cultural details of pre-Imperial Kothringi life, including supplication to Dibe-Mara-Kin and 'Around-Us' cosmology.
topic_desc_basic: A traditional Kothringi folk-tale about a girl named Perrif and a strange tiger-like stone, widely known as Tiber Septim's favorite childhood bedtime story.

title: The Wealth of Wayrest
topic_desc: The Wealth of Wayrest is a western classic play set among the royalty of High Rock. Its scenes depict Breton lords attended by musicians and retainers, featuring roles such as a court fool, a mysterious cloaked figure, a nurse, and an old bookkeeper. The work is currently being staged by a Dunmer theater company in Morrowind. The production faces practical challenges outfitting Breton characters, relying on Cyrodiilic fashions and Nord props to suggest western settings. The director delegates much of the work to focus on her own writing, considering the piece unremarkable but necessary to satisfy outlander audiences and secure revenue. The staging also draws visual inspiration from a book about Daggerfall for its backdrops.
topic_desc_basic: The Wealth of Wayrest is a classic western play about High Rock royalty. A Dunmer theater company in Morrowind currently stages it to satisfy outlander audiences, using Cyrodiilic clothing and Nord props to approximate Breton fashions.

title: The Wealth of Wayrest, Act I
topic_desc: The Wealth of Wayrest, Act I is the opening segment of a four-act play by Muncia Naintes. Set in Wayrest during the New Year, it dramatizes a pivotal visit by Prince Gothryd of Daggerfall to the court of King Eadwyre. The scenes depict political discussions regarding Imperial funding for a Wrothgarian fort and Wayrest's commercial ambitions, alongside the court's mourning for the late Queen Carolyna. A court fool provides allegorical commentary on Dunmer and Dwemer history. The act culminates in ominous prophecy from the bookkeeper Palathinian, who warns of the city's destruction and Eadwyre's death by a betrayer before a daedric fire engulfs the streets.
topic_desc_basic: The Wealth of Wayrest is a four-act play by Muncia Naintes. Its first act dramatizes Prince Gothryd's visit to King Eadwyre's court in Wayrest, covering their political alliance and the court's grief over the late Queen Carolyna, before a prophetic warning of betrayal and a destructive fire cuts the festivities short.

record_links.display_name: The Wealth of Wayrest, Act I
The Wealth of Wayrest, Act I

title: The Wealth of Wayrest, Act II
topic_desc: The second act of Muncia Naintes's four-act drama The Wealth of Wayrest. King Eadwyre survives a palace fire, claiming Kynareth appeared to bless his planned eastern invasion and grant him invincibility by Akatosh. To fund this war despite his depleted military, Eadwyre schemes with Marithyn to strand Prince Gothyrd in the Gro-Kar Forest, fabricate a barbarian kidnapping, and extort funds from King Lysandus of Daggerfall. Meanwhile, Gothyrd's retinue traverses the Wrothgar gap, where he and Banthas reflect on the impermanence of gods and mortal memory near the Cauisian cliffs. Banthas privately doubts the prince's leadership, sensing impending disaster. The act explores divine mandate as a mask for political conspiracy and the fragility of historical truth.
topic_desc_basic: The second act of Muncia Naintes's play The Wealth of Wayrest, a drama of High Rock court intrigue. It depicts King Eadwyre claiming a divine vision to justify war while secretly plotting to strand Prince Gothyrd and extort King Lysandus of Daggerfall for funds.

record_links.display_name: The Wealth of Wayrest, Act II

title: The Wealth of Wayrest, Act III
topic_desc: The third act of Muncia Naintes's four-act drama, depicting the martial and political tensions among the allied forces of the Iliac Bay during a campaign against the Nords. The scenes follow Wulfharth's Nordic army descending into Wrothgar, the fractious strategic councils between Eadwyre of Wayrest, Tarinketh's Camoran forces, and Fatian of Daggerfall, and the growing suspicion of betrayal. A dark cloaked figure separately visits Eadwyre and Wulfharth, promising each ruler absolute victory and manipulating their movements, while Daggerfall's leadership grows distrustful of Wayrest's motives after a prophet warns of Eadwyre's betrayal.
topic_desc_basic: The third act of Muncia Naintes's four-act play, depicting the fractious Breton and Nord campaign in the Wrothgar highlands and the manipulation of its leaders by a mysterious cloaked figure.

record_links.display_name: The Wealth of Wayrest, Act III

title: The Wealth of Wayrest, Act IV
topic_desc: The Wealth of Wayrest, Act IV is the concluding installment of Muncia Naintes's dramatic cycle, staging the Breton defeat at Wrothgar and its political aftermath. The narrative follows King Eadwyre's disastrous military campaign against Nordic forces, where a cloaked figure's sorcery buries the Wayrest army in ice. In Wayrest, King Lysandus receives news of the loss and arranges border adjustments with the Empire, reflecting on the burdens of endurance over mere rule. General Marithyn assumes public blame for the retreat, dissolving his oath to Eadwyre. Meanwhile, the Nord leader Wulfharth halts his advance at the reclaimed borders, citing divine mandate. A closing monologue by the cloaked figure implies Wulfharth's supernatural return. The work examines the limits of ambition, the weight of sovereignty, and the intersection of mortal conflict and otherworldly intervention.
topic_desc_basic: The Wealth of Wayrest, Act IV is the final part of Muncia Naintes's historical play. It dramatizes King Eadwyre's military defeat in Wrothgar against Nordic forces, the political fallout in Wayrest, and Wulfharth's decision to halt his advance at the reclaimed borders.

record_links.display_name: The Wealth of Wayrest, Act IV

title: The Wider Empire
topic_desc: The Wider Empire is a scholarly classification for historical and biographical literature concerning the human provinces of Tamriel, the southern provinces of Summerset Isle, Valenwood, Elsweyr, and Black Marsh, and lands beyond Tamriel. This category encompasses events and peoples external to Morrowind. Texts addressing the general history of Morrowind or the Empire are classified separately.
topic_desc_basic: The Wider Empire is a library classification for historical and biographical texts about the human and southern provinces of Tamriel, including Summerset Isle, Valenwood, Elsweyr, and Black Marsh, as well as lands beyond Tamriel. It covers events and peoples outside Morrowind.

title: The Woodcutter's Wife
topic_desc: A folk tale attributed to Mogen Son of Molag, recounting a story of mistrust, murder, and magic. It tells of a starving woodcutter's family given magical aid by a traveler, and the wife who feared a hidden price and murdered their benefactor. With his dying breath, the mage cursed her to walk the pine forest as a weeping, axe-wielding specter that burns at sunrise. The tale serves as both a moral warning against suspicion and a local explanation for a nocturnal apparition.
topic_desc_basic: A folk tale by Mogen Son of Molag about a woodcutter's wife who murders a mage aiding her starving family, earning a curse that dooms her to haunt the pine forest as a weeping specter.

title: The Worship of the Ashlanders
topic_desc: A scholarly text preserving the lectures of a Kushimmu Wise Woman on Ashlander Daedra veneration, translated by the Altmer Cantur Caelmoryn. The work rejects the Temple's dichotomy of Good and Bad Daedra, asserting that the Daedra simply exist as teachers and testers whose power mortals must engage with cautiously. It presents a distinct Ashlander cosmology: Mephala embodies duality and creation-destruction; Boethiah teaches relentless cunning and perseverance; Azura governs transitions and balance; Malacath serves as a warning against rigidity and exile; Mehrunes Dagon acts as a destructive sculptor clearing the way for renewal; Molag Bal represents corrupted authority and the vital counterbalance of wise counsel; and Sheogorath is a dangerous, chaotic force to be directed at enemies but kept from the tribes. The text is a significant record of Ashlander theology contrasting sharply with Tribunal doctrine.
topic_desc_basic: A translated record of a Wise Woman's teachings on Ashlander Daedra worship. It explains that Ashlanders reject the Temple's division of Daedra into good and evil, instead revering them all as teachers and testers who embody dualities of creation, destruction, and change.

title: Thirrine Water Lily
topic_desc: Thirrine water lilies are pink-petaled flowers growing in the waters along the banks of the Thirr River in Morrowind, surrounded by distinctive orange lily pads. The harvested petals serve as an alchemical ingredient valued for their riverine origin and floral properties.
topic_desc_basic: Thirrine water lilies are pink flowers with orange lily pads that grow along the Thirr River in Morrowind. Their petals are used as an alchemical ingredient.

title: Thoricles' Bane
topic_desc: Thoricles' Bane is a grandiosely named but brutally functional executioner's axe that played a notorious role in Imperial history. It was used to execute Councilman Thoricles Romus for treason against the Empire. The weapon bears a powerful enchantment, though its utility is constrained by a single charge. The axe is currently a sought-after collector's piece, valued at tens of thousands of septims by those with esoteric or antiquarian interests.
topic_desc_basic: Thoricles' Bane is a large executioner's axe famous for its role in Imperial history, having been used to execute the treasonous Councilman Thoricles Romus.

title: Thorntail Berry
topic_desc: Thorntail berries are harvested from thorntails, a plant species native to Elsweyr. As a regional floral ingredient, they are commonly categorized among the fruit and edible flora of the Khajiiti homeland. Alchemists and hunters value them for their alchemical properties, and they circulate through Elsweyr's supply networks via general ingredient and food distributions.
topic_desc_basic: Thorntail berries grow on thorntail plants native to Elsweyr. They serve as both a food fruit and an alchemical ingredient in the region.

title: Three Deaths of House Mora
topic_desc: A lament by Queen Lian Mora, self-proclaimed last of House Mora's line, recounting the destruction of her house through successive betrayals and deaths. The work frames each ancestor—Mora Kronin, Mora Cruethys, and the Witch-King Mora Elyn—as dying twice: first through spiritual or moral failure, then through physical demise or supernatural return. Lian mourns her brother Mora Nerevar and a mysterious 'skin-stranger,' and describes House Mora's collective deaths at the hands of 'northern men' and a catastrophic flood of fire and sea. The text concludes with the assertion that three deaths are required for rebirth, as Lian faces her own second death.
topic_desc_basic: A lament by Queen Lian Mora, last of her line, chronicling the fall of House Mora. It describes how her ancestors each died twice—first through moral or spiritual failure, then physically—and recounts the house's destruction by northern conquerors and catastrophe, concluding that three deaths bring rebirth.

title: Thresher Claw
topic_desc: Thresher claws are harvested from canyon threshers, predatory fauna indigenous to the Shipal-Shin region of Morrowind. Alchemists prize these claws for their inherent properties, which are extracted through standard preparation techniques. The ingredient circulates reliably through regional supply networks, particularly around Narsis, and is commonly stocked via trade lists specializing in local fauna and regional alchemical reagents.
topic_desc_basic: Thresher claws are taken from canyon threshers, predators native to the Shipal-Shin region of Morrowind. They are a familiar regional alchemical ingredient.

title: Thungleweed Flower
topic_desc: Thungleweed flowers are the white blossoms of thungleweed plants, a species commonly found growing along the Strident Coast of Cyrodiil. The pale flowers are collected from these coastal plants and recognized as an alchemical ingredient. The Strident Coast's environment supports the common growth of thungleweed, making its blossoms readily available to those familiar with Cyrodilic coastal flora.
topic_desc_basic: Thungleweed flowers are white blossoms from thungleweed plants that grow along the Strident Coast in Cyrodiil. They are used as an alchemical ingredient.

title: Ticklebritch
topic_desc: Ticklebritch is a serious disease that provokes itchy rashes on intimate parts of the anatomy. Despite its misleading name, it demands proper medical attention. It is transmitted through the bites of muskflies, swampspiders, and ornadas, though its symptoms often cause infected individuals to feel reluctant to seek the help of a healer. Healers and alchemists provide the necessary treatments for the affliction.
topic_desc_basic: Ticklebritch is a serious disease that causes itchy rashes on intimate parts of the anatomy. It can be contracted through the bites of muskflies, swampspiders, or ornadas.

title: Tiger Guar
topic_desc: Tiger guars are larger, aggressive cousins of the common guar. They are distinguished from their domesticated relatives by their heightened hostility and formidable melee attacks. Like common guars, they yield tiger guar hide when slain. In the wild, they pose a significant threat to travelers, justifying their classification as dangerous predators. Afflicted specimens are known to carry diseases such as Yellow Tick, making encounters with them particularly hazardous.
topic_desc_basic: Tiger guars are large, aggressive cousins of the common guar found in the wilds of Morrowind. They are hostile predators that attack travelers on sight.

title: Tiger Guar Hide
topic_desc: Tiger guar hide is the striped pelt of the tiger guar, a rarer and far more dangerous cousin of the common guar. Tiger guars principally inhabit the Deshaan plains far to the southeast, though some range northward toward Othrenis. Tiber Septim himself is said to have named them after the Nibenese tiger for their comparable ferocity. The hides are valued both as display pieces celebrating Morrowind's unique wildlife and as alchemically useful materials; scrapings yield potions that augment strength, restore speed, and confer resistance to poison. Dres merchants in the Othrenis area are known to stock them, though dealings with House Dres prove disagreeable to outlanders. Hunting wild specimens offers an alternative to purchase, though one not undertaken lightly.
topic_desc_basic: Tiger guar hide is the striped pelt of the tiger guar, a fierce creature of the Deshaan plains southeast of settled Morrowind. The hides are traded by Dres merchants and prized both as decorative trophies and as alchemically valuable material.

title: Tiger Lily Nectar
topic_desc: Tiger lily nectar is a floral ingredient harvested from tiger lilies and lilies of the valley. In the wild, tiger lilies commonly grow on Stirk Isle and the Strident Coast of Cyrodiil, while lilies of the valley are more frequently cultivated in urban gardens and pots. The nectar is valued by alchemists for its soluble properties.
topic_desc_basic: Tiger lily nectar is an alchemical ingredient harvested from tiger lilies and lilies of the valley. The flowers grow wild on Stirk Isle and the Strident Coast, or are cultivated in urban gardens.

title: Tinder Polypore Cap
topic_desc: Tinder Polypore Caps are shelf mushrooms that grow in the Dasek Marsh and very occasionally in old ruins in Cyrodiil. They are valued by alchemists and hunters for their properties.
topic_desc_basic: Tinder Polypore Caps are a type of shelf mushroom found growing in the Dasek Marsh and occasionally in old Cyrodiilic ruins.

title: Tobacco
topic_desc: Tobacco is a floral ingredient of uncertain natural origin. Alchemists prize it for its useful properties, and it sees common use across various preparations. Hunters and herbalists occasionally encounter it in the wild, and it circulates through general trade channels.
topic_desc_basic: Tobacco is a plant ingredient valued by alchemists and commonly traded.

title: Tojay
topic_desc: The Tojay are a furstock of the Khajiit people, inhabiting the southern marshes and jungle regions of Elsweyr, such as the Tenmar Forest. Their physical form is subject to conflicting accounts; while sometimes depicted with digitigrade legs, they are also described as having plantigrade legs, though they are generally said to be much like the Cathay. The Tojay-raht is a larger, bipedal variant of this furstock possessing digitigrade legs and renowned for exceptional combat skills. Older stories grant the Tojay the title of
topic_desc_basic: The Tojay are a furstock of Khajiit native to the southern marshes and jungles of Elsweyr, such as the Tenmar Forest. They are generally said to resemble the Cathay furstock.

title: Tomato
topic_desc: The tomato is a common edible fruit utilized as a foodstuff throughout Tamriel. Its widespread culinary presence is reflected in its inclusion among general food supplies and provisions. While primarily valued for sustenance, alchemists recognize the tomato's inherent properties, and hunters may encounter the plant growing in the wild. The fruit's natural distribution allows it to appear in varied flora across the regions.
topic_desc_basic: A tomato is a common edible fruit widely eaten as food across Tamriel.

title: Tombs of the West
topic_desc: Machil Coridale's scholarly study, written for the Imperial Seminary, tracing Colovian burial practices. He argues that earth interment and Nordic-style stone tombs arose in Colovia after its cultural split from Nibenay, as the west lacked the riverways and moth populations needed for traditional Nedic rites. Nordic aristocratic customs heavily influenced early Imperial society, including tomb-building. Alessia's entombment established a precedent for Nedic nobility, spreading crypt burial across Cyrodiil despite older Nibenese doctrines favoring water disposal. Nibenese families adapted through symbolic gestures like boat-shaped coffins and ceremonial sailing, illustrating the flexibility of Niben myth.
topic_desc_basic: Machil Coridale's study for the Imperial Seminary on how Colovian burial customs shifted from traditional Nedic water and moth rites to earth and tomb interment influenced by Nordic practices and Alessia's entombment.

title: Topaz
topic_desc: Topaz is a bright yellow to orange crystal mined in Morrowind and Cyrodiil and commonly used in jewelry. It holds little value in enchanting or alchemy. When ground to dust and ingested, topaz fortifies personality but damages agility and luck.
topic_desc_basic: Topaz is a bright yellow to orange gemstone mined in Morrowind and Cyrodiil, commonly used in jewelry.

title: Tower or Tomb
topic_desc: Olsia Corantha's account follows Antera, a Mages Guild scholar stationed at the Virimoor chapter, whose fascination with Imgan culture leads her to witness the Nab'Angoorfet—a soul-stretching practice the Guild dismisses as hedge-magick—and to explore Uurgelgra, an Under-Tower or Gai'Devag. These dilapidated relics of the Ime Period hold ancient chambers bearing signs of the Fey and depleted enchantments that may illuminate the Imga's Merethic-era role. Ignoring warnings that Under-Towers are death sentences even for the Imga, Antera descends into Uurgelgra and discovers an advanced yet primitive chamber. While attempting to escape through a collapsing crevice, she is crushed by falling stone. Her desperate, pain-wracked casting of Recall returns her not to her spiritual anchor at the Guild but to the subterranean altar itself, sealing her fate. The work stands as a cautionary narrative on the perils of obsessive scholarly ambition and the poorly understood dangers of Imgan ruins.
topic_desc_basic: A book by Olsia Corantha recounting a Mages Guild scholar's fatal expedition into an Imgan Under-Tower, or Gai'Devag, in Valenwood. It describes the ancient, sacred ruins of the Ime Period and the mysterious Nab'Angoorfet soul-stretching practice.

title: Transmuted Flesh
topic_desc: Transmuted Flesh is an alchemical ingredient of uncertain natural or animal origin, its very name suggesting tissue altered by magical or unnatural processes. The substance is associated with certain transmuted fauna, most notably the so-called Red Servants. Alchemists prize such materials for their inherent instability and the distinctive properties imparted by whatever transformative process produced them, though the exact alchemical character remains a matter of specialist study rather than common knowledge.
topic_desc_basic: Transmuted Flesh is an uncommon alchemical ingredient obtained from certain unnatural creatures, including those known as Red Servants. Its properties are of interest to alchemists and hunters familiar with such transmuted fauna.

title: Transpontine Circumpenetrations
topic_desc: Transpontine Circumpenetrations is a theoretical treatise exploring the creation of direct, transliminal bridges between Mundus and extramundial realms, a process it distinguishes from conjuration. The author postulates that while the liminal barrier erected by Akatosh renders such gateways virtually impossible, a sufficient wound in this barrier could allow them to form. Comparing the barrier to skin protecting a frail body, the work argues that breaching it risks metaphysical infection from Oblivion. It concludes that without Akatosh's protection, Mundus would suffer catastrophic Daedric invasion. The text becomes increasingly unsettling, preventing further reading.
topic_desc_basic: A treatise theorizing that direct gateways to Oblivion could be created if the liminal barrier protecting Mundus is wounded, risking catastrophic Daedric invasion.

title: Trefoil Flower
topic_desc: The trefoil flower is a bright purple bloom distinguished by its fern-like leaves. Native to High Rock, it grows in that province's wilds and is gathered as an alchemical ingredient. Its properties make it a recognized resource among herbalists and apothecaries familiar with Breton flora.
topic_desc_basic: The trefoil flower is a bright purple flower with fern-like leaves native to High Rock. It is gathered as an alchemical ingredient.

title: Tremble Weed Sap
topic_desc: Tremble weed sap is an alchemical ingredient harvested from the tremble weed, a plant growing in the Druadach Highlands and the Sundered Hills of Skyrim. As a floral extract, it holds significance for practitioners and procurers familiar with Reach-region botany.
topic_desc_basic: Tremble weed sap is an ingredient harvested from the tremble weed, a plant found in the Druadach Highlands and the Sundered Hills of Skyrim.

title: Trichobezoar
topic_desc: A trichobezoar is a dense mass of accumulated hair formed within a mammal's digestive system, typically resulting from trichophagia. While rare in men and mer, such blockages prove fatal if untreated. Khajiit are notoriously susceptible to terminal trichobezoars, whereas no case—however mild—has ever been recorded in an Argonian. The condition is commonly addressed through surgery, though Ashlander tradition holds that less destructive results can be achieved with the application of Troll Fat and considerable effort. As an alchemical ingredient, the trichobezoar is valued by practitioners for its exotic properties, though it occurs rarely and is not found through common supply channels.
topic_desc_basic: A trichobezoar is a hair mass that accumulates in a mammal's digestive system, often from swallowing hair. It is rare in men and mer but notoriously common and fatal in Khajiit, while Argonians are immune. Ashlander tradition holds it can be treated with Troll Fat.

title: Trickster Knight
topic_desc: The Trickster Knight, known as Sir Sienne, is a figure associated with a jester heraldic symbol on his shield. In Breton heraldic tradition, such symbols carry specific significance, though no known petty kingdom in High Rock claims him. A ballad titled Sir Sienne's Travels recounts a story matching his activities, suggesting the figure originates in Jehannan folklore rather than authentic nobility. He appears at tourneys, where his deception causes disruption before his true nature is uncovered. The High Rock Mission in the Ebon Tower maintains experts who can interpret such heraldic anomalies.
topic_desc_basic: The Trickster Knight, or Sir Sienne, is a mysterious figure who appears at tourneys bearing a jester symbol on his shield. No Breton kingdom claims him, but a ballad called Sir Sienne's Travels tells a story much like his deeds.

title: Trinity Fruit
topic_desc: Trinity Fruit is the edible fruit harvested from the trinity plant, a flora known to grow in abundance on Stirk Isle. Valued as a foodstuff, the fruit is commonly gathered by foragers and hunters traversing the island's wilderness. Alchemists also prize Trinity Fruit for its inherent properties, utilizing it alongside other reagents in the preparation of various concoctions. Its reliable presence on Stirk ensures a steady supply for both culinary and alchemical purposes throughout the region.
topic_desc_basic: Trinity Fruit grows on the trinity plant and is found in abundance on Stirk Isle, where it is commonly gathered as food.

title: Troll Fat
topic_desc: Troll fat is a substance harvested from the various species of troll found across Tamriel. It is notably the densest fat known in the region, exceeding even horker fat in density. Alchemists value it as an ingredient in poultices and potions, while others exploit its diverse practical properties: it serves as an excellent cold-weather lubricant, an armor polish, a strong adhesive when boiled, a window-sill vermin repellent, and a dried jerky. Certain Orcish traditions hold that rubbing troll fat upon an idol of Malacath allows a supplicant to commune with the Daedric Prince directly. More outlandish claims attribute curative powers against vampirism to the substance, though such assertions remain unverified.
topic_desc_basic: Troll fat is a dense substance harvested from trolls. It sees wide use in alchemy, as well as in practical applications such as cold-weather lubrication, armor polish, strong glue, and even as a repellent for household vermin.

title: Trollroot Fiber
topic_desc: Trollroot fiber is a botanical ingredient harvested from the trollroot plant. It grows in the Reach and other regions of Skyrim, where foragers and hunters gather it from the wild. Alchemists value the fibrous root for its properties in potion-making, and it circulates through regional supply lists as a standard alchemical reagent.
topic_desc_basic: Trollroot fiber is a plant ingredient gathered from the wilds of Skyrim, particularly the Reach. Alchemists and hunters commonly harvest it for use in potions.

title: Trout Meat
topic_desc: Trout meat is harvested from the trout, a species of freshwater fish inhabiting the Karth River in Skyrim. Valued as a foodstuff, it is commonly procured by hunters and fishermen familiar with the region's waterways. Alchemists recognize the substance for its inherent properties, utilizing it in various preparations alongside its culinary applications. As a regional ingredient, its availability is generally tied to the river's bounty and the trade of harvested fauna.
topic_desc_basic: Trout meat is taken from the trout, a freshwater fish found in the Karth River in Skyrim. It is commonly used as food.

title: True Witbane
topic_desc: True Witbane is a common disease that drains the victim's magicka reserves, diminishing their capacity to cast spells. Like other common ailments of Morrowind, it responds to standard curative magic and alchemical remedies.
topic_desc_basic: True Witbane is a common disease that saps a spellcaster's magicka, reducing their ability to cast spells. It can be cured through standard restoration magic or alchemical remedies.

title: Tsaesci Artifacts
topic_desc: Rare Akaviri items held by the College of Firewatch museum, recovered during the Imperial retreat from Septimia in 289.
topic_desc_basic: Rare Akaviri items recovered during the Imperial retreat from Septimia in 289 are displayed at the College of Firewatch museum. The collection includes two finely detailed Tsaesci urns from the Emperor's personal collection and a sword of disputed origin.

title: Tunnel Cough
topic_desc: Tunnel Cough is a mild disease characterized by violent, repeated coughing fits. It is contracted from tunnel-dwelling creatures, most notably cave rats, kwama foragers, and ornadas. Due to frequent contact with these hosts, it is a common affliction among eggminers working in the subterranean kwama mines.
topic_desc_basic: Tunnel Cough is a mild disease that causes violent, repeated coughs. It is caught from tunnel-dwelling creatures like cave rats, kwama foragers, and ornadas, making it a common illness among eggminers.

title: Turmeric Powder
topic_desc: Turmeric Powder is a spice of culinary and alchemical use. Its natural origin and precise alchemical properties remain matters of specialist knowledge rather than common record.
topic_desc_basic: Turmeric powder is a spice used in cooking and alchemy.

title: Turnip
topic_desc: A turnip is a root vegetable of floral origin, recognized for its rounded, edible taproot. It serves as a common foodstuff across Tamriel, sustaining the general populace as a staple crop. In alchemical practice, the turnip possesses modest properties that make it a serviceable reagent, though it is primarily valued as sustenance rather than a potent source of magical virtue. Its widespread cultivation ensures steady availability to herbalists and alchemists seeking mundane ingredients for foundational preparations.
topic_desc_basic: A turnip is a common root vegetable widely cultivated as a food staple across Tamriel.

title: Turquoise
topic_desc: Turquoise is a blue-green gemstone valued for decorative purposes and weapon ornamentation. It is mined in Eastmarch. Within the Psijic Order, three vertically arranged turquoise discs symbolize the Three Kinetic Forces represented in archery; the Order decorates certain quivers and belt buckles with this motif. Unscrupulous merchants sometimes treat turquoise glass with glow-spells to pass it off as Welkynd Stones. Alchemists and hunters occasionally handle turquoise alongside gems and ores, though its specific alchemical properties remain obscure.
topic_desc_basic: Turquoise is a blue-green gemstone commonly used for decoration and weapon ornamentation. It is mined in Eastmarch.

title: Two Stances on Knife-Fighting
topic_desc: Two Stances on Knife-Fighting presents opposing Dunmeri perspectives on dagger combat. Galeni Rothrilis, a Mournhold knife-scholar, argues that knife-fighting is a High Art governed by the codified laws of the Guild of Daggerlads, where victory stems from moral clarity and mastery of orthodox technique. He dismisses the Hlaalu reverse grip as a backstabber's posture suited only for amateurs or masters. An anonymous Daggerlad from Narsis offers a pragmatic counterpoint, treating duels as profitable spectacles where success depends on reading an opponent's psychology and masking one's own intent, favoring improvisation over rigid doctrine.
topic_desc_basic: Two Stances on Knife-Fighting is a book contrasting two Dunmeri views on dagger combat: a Mournhold scholar's defense of codified, orthodox technique as a moral High Art, and a Narsis brawler's pragmatic emphasis on improvisation and psychological deception.

title: Ultramarine Dye
topic_desc: Ultramarine Dye is a costly bright blue pigment valued for coloring paints and textiles. It does not appear in common leveled lists, making it a relatively rare commodity sought by artisans and alchemists familiar with fine coloring agents.
topic_desc_basic: Ultramarine Dye is a costly bright blue pigment used for coloring paints and textiles.

title: Umber Morchella
topic_desc: Umber Morchella is a species of mushroom native to Morrowind. Alchemists value it for its stable properties, and it sees common use in local apothecary and huntsman practices. Foragers gather it from the wild, and it circulates readily among regional ingredient supplies.
topic_desc_basic: Umber Morchella is a kind of mushroom native to Morrowind.

title: Umber Moth Wing
topic_desc: Umber Moth Wings are the wings of the Umber Moth, a nocturnal moth native to Skyrim. These insects emerge only at night, and their wings are valued by alchemists and hunters familiar with Skyrim's fauna. As with other moth and butterfly species, each specimen typically yields two wings. No reliably documented samples exist in fixed collections, and the ingredient circulates primarily through chance encounters with the living insect rather than cultivated or stored supply. The wing's alchemical character is known to practitioners who gather nocturnal insect reagents, though its properties remain a matter of specialist knowledge rather than common household familiarity.
topic_desc_basic: Umber Moth Wings come from the Umber Moth, a nocturnal moth found in Skyrim. The insects appear only at night, and each typically yields two wings when caught. The wings are used as alchemical ingredients.

title: Unarmed Traditions of Morrowind
topic_desc: Kevaar Asurani's treatise surveys three Dunmeri hand-to-hand traditions. Golden Reed, the oldest and most widespread, blends familial Redoran, Dres, and Ashlander techniques against armed foes; Ordinators study it before weapons training. Marshmerrow, founded by Taren Omathan from his observation of Khajiiti arena combat, employs flowing, plant-inspired forms honoring ancestor spirits; originally favored by Indoril priests, it is now increasingly practiced by the Mages Guild and Imperial Cult, who value its spiritual invigoration for magicka replenishment. Salt Rice, developed by the Morag Tong for close-quarters assassination, emphasizes brutal grappling, disarms, and silent heel-to-toe movement; it has filtered into the criminal underworld, influencing Camonna Tong brawling and absorbing foreign pirate techniques. Asurani writes from a patriotic Dunmer perspective, dismissing Imperial practitioners as Akaviri-fad followers and defending Omathan against rumors of Dissident Priest sympathies.
topic_desc_basic: A treatise by Kevaar Asurani describing three Dunmeri martial traditions: the widespread Golden Reed style used against armored foes, the flowing Marshmerrow style founded by Taren Omathan, and the brutal Salt Rice style developed by the Morag Tong.

title: Unbiased Appraisal of Abolition
topic_desc: A polemical treatise by Llerns Teisen defending Dunmer slavery of beastfolk against Imperial abolitionist arguments. Teisen contends that Argonians and Khajiit are culturally inferior to the Dunmer, comparing their societies unfavorably to enduring Dunmer civilization. He argues that freed beastfolk cannot survive without masters, claiming Argonians lack aspiration and Khajiit require supervision due to moonsugar addiction. He dismisses the concept that slaves desire freedom, equating beastfolk with pack guars, and rejects the Imperial principle that the strong lack privilege to exploit the weak, framing slavery as the natural extension of authority. The work concludes that resisting abolition serves both Dunmer self-interest and the welfare of the enslaved.
topic_desc_basic: A book by Llerns Teisen arguing against the Imperial abolition of slavery, claiming Dunmer superiority over beastfolk and that enslaved Argonians and Khajiit benefit from their masters.

title: Unending
topic_desc: Unending is a historical axe of the Fighters Guild, wielded by the hero Constantius during the Tiber Septim era. It was forged specifically to counter the spells of the infamous lich Galmyne Dobar and proved instrumental in her defeat. Shortly after this victory, the axe was stolen and remained lost for centuries. Unending possesses a unique reactive property rather than a fixed enchantment: it confers positive effects on its wielder in response to specific negative conditions afflicting them. Recently, credible reports placed the weapon in the Shipal-Shin region, held by rogue wizards occupying the cave of Ashir-Ahat near Narsis, prompting efforts to recover it. With Galmyne Dobar's apparent reappearance, the Guild seeks the axe once more to aid in her defeat.
topic_desc_basic: Unending is a renowned axe of the Fighters Guild, wielded by the hero Constantius during the era of Tiber Septim. Forged to counter the magic of the lich Galmyne Dobar, it helped defeat her before being stolen and lost for centuries. It is currently believed to be held by rogue wizards in the cave of Ashir-Ahat near Narsis.

title: Vampires of Telvannis
topic_desc: This scholarly work examines vampiric presence in the Telvanni peninsula, contrasting the region's tolerance with the Temple-guarded heartlands of Morrowind. It argues that the Tribunal's retreat from the anarchic northeast and the mage-lords' apathy allow vampires to operate openly, with some Telvanni leaders rumored to be undead. The text identifies three local bloodlines spurned by better-known vampiric kin: the Rudhagor, agile spellcasters who bewitch victims in the southern borderlands; the Ehad, psychotic axe-wielding killers preying on traders in the northern dustlands; and the Draneth, the oldest clan of summoners and enchanters who stalk the northeastern isles and feed on stray mages. The author warns that further inquiry is dangerous, though the undead may be directly encountered in Port Telvannis.
topic_desc_basic: A treatise on the three vampiric bloodlines of the Telvanni peninsula, detailing their territories and magical practices while contrasting the region's undead tolerance with the rest of Morrowind.

title: Vampires of The Iliac Bay, v I
topic_desc: An anonymous former vampire's first-hand account of vampirism's nature and his own transformation. The author spent ten years researching the condition after seven years as a vampire. He describes vampirism as an insidious disease typically spread by a vampire's bite or scratch, noting that over one hundred distinct vampire kinds exist across Tamriel, with nine variations in the Iliac Bay alone. He explains that infected victims experience nightmares if they sleep during a two-to-four-day window before death, during which temple healers can still cure the affliction. The narrative recounts his infection while scouting for a knightly order, his death and awakening in a mausoleum, his unrecognized altered appearance, and his first kill driven by an overpowering hunger. The account continues in a second volume.
topic_desc_basic: A first-hand account by an anonymous former vampire describing the nature of vampirism and his own transformation. It notes over one hundred vampire kinds across Tamriel, nine in the Iliac Bay, and explains that temple healers can cure the disease during a brief window before the victim dies and turns.

record_links.display_name: Vampires of The Iliac Bay, v I

title: Vampires of The Iliac Bay, v II
topic_desc: The second installment of an anonymous first-person memoir recounting the author's transformation into a vampire in the Iliac Bay region. The narrator describes discovering heightened strength, speed, and magical abilities alongside crippling vulnerabilities: sunlight burns, holy places cause pain, and a nightly blood thirst must be slaked or wounds will not heal. After initial exhilaration in undeath, the author is contacted by the Montalion—one of nine vampire clans differentiated by geography and unique powers, with the Montalion alone possessing teleportation. Growing horrified at the clans' collective predation upon Tamriel, the narrator seeks a cure and ultimately learns of a secretive network of former vampires who anonymously contact afflicted individuals wishing to end the curse. The work stands as a rare firsthand testimony of vampiric society, clan structure, and the perilous possibility of curing the affliction.
topic_desc_basic: A widely circulated memoir by an anonymous vampire describing undeath in the Iliac Bay. The author recounts vampiric powers and weaknesses, involvement with the Montalion vampire clan, and the eventual discovery that a secretive network of former vampires can help cure the affliction.

record_links.display_name: Vampires of The Iliac Bay, v II

title: Varieties of Thought Volume I
topic_desc: Varieties of Thought Volume I: The Discovery of Reason, authored by Maelix Pallania, opens an attempted Tamrielic history of ideas by tracing philosophical roots to three mythical Altmeri figures: Xarxes, Oghma, and Phynaster. Pallania argues that contemporary Imperial science rests upon Aldmeri foundations, however indemonstrable their divine authorship claims. Xarxes, revered as the inventor of writing and history, allegedly authored the Xarxean Cycle—whose original existence remains unconfirmed by Imperial academia—divided into the Books of War, Seas and Stars, Paradise, and Law. Oghma, his consort, embodies aesthetics, astronomy, and mathematics, disciplines through which Aldmeri scholars sought attunement with the Aedra. Phynaster, covering medicine and biology, authored proverbs whose hygienist exegesis underpins rigid Elven social hierarchies and eugenic policies. Pallania contends that by equating knowledge with worship, Aldmeri thought stagnated into perpetuating ancestral divine spark rather than studying reality, a dead end human thought must escape.
topic_desc_basic: Varieties of Thought Volume I, by Maelix Pallania, is a scholarly work tracing Tamrielic philosophical roots to the mythical Altmeri figures Xarxes, Oghma, and Phynaster. It argues that modern Imperial science descends from Aldmeri foundations, though Elven thought later stagnated by prioritizing ancestral worship over inquiry.

title: Varieties of Thought Volume II
topic_desc: Varieties of Thought Volume II is the second installment of Maelix Pallania's historical survey of Tamrielic ideas. It examines the Aldmeri iconoclasts who rejected the normative dogmatism and genetic fixation of early Altmeri philosophy. The work credits the Psijic Order, Velothi exiles, Direnni experimenters, and reformers like Vanus Galerion with redirecting inquiry toward the material world, thereby founding modern spellcasting, academia, and science. The volume also includes a separate epistemological treatise questioning sensory reliability and the divine status of the Daedra, arguing that true divinity must be an unbound, perfect creator distinct from the beings worshipped in Oblivion.
topic_desc_basic: A scholarly work examining the Aldmeri iconoclasts who rejected Altmeri dogma and a philosophical treatise questioning the true divine nature of the beings commonly called gods.

title: Varieties of Thought Volume III
topic_desc: Varieties of Thought Volume III is the final installment of Maelix Pallania's scholarly series Attempt at a Tamrielic History of Ideas. The treatise argues that contemporary Imperial civilization arose from the synthesis of Aldmeri rationalism, Nordic individualism, and Tsaesci political philosophy. Pallania posits that the formal genius of the Elves—originating with early Altmer thinkers like Meryaran—provided logical tools, while the Nordic spirit introduced progress and self-fulfillment, and Tsaesci statesmanship supplied the institutional framework for universal order. The work frames Cyrodiilic intellectual history as a millennia-long progression from Elven dogmatism through Alessian stagnation to a modern golden age of epistemic efficiency, free trade, and universal humanism, while also surveying foundational Merethic Era philosophers including Erundil, Volanaro, Imare, and the Dwemer Barik Nzalaf.
topic_desc_basic: Varieties of Thought Volume III is the final book in Maelix Pallania's history of ideas. It examines how Imperial civilization formed from the synthesis of Aldmeri rationalism, Nordic individualism, and Tsaesci political philosophy, tracing Cyrodiilic intellectual progress from early Altmer thinkers to a modern golden age of science and universal order.

title: Veiled Urnula
topic_desc: Veiled Urnula is a species of mushroom native to Morrowind, commonly found growing in the Shipal-Shin region and within many caves throughout that territory. Its prevalence in subterranean and damp environments makes it a familiar sight to foragers and alchemists operating in the south-western reaches of the province. The fungus is recognized for its reliable alchemical properties and is routinely harvested as an ingredient by practitioners of the craft.
topic_desc_basic: Veiled Urnula is a common mushroom found growing in the Shipal-Shin region and throughout many caves in Morrowind. It is widely gathered as an alchemical ingredient.

title: Velk
topic_desc: Velk are long-legged nectivorous creatures native to the lands of Great House Indoril east of the upper Thirr River. They hold profound religious significance for the Indoril Dunmer, who consider the animals sacred. Nectar harvested from velk livers is used to produce punavit, a substance the Indoril consume during ritual communion with their ancestors. Because of this sacred status, the Temple views the killing of a velk or the collection of its soul as sacrilege, an act liable to draw Ordinator censure. Wizards who covet velk souls for their calming, mellow aura risk severe conflict with Temple authorities.
topic_desc_basic: Velk are long-legged nectivorous animals found in Indoril lands east of the upper Thirr River. They are considered sacred by the Indoril, who harvest nectar from their livers to make punavit for ancestral rituals.

title: Velk Nectar Sac
topic_desc: The Velk nectar sac is the extracted liver of the Velk, a nectar-drinking creature native to Morrowind. The organ's alchemical character is tied to the creature's nectar-feeding biology, and it is recognized among practitioners as a regional ingredient derived from Morrowind's indigenous fauna.
topic_desc_basic: The Velk nectar sac is the liver of the Velk, a nectar-drinking creature native to Morrowind. It is used as an alchemical ingredient.

title: Venison
topic_desc: Venison is meat obtained from deer and elk. It serves as a common foodstuff across Tamriel and is also utilized in alchemical practice. The animals from which venison is sourced are notably prevalent within the Vorndgad Forest of Skyrim.
topic_desc_basic: Venison is meat taken from deer and elk, commonly used as food.

title: Verdigris Dye
topic_desc: Verdigris dye is an expensive green-blue pigment employed in giving color to paints and textiles. Its costly nature makes it a valued commodity among artisans and dyers seeking vibrant, lasting hues.
topic_desc_basic: Verdigris dye is an expensive green-blue pigment used to color paints and textiles.

title: Vermilion Dye
topic_desc: Vermilion dye is a deep red pigment employed in giving color to paints and textiles. Sourced as a specialty ingredient, it holds practical value for artisans and dyers. Alchemists and hunters occasionally handle the substance, though it remains uncommon and is not typically found in general supply or foraging stocks.
topic_desc_basic: Vermilion dye is a deep red pigment used to color paints and textiles.

title: Vicar Herb Leaves
topic_desc: Vicar herb leaves are gathered from vicar herbs, a plant native to the Druadach Highlands and the Vorndgad Forest of Skyrim. The leaves are used as an alchemical ingredient, valued by practitioners for their properties in potion-making. The plant thrives in the rugged, highland terrain of western Skyrim, where it can be found growing wild.
topic_desc_basic: Vicar herb leaves are gathered from vicar herbs, a plant that grows in the Druadach Highlands and the Vorndgad Forest of Skyrim. They are used as an alchemical ingredient.

title: Vile Morchella
topic_desc: Vile Morchella is a species of mushroom native to Morrowind. It occurs sporadically across the region rather than growing in concentrated, guaranteed clusters. Alchemists and hunters value the fungus for its alchemical properties, though its unpredictable distribution makes consistent harvesting difficult.
topic_desc_basic: Vile Morchella is a species of mushroom native to Morrowind.

title: Vinegar
topic_desc: Vinegar is an odorous liquid produced through the fermentation of various crops. While commonly employed as a culinary condiment and food preservative, its acidic nature also renders it a staple reagent in alchemical practice. The substance is widely associated with Cyrodiil, where suitable crops for its fermentation are cultivated.
topic_desc_basic: Vinegar is an odorous liquid fermented from various crops. It is commonly used as a foodstuff and is widely found in Cyrodiil.

title: Viper Bugloss Leaves
topic_desc: Viper bugloss leaves are harvested from viper's bugloss, a plant distinguished by its purple flowers. The flora is primarily cultivated as an indoor plant in Cyrodiil, where alchemists and hunters value the foliage for its useful properties.
topic_desc_basic: Viper bugloss leaves come from a purple-flowered plant commonly grown indoors in Cyrodiil and are used in alchemy.

title: Voyage of the Three Winds, I
topic_desc: A legendary saga adapted by Hama the Skald, recounting the departure of the Nordic gods from Skyrim during the reign of High King Borgas. After Borgas forced the worship of a maimed dragon, the land suffered, prompting the Hjaal clans to send three siblings to find the missing deities. Haakl sought Kyne through slaughter, Frokl sought Dibella through song, and Grykl underwent a ceremony to become Gryfa, a shieldmaiden of Mara, seeking her through devotion. Driven off course by storms, they reached Roscrea. There, Haakl's berserker fury and mass slaughter transformed him into a monstrous ruk that turned on his own crew before fleeing north. The remaining siblings sailed west, unaware of his true fate.
topic_desc_basic: A Nordic saga by Hama the Skald about the gods abandoning Skyrim under High King Borgas. Three siblings sail west to find them: Haakl seeks Kyne through violence, Frokl woos Dibella with song, and Grykl becomes the shieldmaiden Gryfa to serve Mara. Their voyage reaches Roscrea, where Haakl's bloodlust transforms him into a monstrous bird.

record_links.display_name: Voyage of the Three Winds, I

title: Voyage of the Three Winds, II
topic_desc: The second part of the saga adapted by Hama the Skald, concluding the voyage of the Three Winds. It recounts the Nords' arrival in Jokuud, where Frokl's gluttonous desecration of a famine-relief feast—mistaking it for Dibella's bounty—provokes the villagers into slaughtering the crews. Only Gryfa and a few survivors escape. Through meditative devotion to Mara, Gryfa receives a vision: the gods have not vanished but withdrawn due to impiety under King Borgas, and will return only with the coming of the great Ashen Tongue. The work serves as a mythic explanation for the Nordic gods' absence and a cautionary tale against hubris.
topic_desc_basic: The second part of the Nordic saga adapted by Hama the Skald. It concludes the Three Winds voyage, recounting Frokl's fatal gluttony among the Jokuudans and Gryfa's vision of Mara, who declares the gods will return only with the coming of the Ashen Tongue.

record_links.display_name: Voyage of the Three Winds, II

title: Vvardenfell's Epidemic: Corprus
topic_desc: A medical bulletin co-authored by the East Empire Board of Medical Health and senior clerics of the Imperial Cult, addressing the corprus epidemic on Vvardenfell. The work identifies the affliction as the "divine disease," attributing its spread to ash storms originating from Red Mountain that the Ghostfence cannot contain. It holds Dagoth Ur and his ash creatures responsible for the outbreak and details the disease's progression from rashes and irritated skin to bone deformation, swollen growths, starvation, and mental deterioration ending in violent hostility. The document notes no cure exists, though healers can briefly delay symptoms. It directs infected individuals on Vvardenfell to Divayth Fyr at Tel Fyr for his ongoing research, and those outside the district to the Imperial Cult. It also credits mainland containment measures for preventing the disease's spread beyond Vvardenfell.
topic_desc_basic: A joint medical bulletin by the East Empire Board of Medical Health and Imperial Cult clerics on Vvardenfell's corprus epidemic. It attributes the incurable "divine disease" to Dagoth Ur, details its horrific physical and mental progression, and directs the infected to seek Divayth Fyr at Tel Fyr or Imperial Cult shrines.

title: Wabbajack
topic_desc: Wabbajack is a Daedric artifact associated with Sheogorath, the Prince of Madness. It takes the form of a highly enchantable staff. Accounts of its origin describe it being bestowed by Sheogorath or his servants upon those who summon the Prince, sometimes deliberately mistaken for a different Daedra. The artifact embodies its creator's chaotic nature; those who receive it often descend into madness, perceiving transmutative connections between unrelated things. The staff is linked to the Ashurbalipal shrine in Morrowind, where it rests beneath a statue of Sheogorath.
topic_desc_basic: Wabbajack is a Daedric staff created by Sheogorath, the Prince of Madness. It is known for its chaotic, transmutative properties and is said to drive its wielders mad.

title: War-Banner of Prince Bashomon
